title: IV. A Hymn And A Secret
paragraphs: It was already quite late—days are short in November—when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. Dusk was coming on. But Alyosha knew he'd be let in without any trouble. Things worked that way in our little town, as they do everywhere. At first, right after the preliminary inquiry, relatives and a few others could only get interviews with Mitya by going through certain unavoidable formalities. But later, though the formalities were never officially relaxed, exceptions were made for a few of Mitya's visitors—so much so that sometimes his meetings with the prisoner, in the room set aside for that purpose, were practically private.

Still, these exceptions were few: only Grushenka, Alyosha, and Rakitin were treated this way. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, had grown quite fond of Grushenka. His treatment of her at Mokroe weighed on the old man's conscience, and once he learned the whole story, he changed his opinion of her completely. And strangely enough, though he was firmly convinced Mitya was guilty, the old man had come, since Mitya's imprisonment, to take an increasingly lenient view of him. "He's probably a good-hearted man," he thought, "who came to grief through drink and dissipation." His initial horror had given way to pity. As for Alyosha, the police captain liked him a great deal and had known him for years. Rakitin, who had lately taken to visiting the prisoner very often, was one of the closest friends of what he called the "police captain's young ladies," and was constantly hanging around their house. He also gave lessons at the home of the prison superintendent—a man scrupulous about his duties but kind-hearted underneath. Alyosha, in turn, had a long-standing friendship with the superintendent, who enjoyed talking with him, usually about religious matters. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and was somewhat in awe of his opinions, even though he considered himself something of a philosopher too—self-taught, naturally. But Alyosha held an irresistible appeal for him. Over the past year the old man had taken up studying the Apocryphal Gospels and was forever discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit him at the monastery, and the two of them, along with the monks, would talk for hours. So even when Alyosha arrived at the prison late, he had only to go to the superintendent and everything was smoothed over. Besides, everyone at the prison, down to the lowliest guard, had grown used to Alyosha. The sentry, of course, gave him no trouble as long as the authorities were satisfied.

When Mitya was summoned from his cell, he always went downstairs to the room set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered, he found Rakitin just taking his leave of Mitya. Both were talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw him out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin didn't care for running into Alyosha these days, especially lately. He barely spoke to him and gave him only a stiff nod. Seeing Alyosha come in now, he scowled and looked away, as if entirely absorbed in buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began at once hunting for his umbrella.
"I'd better not forget my things," he muttered, just to say something.
"Mind you don't forget other people's things," Mitya joked, and immediately burst out laughing at his own wit. Rakitin flared up instantly.
"Save that advice for your own family—they've always been a bunch of slave-drivers—and not for Rakitin," he snapped, suddenly shaking with anger.

"What's wrong with you? I was joking," Mitya cried. "Damn it, they're all like that," he said, turning to Alyosha and nodding toward Rakitin's hastily retreating back. "He was sitting right here, laughing, in a good mood, and all of a sudden he boils over like that. Didn't even nod to you. Have you two broken off completely? Why are you so late? I haven't just been waiting—I've been dying for you to come, all morning. But never mind. We'll make up for it now."
"Why does he come here so often? Surely you two aren't such great friends?" Alyosha asked, nodding too toward the door Rakitin had gone through.

"Great friends with Rakitin? Hardly. Him? A pig like that? He thinks I'm... a blackguard. They can't take a joke, that's the trouble with people like that. Never get a joke, their souls are dry—dry and flat, they remind me of these prison walls when I first got here. But he's a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it's all over for me now."
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit beside him.
"Yes, the trial's tomorrow. Are you really without hope, brother?" Alyosha asked, with a rising sense of dread.

"What are you talking about?" Mitya said, looking at him uncertainly. "Oh, you mean the trial! Damn the trial! Until now we've just been talking about things that don't matter—about this trial—but I haven't said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial's tomorrow, but the trial isn't what I meant when I said it was all over for me. Why are you looking at me like that?"
"What do you mean, Mitya?"
"Ideas—ideas, that's all! Ethics! What is ethics?"
"Ethics?" Alyosha asked, puzzled.
"Yes—is it a science?"
"Yes, there's such a science... but... I have to admit I can't really explain to you what kind of science it is."

"Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows a great deal, damn him! He's not going to be a monk. He plans to go to Petersburg. There he'll take up criticism with an uplifting slant. Who knows, maybe he'll actually make himself useful and build a career out of it too. Ugh, these people are first-rate at building careers! To hell with ethics, Alexey, I'm finished, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. Just looking at you makes my heart ache. Who was Karl Bernard?"
"Karl Bernard?" Alyosha was startled again.
"No, not Karl. Wait, I got it wrong. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist or something?"
"He must be some kind of scholar," Alyosha answered, "but I have to admit I can't tell you much about him either. I've heard the name as a scholar, but I don't know what field."

"Well, to hell with him, then! I don't know either," Mitya swore. "Some kind of scoundrel, most likely. They're all scoundrels. And Rakitin will get ahead. Rakitin gets ahead anywhere—he's another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They're everywhere."
"But what's wrong?" Alyosha pressed.

"He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and launch his literary career with it. That's what he comes here for—he told me so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to argue 'he couldn't help murdering his father, he was corrupted by his environment,' and so on. He explained the whole thing to me. He's going to give it a tinge of socialism, he says. Well, to hell with it, he can give it whatever tinge he likes, I don't care. He can't stand Ivan, he hates him. He's not fond of you either. But I don't kick him out, because he's a clever fellow. Terribly conceited, though. I told him just now, 'The Karamazovs aren't blackguards, we're philosophers—because every real Russian is a philosopher—and though you've studied, you're no philosopher, you're a lowlife.' He laughed, very spitefully. And I said to him, 'De ideabus non est disputandum.' Not bad, eh? I can pass for a classicist myself, you see!" Mitya suddenly burst out laughing.
"Why is it all over for you? You said so just now," Alyosha put in.
"Why is it all over for me? Hm!... The fact is... taking it all together, I'm sorry to lose God—that's why."
"What do you mean, 'sorry to lose God'?"

"Picture it: inside, in the nerves, in the head—that is, these nerves are there in the brain... (damn them!)—there are these little tails, tiny tails on the nerves, and the moment they start quivering... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes and then they start quivering, these little tails... and when they quiver, an image appears... it doesn't appear right away, an instant passes, a second... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment—to hell with the moment!—but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That's why I see something and then think about it—because of those tails, not because I've got a soul, not because I'm some kind of image and likeness of God. All of that's nonsense! Rakitin explained the whole thing to me yesterday, brother, and it simply knocked me flat. It's magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new kind of man is coming—that much I understand.... And still I'm sorry to lose God!"
"Well, that's something in your favor, anyway," said Alyosha.

"That I'm sorry to lose God? It's chemistry, brother, chemistry! Nothing to be done about it, your reverence, you'll have to make way for chemistry. And Rakitin really does hate God. Oh, how he hates Him! That's the sore spot with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. 'Will you preach that in your journals?' I asked him. 'Oh, well, if I said it outright, they wouldn't let it through,' he said. He laughed. 'But what becomes of men then,' I asked him, 'without God and eternal life? Then everything's permitted—they can do whatever they like?' 'Didn't you know?' he said, laughing. 'A clever man can do whatever he likes,' he said. 'A clever man knows how to work the angles, but you put your foot in it—committed a murder—and now you're rotting in prison.' He says that right to my face! A regular pig! I used to throw people like that out, but now I listen to him. He does talk a lot of sense, too. Writes well. He read me an article last week. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a moment. Here it is."
Mitya hurriedly pulled a piece of paper from his pocket and read:
"'In order to settle this question, it's above all essential to set one's personality in opposition to one's own reality.' Do you understand that?"
"No, I don't," Alyosha said. He watched Mitya, listening to him with curiosity.

"I don't understand it either. It's murky and obscure, but intellectual. 'Everyone writes like that now,' he says, 'it's the effect of environment.' They're afraid of the environment. He writes poetry too, the rascal. Wrote something in honor of Madame Hohlakov's foot. Ha ha ha!"
"I've heard about it," said Alyosha.
"Have you? And have you heard the poem?"
"No."

"I've got it. Here—I'll read it to you. You don't know—I haven't told you—there's quite a story behind it. He's a rascal! Three weeks ago he started teasing me. 'You've gone and gotten yourself into trouble like a fool over three thousand roubles, while I'm going to pocket a hundred and fifty thousand. I'm going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.' And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She never had much sense even in her youth, and now at forty she's lost what little she had. 'But she's terribly sentimental,' he says, 'that's how I'll get hold of her. Once I marry her, I'll take her off to Petersburg and start a newspaper there.' And his mouth was practically watering, the beast—not for the widow, but for the hundred and fifty thousand. And he had me half believing it. He came to see me every day. 'She's coming around,' he'd announce, beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he got thrown out of the house. Perhotin's carrying the day now, bravo! I could kiss that silly old fool for throwing him out. And he'd written this doggerel for her. 'It's the first time I've ever dirtied my hands with poetry,' he said. 'It's to win her heart, so it's in a good cause. Once I've got hold of the silly woman's fortune, I can do a great deal of good for society.' They've always got some social justification ready for every rotten thing they do! 'Anyway, it's better than your Pushkin's poetry,' he said, 'because I've managed to work in a plea for enlightenment even there.' I see what he means about Pushkin, I understand that much—if the man really did have talent and only wrote about women's feet. But wasn't Rakitin puffed up about his own doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! 'On the Recovery of the Swollen Foot of the Object of My Affections'—that's the title he came up with. He's a droll one.
A charming little foot it is, Though swollen now, and red, and tender! The doctors come, apply their salves, Yet still they cannot mend her.
And yet it's not her foot I fear— A theme more fit for Pushkin's pen— It's not her foot, it is her mind: I dread the loss of wit in her!
For as her foot swells more and more, Her intellect grows ever thinner— Oh, for some remedy, I pray, To mend the foot and mind together!
He's a pig, a real pig, but he's sly, the rascal! And he really did work a progressive idea into it. And wasn't he furious when she kicked him out! He was grinding his teeth!"
"He's already gotten his revenge," said Alyosha. "He's written a piece about Madame Hohlakov."
And Alyosha told him briefly about the item in Gossip.

"That's his doing, that's his doing!" Mitya said, scowling in agreement. "That's him! These little items... I know... the insulting things they've written about Grushenka, for instance.... And about Katya too.... Hm!"
He paced across the room, looking harassed.

"Brother, I can't stay long," Alyosha said after a pause. "Tomorrow will be a great and terrible day for you—God's judgment will be carried out... I'm amazed at you, walking around here talking about I don't know what..."

"No, don't be amazed at me," Mitya broke in warmly. "Am I supposed to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We've talked enough about him. I don't want to say another word about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will strike him down, you'll see. Hush!"
He went up to Alyosha excitedly and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

"Rakitin wouldn't understand this," he began, in a kind of exaltation, "but you—you'll understand all of it. That's why I was longing for you. You see, there's so much I've been wanting to tell you for a long time now, here within these peeling walls, but I haven't said a word about the thing that matters most—the moment never seemed to have come. Now I can't wait any longer. I have to pour out my heart to you. Brother, these last two months I've discovered a new man in myself. A new man has risen up inside me. He was hidden in me, and he'd never have come to the surface if it hadn't been for this blow from heaven. I'm afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I'm not the least bit afraid of that—what I'm afraid of now is something else: that this new man might leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I might find a human heart in some other convict and murderer beside me, and I might become his friend, because even there one can live and love and suffer. One can thaw out and revive a frozen heart in that convict, one can wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature; one can bring forth an angel, forge a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we're all to blame for what they've become. Why did I dream of that 'babe' at such a moment? 'Why is the babe so poor?' That was a sign to me, right then. It's for the babe that I'm going. Because we're all responsible for everyone. For all the 'babes'—because there are grown babies as well as little ones. Everyone is a 'babe.' I'm going for all of them, because someone has to go for all of them. I didn't kill father, but I have to go. I accept it. It's all come to me here, here within these peeling walls. There are crowds of them down there, hundreds of them underground, hammers in their hands. Oh yes, we'll be in chains, there'll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we'll rise again into joy—without which man cannot live and God cannot exist, because God gives joy: that's His privilege, a grand one. Ah, man ought to dissolve himself in prayer! What would I be down there underground without God? Rakitin's laughing! If they drive God off the face of the earth, we'll shelter Him underground. A man can't exist in prison without God—it's even less possible than out of prison. And then we men underground will sing a glorious hymn to God from the bowels of the earth, to Him in whom is joy. Glory to God and His joy! I love Him!"
Mitya was almost gasping for breath by the end of this wild speech. He'd gone pale, his lips trembled, and tears ran down his cheeks.

"Yes, life is full, there's life even underground," he began again. "You wouldn't believe, Alexey, how much I want to live now, what a thirst for existence and awareness has sprung up in me within these peeling walls. Rakitin doesn't understand that; all he cares about is building a house and renting out flats. But I've been longing for you. And what is suffering? I'm not afraid of it, even if it were beyond measure. I'm not afraid of it now. I used to be afraid of it. Do you know, maybe I won't answer a single question at the trial.... And I seem to have such strength in me now that I think I could stand anything, any suffering at all, just to be able to say and repeat to myself every moment, 'I exist.' Amid a thousand torments—I exist. Racked with pain—but I exist! Chained to a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I don't see the sun, I know it's there. And there's a whole life in that, in just knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—"
"What about brother Ivan?" Alyosha broke in, but Mitya didn't hear him.

"You see, I never used to have any of these doubts, but it was all buried inside me. Maybe it was exactly because ideas I didn't understand kept surging up in me that I used to drink and fight and rage. It was to smother them in myself, to quiet them, to choke them down. Ivan isn't Rakitin, there's an idea in him. Ivan's a sphinx, he keeps silent; he's always silent. It's God that's tormenting me. That's the only thing tormenting me. What if He doesn't exist? What if Rakitin's right—that it's just an idea men made up? Then, if He doesn't exist, man is the master of the earth, of the universe. Magnificent! Only how is he going to be good without God? That's the question. I keep coming back to it. Who is man going to love, then? Who will he be grateful to? To whom will he sing his hymn? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says you can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot could maintain that. I can't understand it. Life's easy for Rakitin. 'You'd do better to think about extending civic rights, or even about keeping the price of meat down. That would show your love for humanity more simply and directly than philosophy.' I answered him, 'Well, but you, without a God, are more likely to raise the price of meat, if it suits you, and squeeze a rouble out of every kopeck.' He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing to me and something else to a Chinaman—so it's relative. Or isn't it? Is it not relative? A treacherous question! You won't laugh if I tell you it's kept me awake two nights straight. I only wonder now how people manage to live without giving it a thought. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It's beyond me. But he stays silent. I believe he's a freemason. I asked him, but he stayed silent. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul—he stayed silent. But once he did let a word slip."
"What did he say?" Alyosha asked quickly.

"I said to him, 'Then everything's permitted, if that's so?' He frowned. 'Fyodor Pavlovitch, our dear papa,' he said, 'was a pig, but his thinking on that was sound enough.' That's what he let slip. That was all he said. That went one better than Rakitin."
"Yes," Alyosha agreed bitterly. "When was he here with you?"

"That's for later; right now I have to talk about something else. I haven't said anything to you about Ivan before now. I put it off till the end. Once my business here is finished and the verdict's been handed down, then I'll tell you something. I'll tell you everything. We've got something enormous on hand.... And you'll be my judge in it. But don't get started on that now, keep quiet. You're talking about tomorrow, about the trial; but would you believe, I know nothing about it."
"Have you talked to your lawyer?"

"What good is the lawyer? I told him everything. He's a soft, city-bred rogue—a Bernard! But he doesn't believe me—not for a moment. Just imagine, he thinks I did it. I can see it. 'In that case,' I asked him, 'why did you come to defend me?' To hell with the lot of them! They've even brought in a doctor, trying to prove I'm mad. I won't have it! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do her 'duty' right to the end, whatever it costs her!" Mitya smiled bitterly. "The cat! Hard-hearted creature! She knows I said, at Mokroe, that she was a woman of 'great wrath.' They repeated it back to her. Yes, the facts against me have piled up like the sands of the sea. Grigory sticks to his story. Grigory's honest, but a fool. A lot of people are honest because they're fools—that's Rakitin's idea. Grigory's my enemy. And there are some people better off as enemies than friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I'm afraid, oh, I'm afraid she'll tell the court how she bowed to the ground after I gave her back that four thousand. She'll pay every last penny of it back. I don't want her sacrifice; they'll shame me with it at the trial. I don't know how I'll stand it. Go to her, Alyosha, ask her not to bring that up in court, will you? But damn it all, never mind! I'll get through somehow. I don't pity her. It's her own doing. She deserves what she gets. I'll have my own story to tell, Alexey." He smiled bitterly again. "Only... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why does she have to suffer so much?" he suddenly cried, with tears. "Grusha's killing me; the thought of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me just now...."
"She told me she was very upset over you today."
"I know. Damn my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry, I kissed her as she was leaving. I didn't ask her forgiveness."
"Why not?" Alyosha exclaimed.
Suddenly Mitya laughed, almost cheerfully.

"God spare you, dear boy, from ever asking forgiveness for a fault from a woman you love. From one you love especially, no matter how much you may have been in the wrong. With a woman—the devil only knows what to make of her! I know a thing or two about it, anyway. But just try admitting you're at fault to a woman. Say, 'I'm sorry, forgive me,' and down comes a shower of reproaches! She'll never forgive you plainly and simply—she'll grind you into the dust, dredge up things that never even happened, remember everything, forget nothing, throw in a few things of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best of them do this—the very best! She'll scrape together every last scrap and pile it on your head. They're ready to flay you alive, I tell you, every single one of them, all these angels without whom we can't live! I'll tell you plainly and openly, dear boy: every decent man ought to be under some woman's thumb. That's my conviction—not conviction exactly, but a feeling. A man should be magnanimous, and there's no shame in it! No shame for a hero, not even for a Caesar! But all the same, never beg her pardon for anything. Remember this rule from your brother Mitya, a man ruined by women. No, I'd rather make it up to Grusha some other way, without begging her pardon. I worship her, Alexey, worship her. Only she doesn't see it. No, she still thinks I don't love her enough. And she torments me, torments me with her love. The past was nothing! In the past it was only those infernal curves of hers that tormented me, but now I've taken her whole soul into mine, and through her I've become a man myself. Will they let us marry? If they don't, I'll die of jealousy. I imagine something new every day.... What did she say to you about me?"
Alyosha repeated everything Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him repeat parts of it, and seemed pleased.

"So she's not angry that I'm jealous?" he exclaimed. "She's a real woman! 'I've got a fierce heart myself!' Ah, I love hearts like that, though I can't bear anyone being jealous of me. Can't stand it. We'll fight. But I'll love her, I'll love her without end. Will they let us marry? Do they let convicts marry? That's the question. And without her I can't exist...."
Mitya paced across the room, scowling. It was nearly dark now. He suddenly seemed terribly troubled.

"So there's a secret, she says, a secret? We've cooked up some plot against her, and Katya's mixed up in it, so she thinks. No, my dear Grushenka, that's not it. You're wide of the mark there, in your foolish feminine way. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes—I'll tell you our secret!"

He looked around, stepped quickly up to Alyosha, who was standing right in front of him, and whispered to him with an air of mystery, though in fact no one could have overheard them: the old guard was dozing in the corner, and not a word could reach the soldiers on duty.

"I'll tell you the whole secret," Mitya whispered hurriedly. "I meant to tell you later, because how could I decide anything without you? You're everything to me. Even though I say Ivan is above us, you're my angel. It's your decision that will settle this. Maybe it's you who's above Ivan, not him. You see, it's a matter of conscience, a matter of the higher conscience—the secret's so important I can't settle it on my own, and I've put it off until I could talk to you. But in any case it's too soon to decide now, we have to wait for the verdict. As soon as the verdict's in, you'll decide my fate. Don't decide now. I'll tell you now. You listen, but don't decide. Just stand there and stay quiet. I won't tell you everything. I'll only give you the idea, without the details, and you keep quiet. No questions, no movement. Agreed? But God, what am I going to do about your eyes? I'm afraid your eyes will give away your decision even if you don't say a word. Oo! I'm afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan is suggesting I escape. I won't give you the details—it's all been worked out, it can all be arranged. Hush, don't decide. I'd go to America with Grusha. You know I can't live without Grusha! What if they won't let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts marry? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha, what would I do underground with a hammer? I'd only smash my own skull with it! But then, on the other hand, my conscience? I'd be running away from suffering. A sign has come to me, and I'd be rejecting the sign. I have a path to salvation, and I'd turn my back on it. Ivan says that in America, 'with good will,' I could be more useful than I'd be underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground then? What is America? America is just more vanity! And there's plenty of swindling in America too, I expect. I'd be running away from my crucifixion! I'm telling you this, you know, Alexey, because you're the only one who can understand it. There's no one else. It's folly, madness to everyone else, all this I've told you about the hymn. They'll say I've lost my mind, or that I'm a fool. I haven't lost my mind and I'm not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he doesn't answer—he doesn't speak. He doesn't believe in the hymn. Don't speak, don't speak. I can see how you're looking at me! You've already decided. Don't decide, spare me! I can't live without Grusha. Wait until after the trial!"
Mitya finished, beside himself. He held Alyosha by the shoulders with both hands, his yearning, feverish eyes fixed on his brother's.
"They don't let convicts marry, do they?" he repeated, for the third time now, in a pleading voice.
Alyosha listened in utter astonishment, and was deeply moved.
"Tell me one thing," he said. "Is Ivan really set on this, and whose idea was it?"

"His, his, and he's very set on it. He didn't come see me at first, and then all of a sudden, a week ago, he showed up and got straight into it. He's terribly set on it. He doesn't ask me—he orders me to escape. He doesn't doubt for a second that I'll obey him, even though I bared my whole heart to him, the way I have to you, and told him about the hymn too. He told me he'd arrange everything; he's looked into every detail. But more on that later. He's simply fixed on it. It's all a matter of money: he'll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says we can arrange a magnificent escape for ten thousand."
"And he told you on no account to tell me?" Alyosha asked again.
"To tell no one, and especially not you—on no account to tell you. He's afraid, no doubt, that you'll stand before me as my conscience. Don't tell him I told you. Don't tell him, whatever happens."
"You're right," Alyosha said. "It's impossible to decide anything before the trial's over. After the trial you'll decide for yourself. Then you'll find that new man in yourself, and he'll decide."
"A new man, or a Bernard who'll decide à la Bernard—because I believe I'm a contemptible Bernard myself," Mitya said, with a bitter grin.
"But, brother, have you no hope at all of being acquitted?"

Mitya shrugged nervously and shook his head. "Alyosha, darling, it's time you were going," he said, with sudden haste. "There's the superintendent shouting out in the yard. He'll be here any minute. We're late; it's against the rules. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Make the sign of the cross over me, darling, for the cross I have to carry tomorrow."
They embraced and kissed.
"Ivan," Mitya said suddenly, "suggests I escape; but of course, he believes I did it."
A mournful smile crossed his lips.
"Have you asked him whether he believes it?" Alyosha asked.
"No, I haven't. I wanted to, but I couldn't. I didn't have the courage. But I could see it in his eyes. Well, good-bye!"
Once more they kissed hurriedly, and Alyosha was just heading out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

"Stand and face me! That's it!" And again he took hold of Alyosha, both hands on his shoulders. His face had gone suddenly quite pale, so pale that it showed clearly even through the gathering dark. His lips twitched, his eyes fixed on Alyosha.
"Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as if before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you—do you, deep down, believe it? The whole truth, don't lie to me!" he cried desperately.
Everything seemed to reel before Alyosha, and he felt something like a knife twist in his heart.
"Hush! What are you saying?" he faltered, helplessly.
"The whole truth, the whole truth, don't lie!" Mitya repeated.
"I have never for one instant believed you were the murderer!" broke from Alyosha in a trembling voice, and he raised his right hand into the air, as if calling on God to witness his words.
Mitya's whole face lit up with bliss.

"Thank you!" he said slowly, as if letting out a breath after fainting. "Now you've given me new life. Would you believe it, until this moment I've been afraid to ask you—you, of all people. Well, go now! You've given me the strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Come on, go! Love Ivan!" were Mitya's last words.

Alyosha went out in tears. Such distrust in Mitya, such a lack of confidence even in him, in Alyosha—all this suddenly opened before Alyosha an unsuspected depth of hopeless grief and despair in the soul of his unhappy brother. An intense, infinite compassion swept over him at once. There was a raw ache in his torn heart. "Love Ivan!"—he suddenly recalled Mitya's words. And he was on his way to see Ivan now. He'd wanted badly to see Ivan all day. He was as worried about Ivan as about Mitya, and now more than ever.

title: V. Not You, Not You!
paragraphs: On his way to Ivan, he had to pass the house where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Light showed in the windows. He stopped suddenly and decided to go in. He hadn't seen Katerina Ivanovna in more than a week. But now it struck him that Ivan might be with her, especially on the eve of this terrible day. He rang, climbed the staircase, dimly lit by a Chinese lantern, and saw a man coming down; as they met, he recognized his brother. So Ivan was just now coming from Katerina Ivanovna's.
"Ah, it's only you," Ivan said dryly. "Well, good-bye! You're going up to her?"
"Yes."
"I don't advise it; she's upset, and you'll only upset her more."
A door flew open above them at once, and a voice cried out:
"No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, have you come from him?"
"Yes, I've just been with him."
"Did he send me any message? Come up, Alyosha—and you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you have to come back, you have to. Do you hear?"
There was such a commanding note in Katya's voice that Ivan, after a moment's hesitation, made up his mind to go back up with Alyosha.
"She was listening at the door," he muttered angrily to himself, but Alyosha caught it.
"Forgive me for keeping my coat on," Ivan said, walking into the drawing room. "I won't sit down. I won't stay more than a minute."

"Sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch," Katerina Ivanovna said, though she herself remained standing. She'd changed very little in this time, but there was an ominous gleam in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered afterward that she'd struck him as especially beautiful in that moment.
"What did he ask you to tell me?"

"Just one thing," Alyosha said, looking her straight in the face, "that you'd spare yourself, and say nothing at the trial about what"—he faltered a little—"...passed between you...when you first met...in that town."

"Ah! That I bowed down to the ground for that money!" She broke into a bitter laugh. "So, is he afraid for me, or for himself? He's asking me to spare—whom? Him, or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!"
Alyosha watched her closely, trying to understand her.
"Both you and him," he answered softly.
"I'm glad to hear it," she snapped, with sudden malice, and then abruptly blushed.
"You don't know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch," she said, almost threateningly. "And I don't know myself yet, either. Maybe after my testimony tomorrow you'll want to trample me underfoot."
"You'll give your testimony honorably," Alyosha said. "That's all that's needed."

"Women are often dishonorable," she snarled. "Only an hour ago I was thinking I couldn't bear to touch that monster...as if he were some reptile...but no, he's still a human being to me! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?" she cried out suddenly, almost hysterically, turning sharply to Ivan. Alyosha realized at once that she'd asked Ivan that question before—maybe only a moment before he'd arrived, and not for the first time, but the hundredth—and that it had ended in a quarrel between them.

"I've been to see Smerdyakov.... It was you, you who convinced me he murdered his father. You're the only one I believed!" she went on, still addressing Ivan. He gave her a strained sort of smile. Alyosha started at her tone. He hadn't suspected such intimacy between them.
"Well, that's enough, anyway," Ivan cut the conversation short. "I'm going. I'll come tomorrow." And turning at once, he walked out of the room and went straight downstairs.
With a commanding gesture, Katerina Ivanovna seized Alyosha by both hands.

"Go after him! Catch up with him! Don't leave him alone for a minute!" she said in a hurried whisper. "He's out of his mind! Don't you know he's out of his mind? He's got a fever, a nervous fever. The doctor told me so. Go, run after him...."
Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not fifty paces ahead of him.
"What do you want?" he turned sharply on Alyosha when he saw him running after him. "She told you to catch me up, because I'm out of my mind. I know it all by heart," he added irritably.
"She's mistaken, of course, but she's right that you're ill," Alyosha said. "I was looking at your face just now. You look very ill, Ivan."
Ivan kept walking without stopping. Alyosha followed him.
"And do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how people actually go out of their minds?" Ivan asked, his voice suddenly calm, with no trace of irritation left in it, just a note of plain curiosity.
"No, I don't. I suppose there are all kinds of madness."
"And can a person tell that they're going mad themselves?"
"I'd imagine one can't see oneself clearly in circumstances like that," Alyosha answered, surprised.
Ivan paused for half a minute.
"If you want to talk to me, please change the subject," he said suddenly.

"Oh, while I think of it, I have a letter for you," Alyosha said timidly, and took Lise's note from his pocket, holding it out to Ivan. They were standing right under a streetlamp. Ivan recognized the handwriting at once.
"Ah, from that little demon!" he laughed maliciously, and without opening the envelope, tore it to pieces and tossed them into the air. The wind scattered the scraps.
"She's not even sixteen yet, I believe, and already throwing herself at people," he said contemptuously, striding on down the street again.
"What do you mean, throwing herself at people?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"The way loose women throw themselves at people, of course."

"How can you say that, Ivan, how can you?" Alyosha cried, warmly, his voice pained. "She's a child; you're insulting a child! She's ill, badly ill. She might be on the verge of madness herself.... I'd hoped to hear something from you...something that would save her."
"You won't hear anything from me. If she's a child, I'm not her nursemaid. Be quiet, Alexey. Don't go on about her. I'm not even thinking about it."
They fell silent again for a moment.
"She'll spend all night now praying to the Mother of God, asking how to act tomorrow at the trial," he said, sharp and angry again.
"You...you mean Katerina Ivanovna?"

"Yes. Whether to save Mitya or ruin him. She'll pray for light from above. She can't make up her own mind, you see. She hasn't had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nursemaid too. She wants me to sing her lullabies."
"Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother," Alyosha said sadly.
"Maybe; but I'm not especially keen on her."
"She's suffering. Then why do you...sometimes say things to her that give her hope?" Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. "I know you've given her hope. Forgive me for saying this to you," he added.

"I can't do the right thing by her—break it off completely and tell her so outright," Ivan said irritably. "I have to wait until sentence is passed on the murderer. If I break with her now, she'll take revenge on me by destroying that scoundrel tomorrow at the trial, because she hates him, and she knows she hates him. It's all lies—lie upon lie! As long as I don't break with her, she keeps hoping, and she won't destroy that monster, knowing how much I want to see him get off. If only that damned verdict would come already!"
The words "murderer" and "monster" echoed painfully in Alyosha's heart.
"But how could she ruin Mitya?" he asked, turning Ivan's words over. "What evidence could she give that would ruin him?"
"You don't know that yet. She's got a document in her hands, in Mitya's own handwriting, that proves beyond doubt that he murdered Fyodor Pavlovitch."
"That's impossible!" Alyosha cried.
"Why is it impossible? I've read it myself."
"There can't be a document like that!" Alyosha repeated fiercely. "There can't be, because he's not the murderer. It wasn't him who killed father, not him!"
Ivan stopped short.
"Then who's the murderer, according to you?" he asked, with a show of coldness. There was even something supercilious in his tone.
"You know who," Alyosha said, in a low, piercing voice.
"Who? You mean that myth about the crazy idiot, the epileptic—Smerdyakov?"
Alyosha suddenly felt himself trembling all over.
"You know who," broke helplessly from him. He could hardly breathe.
"Who? Who?" Ivan cried, almost savagely. All his restraint vanished in an instant.
"I know only one thing," Alyosha went on, still nearly in a whisper, "it wasn't you who killed father."
"'Not you'! What do you mean, 'not you'?" Ivan was thunderstruck.
"It was not you who killed father, not you!" Alyosha repeated firmly.
The silence lasted half a minute.
"I know I didn't. Are you raving?" Ivan said, with a pale, twisted smile. His eyes were fixed on Alyosha. They were standing again under a streetlamp.
"No, Ivan. You've told yourself, several times, that you're the murderer."
"When did I say that? I was in Moscow.... When have I ever said that?" Ivan faltered helplessly.

"You've said it to yourself many times, when you've been alone these last two terrible months," Alyosha went on, softly and distinctly, as before. Yet he was speaking now, it seemed, not on his own behalf, not by his own will, but under some command he couldn't resist. "You've accused yourself, and confessed to yourself, that you're the murderer and no one else. But you didn't do it: you're mistaken: you're not the murderer. Do you hear? It was not you! God has sent me to tell you so."

They were both silent. The silence stretched out a whole long minute. They stood still, staring into each other's eyes. Both were pale. Suddenly Ivan began trembling all over, and clutched Alyosha's shoulder.
"You've been in my room!" he whispered hoarsely. "You've been there at night, when he came.... Confess...have you seen him, have you seen him?"
"Who do you mean—Mitya?" Alyosha asked, bewildered.
"Not him, damn the monster!" Ivan shouted, in a frenzy. "Do you know that he visits me? How did you find out? Speak!"
"Who is he? I don't know who you're talking about," Alyosha faltered, starting to feel alarmed.
"Yes, you do know...or how could you—? It's impossible that you don't know."
He suddenly seemed to catch himself. He stood still and appeared to think it over. A strange grin twisted his lips.

"Brother," Alyosha began again, in a shaking voice, "I've said this to you because you'll believe my word—I know that. I'm telling you once and for all, it's not you. Do you hear, once and for all! God put it in my heart to say this to you, even if it means you'll hate me from this hour on."
But by now Ivan seemed to have regained his self-control.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch," he said, with a cold smile, "I can't stand prophets and epileptics—messengers from God especially—and you know that perfectly well. I'm breaking off all relations with you as of this moment, probably for good. I ask you to leave me here at this corner. It's the way to your lodgings too, anyway. And you'd do especially well not to come see me today! Do you hear?"
He turned and walked on with a firm step, without looking back.
"Brother," Alyosha called after him, "if anything happens to you today, come to me before anyone else!"

But Ivan didn't answer. Alyosha stood under the streetlamp at the crossroads until Ivan had vanished into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan were living in lodgings; neither was willing to live in Fyodor Pavlovitch's empty house. Alyosha had a furnished room in the home of some working people. Ivan lived some distance away from him. He'd taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house belonging to a well-to-do lady, the widow of an official. But his only attendant was a deaf, rheumatic old woman who went to bed at six every evening and got up at six in the morning. Ivan had grown remarkably indifferent to his own comfort of late, and very fond of being alone. He did everything for himself in the one room he lived in, and rarely set foot in any of the other rooms of his lodgings.

He reached the gate of the house and had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He felt himself trembling all over with anger. Suddenly he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse, and walked off rapidly in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a small, leaning wooden house, almost a hut, where Marya Kondratyevna now lodged—the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch's kitchen for soup, and to whom Smerdyakov had once sung songs and played the guitar. She'd sold their little house and was now living here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill—nearly dying—had been staying with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch's death. It was to him Ivan was going now, drawn by a sudden and irresistible urge.

title: VI. The First Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: This was the third time Ivan had gone to see Smerdyakov since coming back from Moscow. The first time he'd seen and talked with him was on the day he arrived; then he'd visited once more, two weeks later. But his visits had stopped after that second one, so that it had now been over a month since he'd seen him. And he'd heard almost nothing about him since.

Ivan hadn't returned until five days after his father's death, so he wasn't there for the funeral, which took place the day before he got back. The reason for the delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his Moscow address, had had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph him, and she, not knowing his address either, had telegraphed his sister and aunt, counting on Ivan visiting them as soon as he arrived in Moscow. But he didn't go to see them until four days after he got there. When he received the telegram, he had, of course, set off for our town at once. Alyosha was the first to meet him, and Ivan was quite surprised to find that, against the general opinion in town, Alyosha refused to suspect Mitya at all, and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later, after seeing the police captain and the prosecutor, and hearing the details of the charge and arrest, he was even more surprised at Alyosha, and put his opinion down only to an exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond of.

Let's say a word or two here about Ivan's feelings toward his brother Dmitri. He genuinely disliked him; at most he sometimes felt a kind of pity for him, and even that was mixed with a great deal of contempt, nearly revulsion. Mitya's whole personality, even his appearance, was deeply unappealing to him. Ivan looked with indignation on Katerina Ivanovna's love for his brother. And yet he went to see Mitya on the very first day he arrived, and that meeting, far from shaking Ivan's belief in his guilt, actually strengthened it. He found his brother agitated, nervously worked up. Mitya had been talkative, but scattered and incoherent. He'd used violent language, accused Smerdyakov, and been terribly confused. He'd talked mostly about the three thousand roubles, which he said had been "stolen" from him by his father.
"The money was mine, it was my money," Mitya kept repeating. "Even if I had stolen it, I'd have had the right to."

He barely disputed the evidence against him, and when he did try to turn some fact in his favor, it was in an absurd, incoherent way. He seemed to have hardly any wish to defend himself, to Ivan or to anyone else. Quite the opposite—he was angry, and proudly contemptuous of the charges against him; he kept flaring up and abusing everyone. He only laughed scornfully at Grigory's testimony about the open door, and declared it was "the devil who opened it." But he couldn't offer any coherent explanation for the fact. He even managed to insult Ivan during their first meeting, telling him sharply that people who declared "everything is permitted" had no business suspecting and questioning him. On the whole he was anything but friendly toward Ivan that day. Right after that meeting with Mitya, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov for the first time.

On the train from Moscow, he'd kept thinking about Smerdyakov and about their last conversation, on the evening before Ivan left. A number of things struck him as puzzling and suspicious. But when he gave his testimony to the investigating lawyer, Ivan said nothing, for the time being, about that conversation. He put it off until he'd seen Smerdyakov, who was in the hospital at the time.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, confidently assured Ivan, in answer to his persistent questions, that Smerdyakov's epileptic attack was unmistakably genuine, and seemed genuinely surprised that Ivan would ask whether he might have faked it on the day of the murder. They gave him to understand that the attack had been an exceptional one, the fits recurring several times, so that the patient's life had actually been in danger, and it was only now, after treatment, that they could say with confidence he would survive. "Though it's quite possible," added Doctor Herzenstube, "that his reason will be impaired for a good while, if not permanently." When Ivan asked impatiently whether that meant he was now insane, they told him that wasn't the case yet, not in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities were noticeable. Ivan decided to find out for himself what those abnormalities were.

At the hospital he was allowed to see the patient right away. Smerdyakov was lying on a narrow bed in a separate ward. There was only one other bed in the room, occupied by a tradesman from town, swollen with dropsy, who was clearly close to death; he'd be no obstacle to their conversation. Smerdyakov gave an uncertain grin on seeing Ivan, and for the first instant seemed nervous—or so Ivan imagined, at least. But that passed quickly. For the rest of the visit, Ivan was struck, instead, by Smerdyakov's composure. From the first glance Ivan had no doubt he was very ill. He was very weak; he spoke slowly, as if his tongue moved with difficulty; he'd grown much thinner and more sallow. Throughout the visit, which lasted twenty minutes, he kept complaining of headache and aching in all his limbs. His thin, sexless face seemed to have shrunk; his hair was disheveled, and the tuft of curls at his forehead stood up in a thin clump. But in the left eye, screwed up as if hinting at something, Smerdyakov remained unchanged. "It's always worth talking to a clever man"—Ivan was reminded of that at once. He sat down on the stool at the foot of the bed. Smerdyakov, with visible effort, shifted his position, but he wasn't the one to speak first. He stayed silent, and didn't even seem especially interested.
"Can you talk to me?" Ivan asked. "I won't tire you out."
"Certainly I can," Smerdyakov mumbled, in a faint voice. "Has your honor been back long?" he added, in a condescending tone, as if reassuring a nervous visitor.
"I only arrived today.... To see the mess you've gotten yourself into here."
Smerdyakov sighed.
"Why are you sighing? You knew about it the whole time," Ivan blurted out.
Smerdyakov stayed stolidly silent for a while.
"How could I not know? It was obvious beforehand. But how could I have known it would turn out like this?"
"What would turn out like what? Don't dodge! You predicted you'd have a fit—on the way down to the cellar, you know. You named the very spot."
"Have you already said that at the inquiry?" Smerdyakov asked calmly.
Ivan suddenly felt a surge of anger.
"No, not yet, but I certainly will. You'll have to explain a great deal to me, my man, and let me tell you, I'm not going to let you play games with me!"
"Why would I play games with you, when I trust you completely, the way I trust God Almighty?" Smerdyakov said, with the same composure, only closing his eyes for a moment.

"In the first place," Ivan began, "I know epileptic fits can't be predicted in advance. I've asked around—don't try to fool me. You can't foretell the day and hour. So how did you tell me the day and the hour in advance, and about the cellar too? How could you know you'd fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, unless you faked the fit on purpose?"

"I had to go down to the cellar anyway, several times a day, in fact," Smerdyakov drawled out slowly. "I fell from the loft the same way a year ago. It's quite true you can't predict the exact day and hour of a fit, but you can always sense one coming."
"But you did predict the day and the hour!"
"When it comes to my epilepsy, sir, you'd do much better to ask the doctors here about it. You can ask them whether it was a real fit or a fake one. There's no use my saying anything more about it."
"And the cellar? How could you know about the cellar in advance?"

"You just can't seem to get past that cellar! As I was going down, I was in a state of terrible dread and doubt. What frightened me most was the thought of losing you and being left with no protection in the whole world. So I went down into the cellar thinking, 'Here it comes, it'll strike me down any second, will I fall?' And it was exactly that fear that brought on the spasm that always comes over me... and down I went. All of that, and everything I'd told you at the gate the evening before—how frightened I was, and what I said about the cellar—I told all of it to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it's all been written down in the record. And Dr. Varvinsky here insisted to all of them that it was precisely the thought of it, the fear that I might fall, that brought it on. That's exactly when the fit seized me. So they wrote it down that this is just how it must have happened, simply from my fear."
As he finished, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as if worn out.

"So you've said all that in your testimony?" Ivan asked, somewhat caught off guard. He'd meant to frighten him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and it turned out Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.
"What would I have to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth," Smerdyakov said firmly.
"And did you tell them every word of our conversation at the gate?"
"No, not every word, I wouldn't say."
"And did you tell them you could fake fits, the way you bragged to me then?"
"No, I didn't tell them that either."
"Tell me now—why did you send me to Tchermashnya, then?"
"I was afraid you'd go off to Moscow; Tchermashnya's closer, anyway."
"You're lying; you suggested my leaving on your own; you told me to get out of the way of trouble."

"That was simply out of affection and genuine devotion to you—foreseeing trouble in the house, I wanted to spare you it. Only I wanted to spare myself even more. That's why I told you to get out of harm's way—so that you'd understand there was going to be trouble in the house, and would stay home to protect your father."
"You could have said it more directly, you blockhead!" Ivan suddenly flared up.

"How could I have said it more directly, at the time? It was pure fear that made me speak at all, and you might have gotten angry too. I might well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and carry off that money, since he considered it his own; but who could have guessed it would end in a murder like this? I thought he'd only carry off the three thousand lying under the master's mattress in the envelope, and instead, you see, he's murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?"
"But if you're telling me yourself it couldn't be guessed, how could I have guessed and stayed home? You're contradicting yourself!" Ivan said, thinking it over.
"You might have guessed it from the fact that I sent you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow."
"How could I have guessed anything from that?"
Smerdyakov seemed quite worn out, and fell silent again for a minute.

"You might have guessed it from my asking you not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya—because I wanted you nearer, since Moscow's a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you weren't far away, wouldn't have dared to be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come to protect me too, since I warned you about Grigory Vassilyevitch being ill, and that I was afraid I'd have a fit. And when I explained those knocks to you, the ones you could use to get in to see the deceased, and how Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you'd realize for yourself that he was sure to do something, and so you wouldn't even go to Tchermashnya, but would stay."
"He talks very coherently," Ivan thought, "even if he does mumble. What's this derangement of his faculties Herzenstube was talking about?"
"You're being sly with me, damn you!" he exclaimed, growing angry.
"But I thought at the time that you'd guessed everything," Smerdyakov parried, with the most innocent air.
"If I'd guessed, I would have stayed," Ivan cried.
"Well, I thought it was exactly because you'd guessed that you left in such a hurry—just to get away from trouble, just to run and save yourself in your fright."
"You think everyone's as much a coward as you are?"
"Forgive me, I thought you were like me."

"Of course, I ought to have guessed," Ivan said, agitated; "and I did guess there was some mischief brewing on your part... only you're lying, you're lying again," he cried, suddenly remembering. "Do you recall going up to the carriage and saying to me, 'It's always worth talking to a clever man'? So you were glad I was leaving, since you praised me for it?"
Smerdyakov sighed, again and again. A trace of color crept into his face.

"If I was pleased," he said, rather breathlessly, "it was simply because you agreed not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya. Because it was closer, anyway. Only when I said those words to you, it wasn't meant as praise—it was a reproach. You didn't understand it that way."
"What reproach?"
"Why, that foreseeing such a disaster, you abandoned your own father, and wouldn't protect us—because I could have been arrested any moment for stealing that three thousand."
"Damn you!" Ivan swore again. "Wait—did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?"
"I told them everything exactly as it was."
Ivan found himself puzzled again.

"If I thought of anything back then," he began again, "it was only some piece of mischief on your part. That Dmitri might kill him, yes—but that he would steal, I didn't believe that at the time.... But I was prepared for any kind of mischief from you. You told me yourself you could fake a fit. Why did you say that?"

"That was pure simplemindedness, and I've never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it then to show off to you. It was just foolishness. I liked you so much back then, and was open with you."
"My brother accuses you outright of the murder and the theft."

"What else is left for him to do?" Smerdyakov said, with a bitter grin. "And who's going to believe him, with all the evidence stacked against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say after that? But never mind him! He's trembling just to save his own skin."
He fell slowly silent; then suddenly, as if on second thought, he added:

"And look at this too. He wants to pin it on me, make it out that it's my doing—I've already heard that. But as for me being clever enough to fake a fit—would I have told you beforehand that I could fake one, if I'd really had such a scheme against your father in mind? If I'd been planning a murder like that, could I have been fool enough to give evidence like that against myself in advance? And to his son, no less! I ask you! Is that likely? As if such a thing could happen—nothing like it ever has. No one's hearing this conversation of ours now except Providence itself, and if you told the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch about it, you could clear me completely just by doing so, because who would be such a criminal, if he's so open about it in advance? Anyone can see that."

"Well," and Ivan got up to cut the conversation short, struck by Smerdyakov's last argument. "I don't suspect you at all, and I think it's absurd, really, to suspect you. On the contrary, I'm grateful to you for setting my mind at ease. Now I'll go, but I'll come again. In the meantime, good-bye. Get well. Is there anything you need?"
"I'm very thankful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn't forget me, and provides whatever I need, out of her kindness. Good people visit me every day."
"Good-bye. But I won't say anything about your being able to fake a fit, and I don't advise you to either," something made Ivan say suddenly.
"I understand completely. And if you don't speak of that, I won't say anything about our conversation at the gate."

With that, Ivan went out, and only after he'd gone a dozen steps down the corridor did he suddenly feel that there'd been an insulting undertone in Smerdyakov's last words. He very nearly turned back, but it was only a passing impulse, and muttering "Nonsense!" he walked out of the hospital.

His main feeling was one of relief at the thought that it wasn't Smerdyakov, but Mitya, who'd committed the murder—though one might have expected the opposite. He didn't want to examine the reason for this feeling, and even felt a genuine reluctance to pry into his own sensations. He felt as if he wanted to hurry up and forget something. In the days that followed, he became convinced of Mitya's guilt, as he learned the full weight of the evidence against him. There was testimony from people of no particular importance, Fenya and her mother, for instance, but its effect was nearly overwhelming. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern, and at Plotnikov's shop, as well as the witnesses at Mokroe, their testimony seemed conclusive. It was the details that were so damning. The secret of the knocks struck the lawyers almost as forcefully as Grigory's testimony about the open door. Grigory's wife, Marfa, in answer to Ivan's questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain the whole night on the other side of the partition wall. "He wasn't three paces from our bed," and that although she was a sound sleeper, she'd woken several times and heard him moaning—"He was moaning the whole time, moaning without stopping."
Talking with Herzenstube, and offering his opinion that Smerdyakov wasn't insane, just rather weak, Ivan got only a subtle smile out of the old man in response.

"Do you know how he spends his time now?" he asked. "Memorizing lists of French words. He's got a notebook under his pillow with the French words written out for him in Russian letters by somebody, heh heh heh!"

Ivan eventually dismissed all his doubts. He couldn't think of Dmitri without revulsion. One thing was strange, though. Alyosha kept insisting that Dmitri wasn't the murderer, and that "in all likelihood" it was Smerdyakov. Ivan always felt that Alyosha's opinion meant a great deal to him, and so he was startled by it now. Another odd thing was that Alyosha made no attempt to talk about Mitya with Ivan—never brought the subject up himself, and only answered when asked. This, too, struck Ivan as particularly strange.

But he was very preoccupied at the time with something quite separate from all this. On returning from Moscow, he'd given himself over hopelessly to his mad, consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This isn't the place to begin describing this new passion of Ivan's, one that left its mark on the rest of his life: it would furnish material for a whole other novel, one I may never write. But I can't leave out the fact that when Ivan, on leaving Katerina Ivanovna's with Alyosha, as I've already told, said to him, "I'm not especially keen on her," it was an outright lie: he loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much he could have killed her. Many things had combined to produce this feeling in him. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she had rushed to meet Ivan on his return as her one salvation. She'd been hurt, insulted, humiliated in her feelings. And here was the man who'd come back to her, the one who had once loved her so ardently before (oh, she knew that very well), and whose heart and mind she considered so far above her own. But this sternly virtuous woman didn't give herself over entirely to the man she loved, despite the Karamazov violence of his passions and the powerful hold he had on her. She was tormented, at the same time, by constant remorse for having abandoned Mitya, and in moments of conflict and violent anger (and there were many of them), she told Ivan so, plainly. This was what he'd called to Alyosha "lie upon lie." There was, of course, plenty that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything else.... But more on this later.

For a time he did, in fact, nearly forget Smerdyakov existed, and yet, two weeks after his first visit to him, he began to be haunted by the same strange thoughts as before. Suffice it to say that he kept asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, he'd crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened to hear what his father was doing below. Why had he recalled that afterward with revulsion? Why, the next morning, had he suddenly grown so depressed on his journey? Why, on reaching Moscow, had he said to himself, "I am a scoundrel"? And now he almost fancied these tormenting thoughts might make him forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so completely did they take hold of him again. It was right after this thought occurred to him that he ran into Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and put a question to him:

"Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterward, out in the yard, I told you I reserved 'the right to desire'?... Tell me, did you think, at the time, that I wanted father dead, or not?"
"I did think so," Alyosha answered softly.

"It was true, too; it wasn't just guesswork. But didn't you also imagine, back then, that what I actually wanted was for 'one reptile to devour another'—that is, exactly for Dmitri to kill father, and as soon as possible... and that I myself was even prepared to help make that happen?"
Alyosha went rather pale, and looked silently into his brother's face.
"Speak!" Ivan cried. "I want more than anything to know what you thought at the time. I want the truth, the truth!"
He drew a deep breath, looking angrily at Alyosha before the answer came.
"Forgive me, I did think that too, at the time," Alyosha whispered, and added no softening word to it.

"Thanks," Ivan snapped, and, leaving Alyosha, walked quickly away. From that time on, Alyosha noticed that Ivan began plainly avoiding him, and seemed even to have taken a dislike to him—so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. Right after that meeting, Ivan hadn't gone home, but had gone straight back to Smerdyakov.

title: VII. The Second Visit To Smerdyakov
paragraphs: By this time Smerdyakov had been discharged from the hospital. Ivan knew his new lodgings, the run-down little wooden house divided in two by a hallway, with Marya Kondratyevna and her mother living on one side and Smerdyakov on the other. No one knew exactly on what terms he lived with them—whether as a friend or a lodger. It was assumed afterward that he'd moved in as Marya Kondratyevna's fiancé, and was living there for the time being without paying for room or board. Both mother and daughter held him in the highest respect and considered him far above themselves.

Ivan knocked, and when the door opened, went straight into the hallway. Following Marya Kondratyevna's directions, he went straight to the better room on the left, the one Smerdyakov occupied. There was a tiled stove in the room, and it was extremely hot. The walls were done in cheerful blue paper, though quite worn, and in the cracks beneath it cockroaches swarmed in astonishing numbers, so that there was a constant rustling sound. The furniture was sparse: two benches along the walls and two chairs by the table. The plain wooden table was covered with a cloth patterned in pink. There was a pot of geraniums on each of the two small windows. In the corner stood a case of icons. On the table sat a little copper samovar, badly dented, and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had already finished his tea and the samovar had gone cold. He was sitting at the table on a bench, looking at a notebook and writing slowly with a pen. There was a bottle of ink beside him and a flat iron candlestick holding a composite candle. Ivan could see at once from Smerdyakov's face that he'd fully recovered from his illness. His face was fresher, fuller; his hair stood up jauntily in front and was slicked down at the sides. He sat in a multicolored, padded dressing gown, though fairly dirty and frayed. He had spectacles on his nose, which Ivan had never seen him wear before. This trivial detail suddenly doubled Ivan's anger: a creature like that, wearing spectacles!

Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and looked intently at his visitor through his spectacles; then he slowly took them off and got up from the bench, though by no means respectfully—almost lazily, doing the bare minimum that ordinary politeness demanded. Ivan took all this in at once, noting every bit of it—above all the look in Smerdyakov's eyes, genuinely malicious, sullen, and haughty. "What are you barging in here for?" it seemed to say. "We settled everything already; why have you come again?" Ivan could barely control himself.
"It's hot in here," he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.
"Take your coat off," Smerdyakov conceded.
Ivan took off his coat and tossed it onto a bench with trembling hands. He grabbed a chair, pulled it up to the table, and sat down. Smerdyakov managed to get himself seated on his bench before him.
"First of all—are we alone here?" Ivan asked, sharp and abrupt. "Can they hear us from in there?"
"No one can hear a thing. You saw for yourself—there's a hallway."

"Listen, my good man—what was that you were mumbling as I was leaving the hospital, that if I kept quiet about your talent for faking fits, you wouldn't tell the investigating lawyer all about our conversation at the gate? What do you mean by all? What were you getting at? Were you threatening me? Have I made some kind of deal with you? Do you think I'm afraid of you?"

Ivan said all this in an absolute fury, making it plain, with obvious intent, that he despised any evasion or indirectness and meant to lay his cards on the table. Smerdyakov's eyes gleamed with resentment, his left eye twitched, and he gave his answer at once, with his usual composure and deliberateness. "You want everything out in the open? Fine, you'll have it," he seemed to be saying.

"What I meant then, and why I said it, was that you, knowing beforehand about this murder of your own father, left him to his fate—and that people, after that, might draw all sorts of conclusions about your feelings, and about something else too. That's what I promised not to tell the authorities."

Though Smerdyakov spoke without hurrying, clearly holding himself in check, there was something in his voice—firm and pointed, resentful and insolently defiant. He stared at Ivan with open impudence. For a moment everything blurred before Ivan's eyes.
"How's that? What? Have you lost your mind?"
"I'm in full possession of all my faculties."
"Do you imagine I knew about the murder?" Ivan finally shouted, slamming his fist on the table. "What do you mean by 'something else too'? Speak, you scoundrel!"
Smerdyakov stayed silent, still fixing Ivan with the same insolent stare.
"Speak, you stinking wretch—what's this 'something else too'?"
"By 'something else,' I meant that you, too, probably wanted your father dead."

Ivan jumped up and struck him with all his strength on the shoulder, knocking him back against the wall. In an instant his face was streaming with tears. Saying, "It's shameful, sir, to strike a sick man," he wiped his eyes with a filthy blue checked handkerchief and sank into quiet weeping. A minute passed.
"That's enough! Stop," Ivan said sharply, sitting back down. "Don't push me past all patience."
Smerdyakov took the rag from his eyes. Every line of his creased face reflected the insult he'd just received.
"So you thought, then, you scoundrel, that I meant to kill my father together with Dmitri?"
"I didn't know what was in your mind at the time," Smerdyakov said resentfully, "so I stopped you there at the gate to sound you out on that exact point."
"Sound me out about what, what?"
"Why, that very thing—whether you wanted your father murdered or not."
What infuriated Ivan more than anything was the aggressive, insolent tone Smerdyakov kept up throughout.
"It was you who murdered him?" he suddenly cried.
Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously.
"You know for a fact yourself that it wasn't me who murdered him. And I'd have thought a sensible man wouldn't need to bring that up again."
"But why, why did you have such a suspicion about me at the time?"

"As you already know, it was simply out of fear. I was in such a state, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought if you wanted the same thing as your brother, then the matter was as good as settled, and I'd be crushed like a fly too."
"Look here—you didn't say any of that two weeks ago."

"I meant the same thing when I talked with you at the hospital, only I thought you'd understand without needing it spelled out, and that being such a sensible man, you wouldn't care to discuss it openly."
"What next! Come on, answer me, answer, I insist: what was it... what could I have done to put such a degrading suspicion into your low soul?"
"As for the murder itself, you couldn't have done it and didn't want to—but as for wanting someone else to do it, that's exactly what you did want."
"And how coolly, how coolly he says it! But why would I have wanted it? What grounds did I have for wanting it?"

"What grounds did you have? What about the inheritance?" Smerdyakov said, sarcastically, almost vindictively. "After your father's death, there'd have been at least forty thousand coming to each of you, likely more—but if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she'd have had all his capital signed over to her right after the wedding, because she's got plenty of sense, and your father wouldn't have left the three of you two roubles between you. And were they far from a wedding? Not by a hair—that lady only had to crook her little finger and he'd have gone running to church after her, tongue hanging out."
Ivan restrained himself with painful effort.
"Very good," he said at last. "You see, I haven't jumped up, I haven't knocked you down, I haven't killed you. Go on. So, according to you, I'd settled on Dmitri to do it—I was counting on him?"

"How could you not count on him? If he killed him, he'd lose every right of a nobleman, his rank, his property, and be sent off to exile—so his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch, split in two. Each of you would get not forty, but sixty thousand. There's not a doubt you were counting on Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"What I have to put up with from you! Listen, you scoundrel—if I'd counted on anyone at the time, it would have been you, not Dmitri, and I swear to you I did expect some piece of villainy from you... at the time.... I remember exactly what I felt!"

"I thought so too, for a minute, at the time—that you were counting on me as well," Smerdyakov said with a sarcastic grin. "And that's exactly how you showed me, more than anything, what was in your mind. Because if you had a premonition about me and still went off, it was as good as saying to me, 'You can go ahead and murder my father, I won't stop you!'"
"You scoundrel! So that's how you took it!"

"It was all that business with Tchermashnya. Think about it! You meant to go to Moscow and refused all your father's pleading to go to Tchermashnya instead—and then, on one foolish word from me, you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? Since you went to Tchermashnya for no reason at all, simply on my say-so, it shows you must have been expecting something from me."
"No, I swear I wasn't!" Ivan shouted, grinding his teeth.

"You weren't? Then, as your father's son, you should have had me hauled off to the lockup and beaten right then for saying that... or at the very least, punched me in the face on the spot. But you weren't the least bit angry, if you please—you went along with my foolish word right there in a friendly way and left, which was utterly absurd, because you should have stayed to save your father's life. How could I not draw my own conclusions?"
Ivan sat there scowling, both fists pressed convulsively against his knees.

"Yes, I'm sorry I didn't punch you in the face," he said, with a bitter smile. "I couldn't have had you hauled to the lockup just then—who would have believed me, and what charge could I have brought against you? But the punch in the face... oh, I'm sorry I didn't think of it. Even though blows are forbidden, I should have pounded your ugly face into pulp."
Smerdyakov looked at him with something like relish.

"In the ordinary run of life," he said, in the same self-satisfied, sententious tone he'd used to taunt Grigory and argue about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch's table, "in the ordinary run of life, blows to the face are forbidden nowadays by law, and people have given them up. But in exceptional circumstances, people still resort to blows—not just among us, but all over the world, even in the fullest republic of France, exactly as in the days of Adam and Eve, and they never will stop doing it. But you, even in an exceptional case, didn't dare."
"What are you learning French words for?" Ivan nodded toward the notebook lying on the table.
"Why shouldn't I learn them, to improve my education, in case I might happen to go one day to those happy parts of Europe?"

"Listen, you monster." Ivan's eyes flashed and he trembled all over. "I'm not afraid of your accusations. Say what you like about me. And if I don't beat you to death, it's simply because I suspect you of that crime, and I'll drag you before the law. I'll expose you."

"If you ask me, you'd do better to stay quiet, because what can you accuse me of, given my complete innocence? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I'll tell everything too, since I have to defend myself."
"Do you think I'm afraid of you now?"
"If the court doesn't believe everything I've just told you, the public will, and you'll be disgraced."
"That's as much as to say, 'It's always worth talking to a sensible man,' isn't it?" Ivan snarled.
"You've hit it exactly. And you'd better be sensible."

Ivan got up, shaking all over with indignation, put on his coat, and without another word to Smerdyakov, without even looking at him, walked quickly out of the house. The cool evening air was a relief. A bright moon hung in the sky. A nightmare of thoughts and sensations filled his soul. "Should I go straight and report Smerdyakov? But what could I report? He's not guilty of anything, anyway. If anything, he'll accuse me. And really, why did I set off for Tchermashnya then? What for? What for?" Ivan asked himself. "Yes, of course—I was expecting something, and he's right...." And for the hundredth time he remembered how, on that last night in his father's house, he'd listened on the stairs. But he remembered it now with such anguish that he stopped dead where he stood, as though he'd been stabbed. "Yes, I expected it then, that's true! I wanted the murder, I did want it! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I have to kill Smerdyakov! If I don't dare kill Smerdyakov now, life isn't worth living!"

Ivan didn't go home, but went straight to Katerina Ivanovna's, and alarmed her with his appearance. He looked like a madman. He repeated his whole conversation with Smerdyakov, word for word. Nothing she tried could calm him: he kept pacing the room, talking strangely, disjointedly. At last he sat down, put his elbows on the table, leaned his head on his hands, and pronounced this strange sentence: "If it's not Dmitri, but Smerdyakov, who's the murderer, then I share his guilt, because I put him up to it. Whether I did—I don't know yet. But if he's the murderer, and not Dmitri, then of course I'm the murderer too."

When Katerina Ivanovna heard this, she rose from her seat without a word, went to her writing table, opened a box sitting on it, took out a sheet of paper, and laid it before Ivan.
