This was the document Ivan later spoke of to Alyosha as "conclusive proof" that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna while drunk, on that very evening he'd met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery, right after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna's, when Grushenka had insulted her. After leaving Alyosha, Mitya had rushed off to Grushenka. I don't know whether he saw her, but that evening he was at the Metropolis, where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he'd asked for pen and paper and written a document that would carry heavy consequences for him. It was a rambling, disjointed, frantic letter—a drunken letter, in fact. It read like the talk of a drunk man who, coming home, launches with tremendous heat into telling his wife or someone in his household how he's just been insulted, what a scoundrel just insulted him, what a fine fellow he is by comparison, and how he'll pay that scoundrel back—all of it at enormous length, worked up and incoherent, with drunken tears and pounding on the table. The letter was written on a dirty piece of cheap ordinary paper, supplied by the tavern, with some figures scrawled on the back. There clearly wasn't enough space for his drunken outpouring, and Mitya had filled not only the margins but written his last line straight across the rest of the text. The letter read as follows:

FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I'll get the money and pay back your three thousand, and farewell, woman of great wrath—but farewell, too, my love! Let's put an end to it! Tomorrow I'll try to get it from everyone, and if I can't borrow it, I give you my word of honor I'll go to my father, break his skull, and take the money out from under his pillow, so long as Ivan's gone by then. Even if it means Siberia, I'll pay back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, because I've been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No—better not forgive me, you'll be happier, and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, because I love another woman, and you got to know her far too well today, so how could you forgive me? I'll murder the man who's robbed me! I'll leave you all and go east, so I never see anyone again. Not her either, because you're not my only tormentor—she is too. Farewell! P.S. I write my curse, but I adore you! I feel it in my heart. One string is left, and it's still vibrating. Better to tear my heart in two! I'll kill myself, but first, that cur. I'll tear three thousand out of him and throw it at your feet. Though I've been a scoundrel to you, I'm not a thief! You can count on the three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, tied with pink ribbon. I'm not a thief, but I'll murder my thief. Katya, don't look at me with contempt. Dmitri is no thief! But a murderer! He'll murder his father and destroy himself to hold his ground, rather than endure your pride. And he doesn't love you. P.P.S. I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S. Katya, pray to God someone gives me the money. Then I won't be drenched in blood—and if no one does, I will be! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy, D. KARAMAZOV.

When Ivan read this "document," he was convinced. So it was his brother, then, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not him, Ivan. In his eyes the letter immediately took on the shape of logical proof. There could no longer be the slightest doubt of Mitya's guilt. It never occurred to Ivan, incidentally, that Mitya might have committed the murder together with Smerdyakov—and indeed, such a theory didn't fit the facts. Ivan was thoroughly reassured. The next morning he thought of Smerdyakov and his taunts only with contempt. A few days later he genuinely wondered how he could have been so horribly shaken by his own suspicions. He resolved to dismiss the man with contempt and forget him. A month went by like this. He made no further inquiries about Smerdyakov, though twice he happened to hear that he was very ill and out of his mind.

"He'll end up mad," the young doctor Varvinsky remarked about him, and Ivan remembered this. During the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel quite ill. He went to consult the Moscow doctor Katerina Ivanovna had sent for just before the trial. And it was around this time that his relations with Katerina Ivanovna grew sharply strained. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna's "returns" to Mitya—her brief but violent swings of feeling back in his favor—drove Ivan to a state of pure frenzy. Strangely enough, right up until that last scene described earlier, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna's, Ivan had never once, during that entire month, heard her express any doubt of Mitya's guilt, despite those "returns" he found so hateful. It's worth noting, too, that while he felt his hatred of Mitya growing daily, he understood that it wasn't because of Katya's "returns" that he hated him, but simply because he was his father's murderer. He was conscious of this, and admitted it fully to himself.

Even so, he went to see Mitya ten days before the trial and proposed a plan of escape to him—a plan he'd clearly thought over for a long time. He was driven to it, in part, by a sore spot still lingering in his heart from a remark of Smerdyakov's: that it was to his, Ivan's, advantage that his brother be convicted, since that would raise his own and Alyosha's inheritance from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He decided to sacrifice thirty thousand toward arranging Mitya's escape. Coming back from that visit, he was deeply mournful and dejected; he suddenly began to sense that he was anxious for Mitya's escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for some other reason too. "Is it because I'm just as much a murderer at heart?" he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride, above all, suffered cruelly that whole month. But more on that later....

When, after his conversation with Alyosha, Ivan suddenly decided, hand on the bell of his lodgings, to go see Smerdyakov instead, he was obeying a sudden, strange surge of indignation. He'd suddenly remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had just cried out to him, in front of Alyosha: "It was you, you, who convinced me of his"—meaning Mitya's—"guilt!" Ivan was thunderstruck, recalling it. He'd never once tried to convince her Mitya was the murderer; on the contrary, he'd suspected himself in front of her, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov's. It was she, she, who had produced that "document" and proved his brother's guilt. And now she'd suddenly cried out: "I've been to see Smerdyakov myself!" When had she gone there? Ivan had known nothing about it. So she wasn't at all so certain of Mitya's guilt after all! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with furious anger. He couldn't understand how, half an hour earlier, he'd let those words slip past without crying out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off toward Smerdyakov's. "Maybe I'll kill him this time," he thought, on the way.

title: VIII. The Third And Last Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: When he was halfway there, the sharp, dry wind that had been blowing early that morning picked up again, and a fine, dry snow started falling thickly. It didn't settle on the ground, but was whipped around by the wind, and soon a real snowstorm was underway. There were hardly any streetlamps in the part of town where Smerdyakov lived. Ivan strode along alone in the dark, oblivious to the storm, picking his way instinctively. His head ached and there was a painful throbbing in his temples. He felt his hands twitching convulsively. Not far from Marya Kondratyevna's cottage, Ivan suddenly came upon a solitary drunk peasant. He wore a rough, patched coat and was weaving from side to side, grumbling and cursing to himself. Then all at once he'd break into song in a hoarse, drunken voice:
"Ah, Vanka's gone off to Petersburg; I won't wait till he comes back."

But every time he'd break off at the second line and start cursing again; then he'd start the same song over. Ivan felt an intense hatred for him before he'd even thought about him at all. Suddenly he became fully aware of him and felt an irresistible urge to knock him down. At that moment they came together, and the peasant, lurching violently, fell full-tilt against Ivan, who shoved him back furiously. The peasant went flying backward and fell like a log onto the frozen ground. He let out one plaintive "O—oh!" and then went silent. Ivan stepped up to him. He lay on his back, without movement or awareness. "He'll freeze to death," Ivan thought, and went on his way to Smerdyakov's.

In the hallway, Marya Kondratyevna, who ran out to open the door with a candle in hand, whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. "It's not that he's bedridden, exactly, but he doesn't seem himself, and he even told us to take the tea away—he wouldn't have any."
"Is he causing trouble, then?" Ivan asked, roughly.
"Oh, dear, no, quite the opposite—he's very quiet. Only please don't talk to him too long," Marya Kondratyevna pleaded. Ivan opened the door and stepped into the room.

It was overheated as before, but the room had changed. One of the benches along the wall had been taken out, and in its place stood a large old mahogany leather sofa, made up as a bed with fairly clean white pillows. Smerdyakov was sitting on the sofa, wearing the same dressing gown. The table had been pulled out in front of the sofa, leaving barely room to move. On the table lay a thick book with a yellow cover, but Smerdyakov wasn't reading it. He seemed to be sitting there doing nothing at all. He met Ivan with a slow, silent gaze, apparently not the least bit surprised at his arrival. There was a great change in his face; he was much thinner and more sallow. His eyes had sunk in, with blue shadows underneath.
"Why—you really are ill?" Ivan stopped short. "I won't keep you long, I won't even take off my coat. Where can I sit?"
He went to the other end of the table, pulled up a chair, and sat down.
"Why are you looking at me without saying anything? I've come with only one question, and I swear I won't leave without an answer. Has the young lady, Katerina Ivanovna, been here to see you?"
Smerdyakov stayed silent, watching Ivan quietly as before. Suddenly, with a wave of his hand, he turned his face away.
"What's the matter with you?" Ivan cried.
"Nothing."
"What do you mean, 'nothing'?"
"Yes, she has. It's none of your business. Leave me alone."
"No, I won't leave you alone. Tell me—when was she here?"

"Why, I'd nearly forgotten about her," Smerdyakov said, with a scornful smile, and turning his face back to Ivan, he stared at him with a look of frenzied hatred—the same look he'd fixed on him at their last meeting, a month before.
"You look pretty ill yourself—your face is sunken, you don't look like yourself," he said to Ivan.
"Never mind my health, answer what I'm asking you."
"But why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are quite yellow. Are you that worried?" He smiled contemptuously and then suddenly burst out laughing.
"Listen—I told you I won't leave without an answer!" Ivan cried, intensely irritated.
"Why do you keep after me? Why do you torment me?" Smerdyakov said, with a look of suffering.
"Damn it! I've got nothing to do with you. Just answer my question and I'll go."
"I've no answer to give you," Smerdyakov said, looking down again.
"You can be sure I'll make you answer!"

"Why are you so on edge?" Smerdyakov stared at him, not merely with contempt, but nearly with disgust. "Is it because the trial starts tomorrow? Nothing's going to happen to you—can't you believe that, finally? Go home, go to bed, sleep in peace, don't be afraid of anything."

"I don't understand you.... What do I have to be afraid of tomorrow?" Ivan said, in astonishment, and suddenly a cold breath of fear did in fact pass through his soul. Smerdyakov looked him up and down.
"You don't understand?" he drawled, reproachfully. "It's a strange thing, a sensible man wanting to keep up such a farce!"

Ivan stared at him, speechless. The startling, unbelievably condescending tone from this man who'd once been his father's valet was extraordinary in itself. He hadn't taken such a tone even at their last meeting.

"I'm telling you, you've got nothing to be afraid of. I won't say a word about you—there's no proof against you. Look how your hands are shaking! Why are your fingers moving like that? Go home—you didn't murder him."
Ivan flinched. He thought of Alyosha.
"I know it wasn't me," he faltered.
"Do you?" Smerdyakov caught him up again.
Ivan jumped up and grabbed him by the shoulder.
"Tell me everything, you snake! Tell me everything!"
Smerdyakov wasn't the least bit frightened. He simply fixed his eyes on Ivan with a kind of deranged hatred.
"Well, then, it was you who murdered him, if that's how it is," he whispered furiously.
Ivan sank back into his chair, as if turning something over in his mind. He laughed, viciously.
"You mean my going away. What you talked about last time?"
"You stood right here last time and understood it all, and you understand it now."
"All I understand is that you're insane."

"Aren't you sick of this? Here we are, face to face—what's the use of going on keeping up a farce between us? Are you still trying to pin it all on me, to my face? You murdered him; you're the real murderer; I was only your instrument, your faithful servant, and I did it following your own words."
"Did it? What—did you murder him?" Ivan went cold.
Something seemed to give way inside his brain, and he shuddered all over with a cold chill. Smerdyakov himself looked at him with wonder now; the genuineness of Ivan's horror seemed to strike him.
"You don't mean to tell me you really didn't know?" he faltered, mistrustfully, looking into his eyes with a forced smile. Ivan just stared at him, seemingly unable to speak.
Ah, Vanka's gone off to Petersburg; I won't wait till he comes back,
suddenly echoed in his head.
"Do you know, I'm afraid you're a dream, a phantom sitting in front of me," he muttered.
"There's no phantom here—just the two of us, and one other. No doubt he's here too, that third one, between us."
"Who is he? Who's here? What third person?" Ivan cried in alarm, looking around, his eyes darting into every corner.
"That third one is God Himself—Providence. He's the third one with us now. Only don't go looking for Him, you won't find Him."
"It's a lie that you killed him!" Ivan cried, wildly. "You're insane, or you're toying with me again!"

Smerdyakov watched him with the same curiosity as before, showing no sign of fear. He still couldn't quite get past his own disbelief; he still imagined Ivan knew everything and was trying to "pin it all on him," to his face.

"Wait a moment," he said at last, in a weak voice, and suddenly bringing his left leg out from under the table, he began rolling up his trouser leg. He had on long white stockings and slippers. Slowly he undid his garter and reached down into the bottom of his stocking. Ivan stared at him, and suddenly shuddered in a fit of terror.

"He's mad!" he cried, and jumping up quickly, backed away until he struck the wall and stood pressed against it, stiff and straight. He looked at Smerdyakov with insane terror, while Smerdyakov, entirely unaffected by it, kept fumbling in his stocking, as if straining to get hold of something with his fingers and pull it out. At last he got a grip on it and started pulling it out. Ivan saw it was a piece of paper, or maybe a roll of papers. Smerdyakov drew it out and set it on the table.
"Here," he said quietly.
"What is it?" Ivan asked, trembling.
"Take a look, if you would," Smerdyakov answered, still in the same low tone.
Ivan stepped up to the table, picked up the roll of paper, and started to unfold it, but suddenly drew his fingers back, as if he'd touched some loathsome reptile.
"Your hands keep twitching," Smerdyakov observed, and deliberately unwrapped the bundle himself. Under the wrapping were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.
"They're all here, the whole three thousand roubles—no need to count them. Take it," Smerdyakov said, nodding at the notes. Ivan sank back into his chair. He was as pale as a handkerchief.
"You frightened me... with that stocking," he said, with a strange grin.
"You really didn't know until now?" Smerdyakov asked again.
"No, I didn't know. I kept thinking it was Dmitri. Brother, brother! Ach!" He suddenly clutched his head in both hands.
"Listen. Did you kill him alone? With my brother's help, or without?"
"Only with you, with your help, I killed him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch is completely innocent."
"All right, all right. Talk about me later. Why do I keep trembling? I can't speak properly."

"You were bold enough back then. You said 'everything is lawful,' and now look how frightened you are," Smerdyakov muttered, in surprise. "Won't you have some lemonade? I'll ask for it right away. It's very refreshing. Only I have to hide this first."

And he gestured at the notes again. He was about to get up and call to Marya Kondratyevna through the door to make some lemonade and bring it in, but looking around for something to cover the notes with so she wouldn't see them, he first pulled out his handkerchief, and finding it very dirty, took the big yellow book Ivan had noticed earlier on the table and laid it over the money. The book was The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian. Ivan read the title without taking it in.
"I won't have any lemonade," he said. "Talk about me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. Tell me everything."
"You'd better take off your coat, or you'll get too hot." Ivan, as if only just remembering, took off his coat and, without getting up from his chair, threw it onto the bench.
"Speak, please, speak."
He seemed calmer now. He waited, certain that Smerdyakov would tell him everything.
"How it was done?" Smerdyakov sighed. "It was done in the most natural way, exactly following your own words."

"About my words, later," Ivan cut in again, seemingly with complete self-possession now, pronouncing his words firmly instead of shouting as before. "Just tell me in detail how you did it. Everything, exactly as it happened. Don't leave anything out. The details, above all—the details, I beg you."
"You'd gone off, and then I threw myself down into the cellar."
"A real fit, or a faked one?"

"A faked one, of course. I faked the whole thing. I went quietly down the steps to the very bottom and lay down quietly, and once I was down, I let out a scream and thrashed around, until they carried me out."
"Wait! And were you faking it all along afterward too—in the hospital?"
"No, not at all. The next morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real attack, and a worse one than I've had in years. For two days I was completely unconscious."
"All right, all right. Go on."

"They laid me on the bed. I knew I'd be on the other side of the partition, because whenever I was ill, Marfa Ignatyevna always put me there, near them. She's always been very kind to me, since I was born. That night I moaned, but quietly. I kept waiting for Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come."
"Waiting for him? To come to you?"

"Not to me. I was waiting for him to come to the house, because I had no doubt he'd come that night—being without me, getting no word, he'd be sure to come and climb over the fence, the way he used to, and do something."
"And if he hadn't come?"
"Then nothing would have happened. I'd never have brought myself to do it without him."
"All right, all right... talk more clearly, don't rush; above all, don't leave anything out!"

"I was expecting him to kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, because I'd prepared him for it... over the last few days.... He knew about the knocks, that was the main thing. With his suspicious nature and the rage that had been building in him all those days, he was bound to get into the house through those signals. It was inevitable, so I was waiting for him."
"Wait," Ivan interrupted. "If he'd killed him, he'd have taken the money and carried it off—you must have thought of that. What would you have gained by it afterward? I don't see it."

"But he never would have found the money. That was only what I told him—that the money was under the mattress. But that wasn't true. It had been sitting in a box. And afterward I suggested to Fyodor Pavlovitch, since I was the only person he trusted, that he hide the envelope with the notes in the corner behind the icons, because no one would ever guess that spot, especially in a hurry. So that's where the envelope lay, in the corner behind the icons. It would have been absurd to keep it under the mattress; the box, at least, could be locked. But everyone believed it was under the mattress. A stupid thing to believe. So if Dmitri Fyodorovitch had committed the murder and found nothing, he'd either have run off in a panic, jumping at every sound, the way murderers always do, or he'd have been caught. So I could always climb up to the icons and take the money the next morning, or even that same night, and it would all get pinned on Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I could count on that."
"But what if he didn't kill him, only knocked him down?"

"If he hadn't killed him, of course, I wouldn't have dared take the money, and nothing would have happened. But I calculated he'd beat him senseless, and I'd have time to take it then, and afterward I'd make out to Fyodor Pavlovitch that no one but Dmitri Fyodorovitch had taken the money after beating him."
"Stop... I'm getting confused. So it was Dmitri after all who killed him, and you only took the money?"

"No, he didn't kill him. Well, I might as well have just told you he was the murderer.... But I don't want to lie to you now, because... because if you really haven't understood until now, as I can see for myself, and aren't pretending, just to pin your guilt on me right to my face—you're still responsible for the whole thing, since you knew about the murder and set me to do it, and went away knowing all about it. And so I want to prove to your face tonight that you're the only real murderer in this whole business, and that I'm not the real murderer, even though I did kill him. You're the rightful murderer."

"Why, why am I a murderer? Oh, God!" Ivan cried, unable to hold himself back any longer, forgetting he'd meant to put off discussing himself until the end of the conversation. "You still mean that business with Tchermashnya? Wait, tell me—why did you need my consent, if you really took Tchermashnya as consent? How will you explain that now?"

"Sure of your consent, I'd have known you wouldn't make a fuss over that three thousand going missing, even if suspicion fell on me instead of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or as his accomplice—on the contrary, you'd have protected me from the others.... And once you got your inheritance, you'd have rewarded me for the rest of your life, whenever you could. Because you'd have gotten your inheritance through me, seeing as, if he'd married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you wouldn't have had a kopeck."
"Ah! So you meant to torment me for the rest of my life," Ivan snarled. "And what if I hadn't gone away then, but had reported you?"

"Reported what? That I talked you into going to Tchermashnya? That's nothing. Besides, after our conversation, you'd either have gone away or stayed. If you'd stayed, nothing would have happened. I'd have known you didn't want it done, and wouldn't have attempted anything. Your leaving meant you were, in effect, assuring me you wouldn't dare report me at the trial, and that you'd overlook my having the three thousand. And in fact, you couldn't have prosecuted me afterward, because then I'd have told the whole court everything—not that I stole the money or killed him, I wouldn't have said that—but that you'd put me up to the theft and the murder, even though I hadn't agreed to it. That's why I needed your consent—so you couldn't corner me afterward, because what proof would you have had? I could always have cornered you instead, exposing how eager you were for your father's death, and I promise you, the public would have believed every word of it, and you'd have been ashamed for the rest of your life."
"Was I really so eager, then? Was I?" Ivan snarled again.

"You certainly were, and by your consent you silently gave your blessing to my doing it." Smerdyakov looked steadily at Ivan. He was very weak, and spoke slowly and wearily, but some hidden inner force kept driving him forward. He clearly had some purpose in mind. Ivan could feel it.
"Go on," he said. "Tell me what happened that night."

"What more is there to tell! I lay there and thought I heard the master shout. And before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly gotten up and gone out, and let out a sudden scream, and then everything went silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart pounding; I couldn't stand it. Finally I got up, went outside. I saw the window open on the left, into the garden, and I moved left to listen and find out whether he was sitting there alive, and I heard the master moving around, sighing, so I knew he was alive. 'Ech!' I thought. I went to the window and called out to the master, 'It's me.' And he called back to me, 'He's been here, he's been here, he's run off.' He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been there. 'He's killed Grigory!' 'Where?' I whispered. 'There, in the corner,' he pointed. He was whispering too. 'Wait a moment,' I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there I found Grigory Vassilyevitch lying by the wall, covered in blood, unconscious. So it's true, Dmitri Fyodorovitch has been here—that's the thought that came into my head, and right there I decided to finish it, since Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, wouldn't see any of it, lying there senseless as he was. The only risk was Marfa Ignatyevna waking up. I felt that in the moment, but the urge to get it done came over me until I could hardly breathe. I went back to the master's window and said, 'She's here, she's come—Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, wants to be let in.' And he started like a child. 'Where is she?' he gasped, but couldn't quite believe it. 'She's standing right there,' I said. 'Open up.' He looked out the window at me, half believing, half doubting, but afraid to open the door. 'So he's afraid of me now too,' I thought. And it struck me as funny. It occurred to me to knock the taps we'd agreed on, on the window frame, as the signal that Grushenka had arrived, right there in front of him, before his eyes. He didn't seem to believe my word, but the moment he heard those knocks, he ran straight to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the way to block me. 'Where is she? Where is she?' He looked at me, trembling all over. 'Well,' I thought, 'if he's this scared of me, it's a bad sign!' And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn't let me in, or would cry out, or Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or something else might happen. I don't remember exactly now, but I must have been standing there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, 'Why, she's there, right there, under the window—how is it you don't see her?' I said. 'Bring her here, then, bring her.' 'She's frightened,' I said; 'the noise scared her, she's hidden in the bushes—go call out to her yourself, from the study.' He ran to the window, set the candle in it. 'Grushenka,' he cried, 'Grushenka, are you there?' Even as he cried out, he didn't want to lean out of the window, didn't want to move away from me, because he was gripped by panic—he was too afraid to turn his back on me. 'Why, there she is,' I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out of it. 'There she is, she's in the bushes, laughing at you—don't you see her?' Suddenly he believed it; he was shaking all over—he was crazy about her, terribly—and he leaned right out the window. I snatched up that iron paperweight from his table—do you remember, the one that weighed about three pounds? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner of it. He didn't even cry out. He just sank down suddenly, and I hit him again, and a third time. And on the third blow I knew I'd broken his skull. He suddenly rolled onto his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked myself over. Not a drop of blood on me, not a spot. I wiped off the paperweight, put it back, went up to the icons, took the money out of the envelope, and threw the envelope on the floor, along with the pink ribbon. I went out into the garden, trembling all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the one. I'd marked it out long before and left a rag and a piece of paper ready inside it. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and stuffed it deep down into the hole. And it stayed there for over two weeks. I took it out later, after I got out of the hospital. I went back to my bed, lay down, and thought: 'If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, that could be bad for me, but if he's not dead and recovers, it'll be perfect, because then he'll testify Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so he must have killed him and taken the money.' Then I started groaning with the strain and the waiting, so as to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as possible. Finally she got up and rushed over to me, but when she saw Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn't there, she ran outside, and I heard her scream in the garden. And that set the whole thing in motion and put my mind at ease."

He stopped. Ivan had listened the whole time in dead silence, not stirring, not taking his eyes off him. As he told his story, Smerdyakov glanced at him now and then, but mostly kept his eyes averted. When he'd finished, he was visibly agitated, breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face. But it was impossible to tell whether what he felt was remorse, or something else entirely.
"Wait," Ivan cried, thinking it over. "What about the door? If he only opened the door for you, how could Grigory have seen it open before that? Grigory saw it open before you even went in."

It was striking that Ivan spoke quite amicably now, in a different tone altogether, no longer angry as before—so that if someone had opened the door at that moment and peeked in at them, they'd certainly have concluded the two were discussing some ordinary, if interesting, matter, on perfectly peaceful terms.

"As for that door, and Grigory Vassilyevitch having seen it open—that's just his fancy," Smerdyakov said, with a wry smile. "He's not a man, I assure you, he's a stubborn mule. He didn't see it, but imagined he had, and there's no shaking him on it. It's just our good luck he got that notion into his head, because now they're sure to convict Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"Listen..." Ivan said, starting to look bewildered again, straining to grasp at something. "Listen. I have a lot of questions I want to ask you, but I keep forgetting them... I keep forgetting and getting mixed up. Yes. Tell me this, at least—why did you open the envelope and leave it lying there on the floor? Why didn't you just carry the whole envelope off?... When you were telling it to me, I thought you spoke of it as though it were the obvious thing to do... but I can't understand why...."

"I did that for a good reason. Because if a man had known all about it, the way I did, for instance—if he'd seen those notes before, and maybe even put them into the envelope himself, and seen it sealed and addressed with his own eyes—if a man like that had done the murder, what would have made him tear open the envelope afterward, especially in such a desperate hurry, when he'd know for certain the notes had to be inside? No—if the robber had been someone like me, he'd simply have put the whole envelope straight into his pocket and gotten away with it as fast as he could. But it would be quite different for Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He only knew about the envelope by hearsay; he'd never seen it, and if he'd found it, say, under the mattress, he'd have torn it open as fast as he could to make sure the notes were really inside. And he'd have tossed the envelope down without stopping to think it would count as evidence against him—because he wasn't a habitual thief, had never outright stolen anything before, being a gentleman born, and even if he'd brought himself to steal, it wouldn't have felt like real stealing to him, just taking back what was his own, since he'd told the whole town beforehand that he meant to, and had even bragged loudly in front of everyone that he'd go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn't say that outright to the prosecutor when he questioned me—quite the opposite, I led him to it with a hint, as if I hadn't thought of it myself, as if he'd come up with it on his own and I hadn't prompted him at all, so that Mr. Prosecutor's mouth was practically watering at my suggestion."
"But could you really have thought all of that through on the spot?" Ivan cried, overcome with astonishment. He looked at Smerdyakov again, with alarm.
"Mercy on us! Could anyone think all that through in such a desperate rush? It was all worked out beforehand."
"Well... well, the devil helped you!" Ivan cried again. "No, you're not a fool, you're far more clever than I thought...."

He got up, clearly meaning to pace across the room. He was in terrible distress. But since the table blocked his way, and there was barely room to pass between the table and the wall, he only turned in place and sat back down. Maybe the impossibility of moving irritated him, because he suddenly cried out again, almost as furiously as before.

"Listen, you miserable, contemptible creature! Don't you understand that if I haven't killed you, it's simply because I'm keeping you alive to answer for it tomorrow at the trial? God sees"—Ivan raised his hand—"maybe I was guilty too; maybe I really did secretly wish for my father's... death—but I swear I wasn't as guilty as you think, and maybe I never urged you on at all. No, no, I didn't urge you on! But it doesn't matter—I'll give evidence against myself tomorrow at the trial. I'm determined to! I'll tell everything, everything. But we'll appear together. And whatever you say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I'll face it—I'm not afraid of you. I'll confirm all of it myself! But you have to confess too! You must, you must; we'll go together. That's how it's going to be!"
Ivan said this solemnly and resolutely, and from his blazing eyes alone one could see that this was how it would be.
"You're ill, I can see; you're quite ill. Your eyes are yellow," Smerdyakov observed, without the slightest irony—in fact, with what seemed like genuine sympathy.
"We'll go together," Ivan repeated. "And if you won't go, it doesn't matter, I'll go alone."
Smerdyakov paused, as if turning it over in his mind.
"None of that's going to happen, and you're not going to go," he concluded at last, with certainty.
"You don't understand me," Ivan said, reproachfully.

"You'll be too ashamed, if you confess to it all. And what's more, it won't do any good at all, because I'll say flatly that I never told you anything of the sort, that you're either ill (and it does look that way) or that you're so sorry for your brother you're sacrificing yourself to save him, and made all of this up against me, since you've never thought more of me than if I were a fly. And who's going to believe you, and what single piece of proof do you have?"
"Listen, you showed me that money just now, to convince me."
Smerdyakov lifted the book off the notes and set it aside.
"Take that money with you," Smerdyakov sighed.
"Of course I'll take it. But why are you giving it to me, if you committed the murder for its sake?" Ivan looked at him with great surprise.

"I don't want it," Smerdyakov said, in a shaking voice, waving it off. "I did have the idea of starting a new life with that money, in Moscow, or better yet, abroad. I did dream of it—mainly because 'everything is lawful.' That's exactly what you taught me, you talked to me about it plenty. Because if there's no everlasting God, there's no such thing as virtue, and no need for it either. You were right about that. So that's how I saw it."
"Did you work that out on your own?" Ivan asked, with a wry smile.
"With your guidance."
"And now, I suppose, you believe in God, since you're giving the money back?"
"No, I don't believe," Smerdyakov whispered.
"Then why are you giving it back?"

"Enough... that's enough!" Smerdyakov waved his hand again. "You used to say yourself that everything was lawful—so why are you so worked up now too? You even want to go and testify against yourself.... Only none of that's going to happen! You're not going to go and testify," Smerdyakov concluded, with conviction.
"You'll see," Ivan said.

"It isn't possible. You're very clever. You love money, I know that. You like to be respected, too, because you're very proud; you're also far too fond of feminine charms, and what matters to you most of all is living undisturbed and comfortable, without having to depend on anyone—that's what you care about above everything. You won't want to ruin your life forever by taking on a disgrace like that. You're like Fyodor Pavlovitch—more like him than any of his other children; you've got the same soul he had."
"You're no fool," Ivan said, seeming struck by this. Blood rushed to his face. "You're being serious now!" he said, suddenly looking at Smerdyakov with a different expression.
"It was your own pride that made you think I was a fool. Take the money."
Ivan took the three rolls of notes and stuffed them into his pocket, without wrapping them in anything.
"I'll show them at the trial tomorrow," he said.
"Nobody will believe you, since you've got plenty of money of your own—you might simply have taken it out of your own cash-box and brought it to court."
Ivan rose from his seat.
"I'll say it again," he said. "The only reason I haven't killed you is that I need you for tomorrow—remember that, don't forget it!"

"Well, kill me then. Kill me right now," Smerdyakov said, suddenly looking at Ivan strangely. "You won't even dare to do that!" he added, with a bitter smile. "You won't dare do anything, you—you who used to be so bold!"
"Until tomorrow," Ivan cried, and turned to go.
"Wait a moment.... Show me that money again."
Ivan took out the notes and showed them to him. Smerdyakov looked at them for ten seconds.
"Well, you can go," he said, with a wave of his hand. "Ivan Fyodorovitch!" he called after him again.
"What do you want?" Ivan turned without stopping.
"Good-bye!"
"Until tomorrow!" Ivan cried again, and walked out of the cottage.

The snowstorm was still raging. He walked the first few steps boldly, but suddenly began to stagger. "It's just something physical," he thought, with a grin. Something like joy was rising up in his heart. He felt an unbounded sense of resolve; he'd put an end, now, to the wavering that had tormented him so much lately. His decision was made, "and now it won't change," he thought, with relief. At that moment he stumbled over something and nearly fell. Stopping short, he made out at his feet the peasant he'd knocked down earlier, still lying senseless and motionless. Snow had nearly covered his face. Ivan grabbed him and lifted him into his arms. Seeing a light in the little house to the right, he went up, knocked on the shutters, and asked the man who lived there to help him carry the peasant to the police station, promising him three roubles. The man got dressed and came out. I won't describe in detail how Ivan managed it, getting the peasant to the police station and arranging for a doctor to see him at once, paying generously for the expense. I'll only say the whole business took a full hour, but Ivan was quite pleased with himself over it. His mind wandered and worked without pause.

"If I hadn't made up my mind so firmly about tomorrow," he reflected with satisfaction, "I wouldn't have spent a whole hour looking after that peasant—I'd have just walked past, not caring whether he froze. I'm quite capable of observing myself, by the way," he thought, in that same instant, with even greater satisfaction, "even though they've decided I'm losing my mind!"

Just as he reached his own house he stopped short, suddenly asking himself whether he oughtn't to go straight to the prosecutor and tell him everything now. He settled the question by turning back toward the house. "All of it together, tomorrow!" he whispered to himself, and, strangely, nearly all his gladness and self-satisfaction vanished in that same instant.

As he entered his own room, he felt something like a touch of ice on his heart—like a memory, or more precisely, a reminder, of something agonizing and repulsive that was in that room now, at this very moment, and had been there before. He sank wearily onto his sofa. The old woman brought him a samovar; he made tea, but didn't touch it. He sat on the sofa and felt dizzy. He felt ill and helpless. He was starting to drift off to sleep, but got up uneasily and paced across the room to shake off the drowsiness. At moments he imagined he was delirious, but it wasn't his illness that occupied his thoughts most. Sitting back down, he began looking around, as if searching for something. This happened several times. At last his eyes fixed intently on one spot. Ivan smiled, but an angry flush spread across his face. He sat a long time in his place, his head propped on both arms, though he kept glancing sideways at that same spot, at the sofa standing against the opposite wall. There was clearly something there, some object, that irritated him, worried him, tormented him.

title: IX. The Devil. Ivan’s Nightmare
paragraphs: I'm not a doctor, but even so I feel the moment has come when I have to give the reader some account of the nature of Ivan's illness. Getting ahead of events, I can say at least this much: he was, at that very moment, on the verge of an attack of brain fever. His health had been affected for some time, but had put up a stubborn resistance to the fever, which in the end gained complete mastery over it. Knowing nothing of medicine, I'll venture the suggestion that he had, in fact, perhaps through a terrible effort of will, managed to delay the attack for a while, hoping, of course, to stop it entirely. He knew he wasn't well, but he loathed the thought of being ill at this fatal moment, at the approaching crisis of his life, when he needed his wits fully about him, to say what he had to say boldly and firmly, and "to justify himself to himself."

He had, however, gone to consult the new doctor, brought from Moscow by one of Katerina Ivanovna's fanciful notions, which I've already mentioned. After listening to him and examining him, the doctor concluded that he really was suffering from some disorder of the brain, and wasn't at all surprised by the admission Ivan reluctantly made him. "Hallucinations are quite likely, given your condition," the doctor said, "though it would be best to verify them.... You need to take steps right away, without a moment's delay, or things will go badly for you." But Ivan didn't follow this sound advice and didn't take to his bed to be nursed. "I'm still walking around, so I'm strong enough—if I collapse, that'll be a different matter, and anyone who wants to can nurse me then," he decided, dropping the subject.

And so he sat there, half-aware himself that he was delirious, and, as I've already said, staring persistently at something on the sofa against the opposite wall. Someone seemed to be sitting there, though goodness knows how he'd gotten in, since he hadn't been in the room when Ivan came in, on his return from Smerdyakov's. This was a person—or, more precisely, a Russian gentleman of a particular type, no longer young, qui faisait la cinquantaine, as the French say, with rather long, still-thick dark hair, faintly streaked with gray, and a small pointed beard. He wore a brownish reefer jacket, somewhat shabby, evidently cut by a good tailor, though at least three years out of fashion—a style that smart, well-off people had abandoned two years before. His linen and his long, scarf-like necktie were of the kind worn by people aiming at style, but on closer look his linen wasn't especially clean, and his wide scarf was quite threadbare. The visitor's checked trousers were excellently cut, but too pale in color and too tight for current fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat was out of step with the season.

In short, he presented every appearance of gentility on limited means. It looked as though the gentleman belonged to that class of idle landowners who once flourished in the days of serfdom. He'd unmistakably moved, at some point, in good, fashionable society, had once had solid connections, quite possibly still kept some of them—but after a lively youth, growing gradually poorer once serfdom was abolished, he'd sunk into the position of a poor relation of the better sort, drifting from one old family friend to another, welcomed for his agreeable, accommodating manner, and as, after all, a gentleman who could be seated with anyone, though of course not in a place of honor. Gentlemen of this accommodating temperament and dependent standing, who can tell a good story, take a hand at cards, and have a distinct aversion to any duty forced upon them, are usually solitary creatures, either bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but if so, the children are always being raised somewhere far off, at some aunt's, whom these gentlemen never mention in good company, seeming ashamed of the connection. They gradually lose track of their children altogether, though now and then they receive a birthday or Christmas letter, and sometimes even answer it.

The unexpected visitor's face wasn't so much good-natured as accommodating, ready to take on any agreeable expression the moment called for. He had no watch, but carried a tortoiseshell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand sat a heavy gold ring set with a cheap opal.

Ivan sat silent, angry, unwilling to start the conversation. The visitor waited, sitting exactly like a poor relation who'd come down from his room to keep his host company at tea, discreetly quiet, seeing that his host was frowning and preoccupied. But he was ready for any friendly conversation the moment his host began it. All at once his face took on a look of sudden concern.

"I say," he began, to Ivan, "forgive me, I only mention it as a reminder. You went to Smerdyakov's to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, but you came away without learning a thing about her—you must have forgotten—"

"Ah, yes," broke from Ivan, his face darkening with unease. "Yes, I'd forgotten... but never mind now, it doesn't matter, till tomorrow," he muttered to himself, "and you," he added, turning to his visitor, "I would have remembered that myself in another minute, since that was exactly what was tormenting me! Why do you butt in, as if I'm supposed to believe you put it in my head, and that I didn't remember it on my own?"

"Then don't believe it," the gentleman said, smiling amiably. "What good is believing against your will, anyway? Besides, proof doesn't help belief along, especially material proof. Thomas believed not because he saw the risen Christ, but because he wanted to believe, before he ever saw. Take the spiritualists, for instance.... I'm quite fond of them... just imagine, they think they're serving the cause of religion, because devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, of the existence of another world. The other world and material proof—what next! And if it comes to that, does proving there's a devil prove there's a God? I'd like to join an idealist society—I'd lead the opposition in it, I'd say I'm a realist, not a materialist, heh heh!"

"Listen," Ivan suddenly got up from the table. "I seem to be delirious.... I am delirious, in fact—say whatever nonsense you like, I don't care! You won't drive me into a fury the way you did last time. But somehow I feel ashamed.... I want to walk around the room.... Sometimes I don't see you and don't even hear your voice the way I did last time, but I can always guess what you're babbling on about, because it's me, it's me myself talking, not you. Only I don't know whether I was dreaming last time or really saw you. I'll wet a towel and put it on my head, and maybe you'll dissolve into thin air."
Ivan went to the corner, got a towel, and did as he'd said, and with a wet towel on his head began pacing up and down the room.
"I'm so glad you're being so familiar with me," the visitor began.

"Fool," Ivan laughed. "Do you think I'm going to stand on ceremony with you? I'm in good spirits right now, even with this pain in my forehead... and at the crown of my head... only please don't talk philosophy, the way you did last time. If you can't take yourself off, talk about something amusing. Gossip—you're a poor relation, you ought to gossip. What a nightmare to have! But I'm not afraid of you. I'll get the better of you. I won't be carted off to a madhouse!"

"C'est charmant, poor relation. Yes, that's exactly my true shape. What else am I on earth but a poor relation? By the way, I'm listening to you, and I'm rather surprised to find you're actually starting to take me for something real, and not simply your own fancy, as you kept insisting last time—"

"Not for one minute have I taken you for reality," Ivan cried, in a kind of fury. "You're a lie, you're my illness, you're a phantom. It's only that I don't know how to destroy you, and I see I'll have to suffer through it for a while. You're my hallucination. You're the embodiment of myself—but only one side of me... of my thoughts and feelings, and only the nastiest and stupidest ones at that. From that angle you might interest me, if only I had time to waste on you—"

"Excuse me, excuse me, I've caught you now. When you flew at Alyosha under the streetlamp tonight and shouted at him, 'You learned it from him! How do you know he visits me?'—you were thinking of me right then. So for one brief moment, you did believe that I really exist," the gentleman laughed, blandly.
"Yes, that was a moment of weakness... but I couldn't believe in you. I don't know whether I was asleep or awake last time. Maybe I was only dreaming, then, and never really saw you at all—"
"And why were you so surly with Alyosha just now? He's a dear boy; I did him wrong over Father Zossima."
"Don't talk about Alyosha! How dare you, you lackey!" Ivan laughed again.
"You scold me, but you laugh—that's a good sign. But you're ever so much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours—"
"Don't speak of my resolution," Ivan cried, savagely.
"I understand, I understand, c'est noble, c'est charmant—you're going to defend your brother and sacrifice yourself... C'est chevaleresque."
"Hold your tongue, or I'll kick you!"

"I wouldn't mind that at all, since it would achieve my object. If you kick me, you'll have to believe I'm real, since people don't kick ghosts. Joking aside, it makes no difference to me—scold away if you like, though you might be a bit more polite even to me. 'Fool, lackey!' Such words!"
"Scolding you, I scold myself," Ivan laughed again. "You are myself, myself, just with a different face. You only say what I'm already thinking... you're incapable of saying anything new!"
"If I think the way you do, that's entirely to my credit," the gentleman said, with delicacy and dignity.

"You only pick out my worst thoughts—and what's more, the stupid ones. You're stupid and vulgar. You're horribly stupid. No, I can't stand you! What am I supposed to do, what am I supposed to do?" Ivan said, through clenched teeth.

"My dear friend, above everything else I want to behave like a gentleman, and to be recognized as one," the visitor began, with a kind of deprecating, simple-hearted pride typical of a poor relation. "I'm poor, but... I won't say very honest, but... it's a generally accepted axiom in society that I'm a fallen angel. I really can't conceive how I could ever have been an angel. If I ever was, it must have been so long ago there's no harm in forgetting it now. These days I only value the reputation of being a gentlemanly sort, and I live as best I can, trying to make myself agreeable. I genuinely love mankind, I've been terribly slandered! Here, staying with you from time to time, my life takes on a kind of reality, and that's what I like best of all. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastical, and so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything's bounded, everything's formulated and geometrical, while over there we've got nothing but indeterminate equations! I wander around here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I turn superstitious. Please don't laugh, that's exactly what I like—turning superstitious. I take on all your habits here: I've grown fond of going to the public baths, would you believe it, and I go steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once and for all, irrevocably, in the shape of some merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing everything she believes. My ideal is to go to church and light a candle in simple, wholehearted faith—upon my word, it is. Then all my suffering would end. I like being treated for illness, too. This spring there was an outbreak of smallpox, and I went and got vaccinated at a foundling hospital—if only you knew how much I enjoyed that day. I subscribed ten roubles to the Slavic cause!... But you're not listening. Do you know, you're not at all well tonight? I know you went to see that doctor yesterday... well, how's your health? What did the doctor say?"
"Fool!" Ivan snapped.
"But you're clever, all the same. Scolding again? I wasn't asking out of sympathy. You don't need to answer. Now the rheumatism's come back again—"
"Fool!" Ivan repeated.
"You keep saying the same thing; but I had such an attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this very day."
"The devil, with rheumatism!"
"Why not, if I sometimes take on fleshly form? I put on flesh, and I take the consequences. Satan sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto."
"What, what—Satan sum et nihil humanum... not bad, for the devil!"
"I'm glad I've finally pleased you."
"But you didn't get that from me." Ivan stopped suddenly, struck. "That never crossed my mind—that's strange."

"C'est du nouveau, n'est-ce pas? This time I'll be honest and explain it to you. Listen: in dreams, and especially in nightmares—from indigestion, or anything else—a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such intricate, real actuality, such events, even a whole world of events woven into such a plot, with such unexpected details, from the most exalted matters down to the last button on a cuff, that I swear Leo Tolstoy himself has never invented the like. And yet such dreams are sometimes had not by writers, but by the most ordinary people—officials, journalists, priests.... The whole subject is a complete mystery. A certain statesman once confessed to me, in fact, that all his best ideas came to him while he was asleep. Well, that's how it is right now—though I'm your hallucination, still, just as in a nightmare, I'm saying original things that hadn't occurred to you before. So I'm not repeating your ideas, and yet I'm only your nightmare, nothing more."
"You're lying. Your whole aim is to convince me you exist separately, and aren't my nightmare, and now you're claiming you're a dream."
"My dear fellow, I've adopted a special method today—I'll explain it to you afterward. Wait, where did I leave off? Oh, yes! I caught cold that time, only not here, but over there."

"Where's over there? Tell me, will you be here long? Can't you go away?" Ivan exclaimed, almost in despair. He stopped pacing, sat down on the sofa, leaned his elbows on the table again, and gripped his head tight in both hands. He yanked off the wet towel and flung it away in irritation. It was clearly no use.

"Your nerves are out of order," the gentleman observed, in an easy, careless, though perfectly polite tone. "You're even angry at me for having caught cold, though it happened in the most natural way. I was rushing off at the time to a diplomatic soirée at the house of a high-ranking lady in Petersburg, one aiming at some influence at the Ministry. Well—evening dress, white tie, gloves—though I was God knows where, and had to fly across space to reach your earth.... Of course it took only an instant, but you know a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes, and imagine, in evening dress and an open waistcoat. Spirits don't freeze, but once you're in fleshly form, well... in short, I didn't think it through, and set off, and you know, out in that ethereal space, in the water above the firmament, there's such a frost... at least, one can hardly call it frost, imagine, a hundred and fifty degrees below zero! You know that game the village girls play—inviting the unwary to lick an axe in thirty degrees of frost, and the tongue freezes to it instantly, and the poor fool tears the skin off, and it bleeds. But that's only at thirty degrees; at a hundred and fifty, I'd imagine just touching your finger to the axe would finish you off... if only there were an axe out there."
"And could there be an axe out there?" Ivan cut in, offhand and disdainful. He was straining with everything he had not to believe in the delusion, not to sink into outright madness.
"An axe?" the guest broke in, surprised.
"Yes—what would happen to an axe out there?" Ivan suddenly cried, with a sort of wild, insistent stubbornness.

"What would become of an axe in space? Quelle idée! If it happened to fall some distance, I imagine it would start flying around the earth without knowing why, like a satellite. Astronomers would calculate the rising and setting of the axe, Gatzuk would put it in his almanac, that's all there is to it."

"You're stupid, horribly stupid," Ivan said, peevishly. "Lie more cleverly, or I won't listen. You want to win me over with realism, to convince me you're real—but I don't want to believe you're real! I won't believe it!"

"But I'm not lying, it's all the truth; the trouble is, the truth is hardly ever amusing. I can see you keep expecting something grand from me, and maybe something fine. That's a great shame, because I can only give what I have—"
"Don't talk philosophy, you jackass!"

"Philosophy, indeed, when my whole right side is numb and I'm moaning and groaning. I've tried the entire medical profession: they diagnose beautifully, they've got the whole of your illness at their fingertips, but they haven't the first idea how to cure it. There was an eager young student here—'You may die,' he told me, 'but you'll know perfectly well what disease you're dying of!' And then there's their way of shunting people off to specialists! 'We only diagnose,' they say, 'go to such-and-such a specialist, he'll cure you.' The old-fashioned doctor who used to cure everything has completely vanished, I promise you—now it's nothing but specialists, and they all advertise in the papers. If something's wrong with your nose, they send you to Paris—there, they say, is a European specialist who cures noses. You go to Paris, he examines your nose; 'I can only treat your right nostril,' he'll tell you, 'I don't treat the left, that's not my specialty—but go to Vienna, there's a specialist there who'll fix your left nostril.' What's a man to do? I turned to folk remedies. A German doctor advised me to rub myself with honey and salt at the bathhouse. Purely to get an extra bath out of it, I went, smeared myself all over, and it did nothing for me at all. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. He sent me a book and some drops, bless him, and just imagine—Hoff's malt extract cured me! I bought it by accident, drank a bottle and a half, and I was ready to dance—it cleared it right up. I decided to write to the papers to thank him, out of pure gratitude, and just imagine, it caused no end of trouble: not a single paper would print my letter. 'It would look far too reactionary,' they said, 'no one will believe it. Le diable n'existe point. You'd better stay anonymous,' they advised me. What good is a thank-you letter if it's anonymous? I laughed it over with the men at the newspaper office. 'It's reactionary to believe in God nowadays,' I said, 'but I'm the devil, so people are allowed to believe in me.' 'We quite understand that,' they said. 'Who doesn't believe in the devil? Still, it won't do, it might damage our reputation. As a joke, if you like.' But I figured as a joke it wouldn't be terribly witty. So it never got printed. And you know, it still stings me to this day. My best feelings—gratitude, for instance—are literally denied me, simply because of my social standing."
"Philosophical reflections again?" Ivan snarled, viciously.

"God forbid, but a man can't help complaining sometimes. I'm a slandered creature. You reproach me every other minute for being stupid. One can tell you're young. My dear fellow, intelligence isn't the only thing! I have, by nature, a kind and cheerful heart. 'I also write vaudevilles of every sort.' You seem to take me for an aged Hlestakov, but my fate is a far more serious one. Before time itself began, by some decree I've never been able to work out, I was predestined 'to deny'—and yet I'm genuinely good-hearted and not the least bit inclined toward negation. 'No, you must go and deny, because without denial there's no criticism, and what would a journal be without a criticism column?' Without criticism there'd be nothing but a single 'hosanna.' But nothing but hosanna isn't enough for life—the hosanna has to be tested in the crucible of doubt, and so on, in that same vein. But I don't meddle in that, I didn't invent it, I'm not answerable for it. Well, they picked their scapegoat, they made me write the criticism column, and so life became possible. We understand that comedy perfectly; I, for instance, simply ask to be annihilated. No, live, they tell me, because there'd be nothing without you. If everything in the universe were sensible, nothing would ever happen. There'd be no events without me, and there have to be events. So against my own grain, I serve to produce events, and do what's irrational, because I'm commanded to. For all their unquestionable intelligence, men take this farce as something serious, and that's their tragedy. They suffer for it, of course... but then again, they live, they live a real life, not a fantastical one, because suffering is life. Without suffering, what pleasure would there be in it? It would turn into one endless church service; it would be holy, but tedious. But what about me? I suffer, and yet I don't live. I'm x in an indeterminate equation. I'm a kind of phantom in life who's lost all beginning and end, and has even forgotten his own name. You're laughing—no, you're not laughing, you're angry again. You're forever angry, all you care about is intelligence, but I'll say it again: I'd give up all this super-stellar existence, all the ranks and honors, just to be transformed into the soul of a merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone, and light candles at God's shrine."
"So even you don't believe in God?" Ivan said, with a smile full of hatred.
"What can I say?—that is, if you're serious—"
"Is there a God, or isn't there?" Ivan cried, with the same savage intensity.
"Ah, so you're serious! My dear fellow, upon my word, I don't know. There! I've said it now!"
"You don't know, but you can see God? No, you're not something apart—you're myself, you're me and nothing more! You're rubbish, you're my fancy!"

"Well, if you like, I hold the same philosophy you do—that much is true. Je pense, donc je suis, that much I know for a fact; everything else, all these worlds, God, even Satan—none of it's proven, to my mind. Does all of that exist on its own, or is it only an emanation of myself, a logical development of my ego, which alone has existed forever? But I'll hurry and stop there, because I believe you're about to jump up and hit me."
"You'd better tell me some story!" Ivan said, wretchedly.

"There's a story on exactly our subject—or rather a legend, not a story. You reproach me with unbelief, you see—you say, but you yourself don't believe. But, my dear fellow, I'm not the only one that way. We're all in quite a muddle over there now, thanks entirely to your science. There used to be atoms, five senses, four elements, and everything hung together somehow. There were even atoms in the ancient world, but since we learned you'd discovered the chemical molecule, and protoplasm, and the devil knows what else, we've had to lower our crest. It's a real mess now—and above all, superstition, scandal; there's just as much scandal among us as among you, you know, a bit more, in fact, and spying too, since we have our own secret police department that takes in private tips. Well, this wild legend belongs to our middle ages—not yours, ours—and no one even among us believes it anymore, except the old ladies weighing eighteen stone, not your old ladies, ours. We have everything you have, I'm letting you in on one of our secrets, out of friendship, though it's forbidden. This legend's about Paradise. There was, they say, here on earth, a thinker and philosopher. He rejected everything—'laws, conscience, faith'—and above all, the afterlife. He died; he expected to go straight into darkness and death, and instead found an afterlife waiting for him. He was astonished and outraged. 'This goes against my principles!' he said. And he was punished for it... that is, forgive me, I'm just repeating what I heard myself, it's only a legend... he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in the dark (we've adopted the metric system, you know), and once he's finished that quadrillion, the gates of heaven will open to him and he'll be forgiven—"
"And what torments do you have over there, besides the quadrillion kilometers?" Ivan asked, with a strange eagerness.

"What torments? Ah, don't ask. In the old days we had every kind, but now they've mostly switched to moral punishments—'the stings of conscience' and all that nonsense. We got that from you too, from the general softening of your manners. And who's better off for it? Only those with no conscience at all, because how can conscience torment someone who hasn't got one? But decent people, with conscience and a sense of honor, suffer for it. Reforms, when the ground hasn't been prepared for them, especially institutions copied wholesale from abroad, do nothing but harm! The old-fashioned fire was better. Well, this man, sentenced to the quadrillion kilometers, stood still, looked around, and lay down across the road. 'I won't go, I refuse on principle!' Take the soul of an enlightened Russian atheist and mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked for three days and nights in the belly of the whale, and you get the character of that thinker lying across the road."
"What did he lie down on, out there?"
"Well, I suppose there was something to lie on. You're not laughing?"
"Bravo!" Ivan cried, still with that same strange eagerness. Now he was listening with unexpected curiosity. "So, is he still lying there now?"
"That's exactly the point—he isn't. He lay there nearly a thousand years, and then he got up and went on."

"What an ass!" Ivan cried, laughing nervously, still seeming to be turning something over intently in his mind. "Does it make any difference whether he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take a billion years to walk it!"
"Much more than that. I don't have a pencil and paper on me, or I could work it out precisely. But he got there long ago, and that's where the story really begins."
"What, he got there? But how did he manage the billion years to do it?"

"Ah, you keep thinking of our present earth! But our present earth may have repeated itself a billion times already. It's gone extinct, been frozen, cracked, shattered into fragments, broken down into its elements, and turned back into 'the water above the firmament,' then a comet again, a sun again, and from the sun it becomes earth once more—and that same sequence may have repeated endlessly, exactly the same down to the last detail, most unseemly and unbearably tedious—"
"Well, well, what happened once he arrived?"

"Why, the very moment the gates of Paradise opened and he walked in, before he'd even been there two seconds by his watch (though to my mind his watch must have long since dissolved into its elements on the way), he cried out that those two seconds alone were worth walking not just a quadrillion kilometers, but a quadrillion quadrillions, raised to the quadrillionth power! In fact, he sang hosanna, and overdid it so thoroughly that some of the more high-minded people there wouldn't shake his hand at first—he'd turned reactionary far too fast, they said. The Russian temperament. I repeat, it's only a legend. Take it for what it's worth. So that's the sort of thinking we still have about such things, even now."

"I've caught you!" Ivan cried, with an almost childish delight, as though he'd finally managed to remember something. "That story about the quadrillion years—I made it up myself! I was seventeen at the time, at the high school. I invented that anecdote and told it to a schoolmate of mine, Korovkin—this was in Moscow.... The story's so distinctive I couldn't have picked it up anywhere else. I thought I'd forgotten it... but I've recalled it without meaning to—I remembered it myself—you didn't tell it to me! A thousand things get remembered like that without a person meaning to, even in men being led to execution... it's come back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You're a dream, not a living creature!"
"From the sheer force with which you deny I exist," the gentleman laughed, "I'm convinced that you believe in me."
"Not in the slightest! I haven't a hundredth of a grain of faith in you!"
"But you do have a thousandth of a grain. Homeopathic doses might be the strongest, after all. Admit it—you've got faith down to the ten-thousandth of a grain."
"Not for a single minute," Ivan cried, furiously. "But I'd like to believe in you," he added, strangely.

"Aha! There's a confession! But I'm good-natured. I'll come to your aid again. Listen, it was I who caught you, not you me. I told you your own forgotten anecdote on purpose, precisely to destroy your faith in me altogether."
"You're lying. The whole point of your visit is to convince me you exist!"

"Just so. But hesitation, suspense, the conflict between belief and disbelief, is sometimes such torture to a conscientious man like yourself that it's better to just go hang oneself. Knowing you're inclined to believe in me, I administered a dose of disbelief by telling you that anecdote. I lead you toward belief and disbelief by turns, and I have my reasons for it. It's the new method. The moment you disbelieve in me completely, you'll turn right around and start insisting to my face that I'm not a dream but a reality. I know you. Then I'll have achieved my goal, which is an honorable one. I'll plant in you only the tiniest grain of faith, and it'll grow into an oak tree—and such an oak tree that, sitting up in it, you'll long to join the ranks of the 'hermits of the wilderness and the holy women,' because that's exactly what you're secretly longing for. You'll dine on locusts, you'll wander off into the wilderness to save your soul!"
"So it's for the salvation of my soul you're working, is it, you scoundrel?"
"One has to do a good deed now and then. How sour-tempered you are!"
"Fool! Did you ever tempt those holy men who ate locusts and prayed seventeen years in the wilderness until they were overgrown with moss?"

"My dear fellow, I've done nothing else my whole existence. One forgets the entire world, and every other world besides, and clings to a single such saint, because he's a very precious diamond. One soul like that, you know, is sometimes worth a whole constellation. We keep our own system of accounting, you understand. The conquest is priceless! And some of them, I promise you, aren't inferior to you in learning, though you won't believe it. They can contemplate such depths of belief and disbelief at the very same instant that sometimes it really does look as if they're a hair's breadth from being 'turned upside down,' as the actor Gorbunov puts it."
"Well, and did you get your nose pulled?"

"My dear fellow," the visitor observed, sententiously, "it's better to get off with your nose pulled than to have no nose at all. As an afflicted marquis once observed, not long ago (he must have been under a specialist's care), confessing to his spiritual father—a Jesuit. I was there myself, it was simply charming. 'Give me back my nose!' he said, beating his breast. 'My son,' the priest said, evasively, 'all things happen according to the inscrutable decrees of Providence, and what looks like misfortune sometimes leads to extraordinary, if unseen, benefits. If stern fate has robbed you of your nose, it works to your advantage that no one can ever pull you by it again.' 'Holy father, that's no comfort,' the despairing marquis cried. 'I'd be delighted to have my nose pulled every single day of my life, if only it were still in its proper place.' 'My son,' the priest sighed, 'you can't expect every blessing all at once. That's grumbling against Providence, which hasn't forgotten you even in this—because if you complain, as you just did, declaring you'd be glad to have your nose pulled for the rest of your life, your wish has already been granted, indirectly, since in losing your nose, you were led by the nose.'"
"Fool, how stupid!" Ivan cried.

"My dear friend, I only meant to amuse you. But I swear that's genuine Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it happened word for word exactly as I've told it. It happened recently, and gave me a great deal of trouble. The unhappy young man shot himself that very night, once he got home. I stayed by his side right to the very end. Those Jesuit confessionals really are my most delightful entertainment in melancholy moments. Here's another incident, from just the other day. A little blonde Norman girl of twenty—a buxom, guileless beauty that would make your mouth water—comes to an old priest. She bends down and whispers her sin through the grating. 'Why, my daughter, have you fallen again already?' the priest cries. 'O Sancta Maria, what am I hearing! Not the same man this time—how long is this going to go on? Aren't you ashamed?' 'Ah, mon père,' the sinner answers, with tears of repentance, 'ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!' Imagine, such an answer! I stepped back. It was the cry of nature, better than innocence itself, if you like. I absolved her sin right there and turned to leave, but was forced to turn back. I heard the priest, through the grating, arranging a meeting with her for that evening—though he was an old man, hard as flint, he fell in an instant! It was nature, the truth of nature asserting its rights! What, turning your nose up again? Angry again? I don't know how to please you—"

"Leave me alone, you're beating on my brain like some haunting nightmare," Ivan moaned, wretchedly, helpless before his own apparition. "I'm bored of you, agonizingly, unbearably bored. I'd give anything to shake you off!"

"I'll say it again, moderate your expectations, don't demand 'everything grand and noble' from me, and you'll see how well we get along," the gentleman said, impressively. "You're really angry with me for not appearing to you in a red glow, with thunder and lightning, with scorched wings, but showing myself instead in such a modest shape. You're wounded, first, in your aesthetic feelings, and second, in your pride. How could such a vulgar devil pay a visit to such a great man as yourself! Yes, there's that romantic streak in you, the one Byelinsky mocked so mercilessly. I can't help it, young man—as I was getting ready to come to you, I did think, as a joke, of appearing in the form of a retired general who'd served in the Caucasus, with the star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat. But I was genuinely afraid to do it, because you'd have thrashed me for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat, instead of at least the Polar Star, or Sirius. And you keep calling me stupid, but mercy on us, I make no claim to be your equal in intelligence. Mephistopheles told Faust he desired evil, but did only good. Well, he can say what he likes—it's quite the opposite with me. I may be the one being in all of creation who loves the truth and genuinely wants good. I was there when the Word, who died on the Cross, rose up into heaven bearing on his breast the soul of the penitent thief. I heard the joyous shrieks of the cherubim, singing and shouting hosanna, and the thunderous rapture of the seraphim that shook heaven and all creation, and I swear to you, by everything sacred, I longed to join the choir and shout hosanna with all of them. The word had all but escaped me, had nearly broken from my lips... you know how susceptible and aesthetically impressionable I am. But common sense—oh, a most unfortunate trait in my character—kept me within proper bounds, and I let the moment pass! Because what would have happened, I thought to myself, what would have happened after my hosanna? Everything on earth would have been snuffed out at once, and no events could have occurred at all. And so, purely out of a sense of duty, and my social position, I was forced to suppress that good moment, and stick to my nasty task. Somebody else takes all the credit for everything good, and nothing but nastiness is left for me. But I don't envy him the honor of a life of idle fraud—I'm not ambitious. Why am I, of all beings in the world, condemned to be cursed by every decent person, even kicked around, since taking on mortal form means I sometimes have to bear those consequences? I know, of course, there's a secret behind it, but they won't tell me the secret for anything, because if I understood its meaning, I might just bellow out hosanna, and the indispensable minus would vanish at once, and good sense would reign supreme over the whole world. And that, of course, would mean the end of everything—even of magazines and newspapers, since who would subscribe to them then? I know that in the end I'll be reconciled. I too will walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until that happens, I sulk and carry out my destiny, even against the grain—which is, to ruin thousands in order to save one. How many souls have had to be ruined, how many honorable reputations destroyed, for the sake of that one righteous man, Job, over whom they made such a fool of me in the old days! Yes, until the secret's revealed, there are two kinds of truth for me—theirs, over there, which I know nothing about so far, and my own. And there's no telling which will turn out to be the better one.... Are you asleep?"
"I might as well be," Ivan groaned, angrily. "All my stupid ideas—outgrown, thrashed out long ago, and tossed aside like a dead carcass—you're serving them back to me as something new!"
"There's just no pleasing you! And here I thought I'd win you over with my literary style. That hosanna in the heavens wasn't bad, was it? And then that ironic tone à la Heine, eh?"
"No, I was never such a lackey! Then how could my own soul have spawned a lackey like you?"
