"My dear fellow, I know a most charming, appealing young Russian gentleman, a young thinker and a great lover of literature and art, author of a promising poem titled The Grand Inquisitor. I was only thinking of him!"
"I forbid you to speak of The Grand Inquisitor," Ivan cried, crimson with shame.
"And the Geological Cataclysm. Remember that? Now that was a poem!"
"Hold your tongue, or I'll kill you!"

"You'll kill me? No, excuse me, I'm going to speak. I came here to treat myself to that very pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of my eager young friends, quivering with hunger for life! 'There are new men,' you decided last spring, right before you set off to come here, 'they propose to tear down everything and start with cannibalism. Foolish fellows—they never asked my advice! I maintain that nothing needs to be torn down, that all we need is to destroy the idea of God in man, that's where the real work begins. That's what we must start with. Oh, blind race, with no understanding! The moment every last man has denied God—and I believe that period, comparable to a geological age, will come to pass—the old conception of the universe will collapse on its own, without any cannibalism, and, what's more, so will the old morality, and everything will begin anew. Men will unite to wring from life everything it can offer, but only for joy and happiness in this present world. Man will be lifted up on a spirit of divine, Titanic pride, and the man-god will appear. Hour by hour, extending his conquest of nature infinitely through will and science, man will feel such lofty joy, hour by hour, in the doing of it, that it will make up for all his old dreams of heavenly joys. Everyone will know he is mortal, and will accept death proudly and calmly, like a god. His pride will teach him it's pointless to grieve that life is only a moment, and he'll love his brother with no need of reward. Love will be enough only for a moment of life, but the very awareness of its brevity will only intensify its fire, fire that today is squandered on dreams of eternal love beyond the grave'—and so on, and so on, in the same vein. Charming!"
Ivan sat with his eyes fixed on the floor, hands pressed to his ears, but he began trembling all over. The voice went on.

"The question now, my young thinker reflected, is whether such a period could ever really come. If it does, everything is settled, and humanity is fixed forever. But since, given man's ingrained stupidity, this can't come about for at least a thousand years, anyone who recognizes the truth even now may fairly order his own life however he pleases, on these new principles. In that sense, 'everything is permitted' for him. What's more, even if this age never arrives at all, since there's no God anyway, and no immortality, the new man may as well become the man-god, even if he's the only one of his kind in the entire world, and, elevated to his new rank, he may cheerfully step over every barrier of the old slave-man's morality, if it comes to that. There's no law for God. Where God stands, that ground is holy. Wherever I stand will become, at once, the foremost place... 'everything is permitted,' and that's the end of it! All very charming; but if you want to swindle someone, why do you need a moral sanction to do it? But that's our modern Russian, through and through. He simply can't bring himself to swindle without a moral sanction for it. He's so terribly in love with the truth—"

The visitor talked on, clearly carried away by his own eloquence, his voice rising louder and louder, watching his host with an ironic eye. But he never got to finish; Ivan suddenly snatched a glass off the table and hurled it at him.

"Ah, mais c'est bête enfin," the man cried, jumping up off the sofa and shaking tea drops off himself. "He remembers Luther's inkstand! He takes me for a dream and throws glasses at a dream! Just like a woman! I suspected you were only pretending to stop up your ears."
A loud, persistent knocking suddenly sounded at the window. Ivan jumped up from the sofa.
"Do you hear? You'd better open it," the visitor cried. "It's your brother Alyosha, with the most interesting and surprising news, I'll bet you anything!"
"Quiet, deceiver, I knew it was Alyosha, I could feel him coming, and of course he hasn't come for nothing—of course he's bringing 'news,'" Ivan exclaimed, frantically.
"Open up, open up for him. There's a snowstorm out there, and he's your brother. Monsieur sait-il le temps qu'il fait? C'est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors."

The knocking went on. Ivan wanted to rush to the window, but something seemed to have chained his arms and legs. He strained with all his might to break free, but in vain. The knocking at the window grew louder and louder. At last the chains broke, and Ivan leapt up off the sofa. He looked around wildly. Both candles had nearly burned out; the glass he'd just thrown at his visitor stood on the table before him, and there was no one on the sofa across the room. The knocking on the window frame continued, insistently, but it was nowhere near as loud as it had seemed in his dream; on the contrary, it was quite muted.
"It wasn't a dream! No, I swear it wasn't a dream, it all just happened!" Ivan cried. He rushed to the window and threw open the sash.
"Alyosha, I told you not to come," he shouted fiercely at his brother. "In two words—what do you want? In two words, do you hear?"
"An hour ago Smerdyakov hanged himself," Alyosha answered, from the yard.
"Come round to the steps, I'll open the door at once," said Ivan, going to let Alyosha in.

title: X. “It Was He Who Said That”
paragraphs: Coming in, Alyosha told Ivan that a little over an hour earlier, Marya Kondratyevna had come running to his rooms to tell him Smerdyakov had taken his own life. "I went in to clear away the samovar, and there he was, hanging from a nail in the wall." When Alyosha asked whether she'd told the police, she said she'd told no one—"but I ran straight to you, I ran the whole way." She seemed completely out of her mind, Alyosha reported, shaking like a leaf. When Alyosha ran with her to the cottage, he found Smerdyakov still hanging there. On the table lay a note: "I end my life of my own will and desire, so that no blame falls on anyone." Alyosha left the note on the table and went straight to the police captain and told him everything. "And from him I came straight here to you," Alyosha finished, looking intently into Ivan's face. He hadn't taken his eyes off him the whole time he told the story, as if something in his expression had struck him.
"Brother," he suddenly cried, "you must be terribly ill. You're looking at me and don't seem to understand what I'm telling you."
"It's a good thing you came," Ivan said, as if brooding, not hearing Alyosha's outburst at all. "I knew he'd hanged himself."
"From whom?"
"I don't know. But I knew it. Did I know it? Yes, he told me. He told me just now."
Ivan stood in the middle of the room, still speaking in that same brooding tone, staring at the floor.
"Who's he?" Alyosha asked, glancing around involuntarily.
"He's slipped away."
Ivan lifted his head and smiled softly.

"He was afraid of you—a dove like you. You're a 'pure cherub.' Dmitri calls you a cherub. Cherub!... the thunderous rapture of the seraphim. What are seraphim, anyway? Maybe a whole constellation. Or maybe that constellation is nothing but a chemical molecule. There's a constellation of the Lion and the Sun. Don't you know it?"

"Brother, sit down," Alyosha said, alarmed. "For goodness' sake, sit down on the sofa! You're delirious—put your head on the pillow, that's it. Would you like a wet towel on your head? It might do you some good."
"Give me the towel—it's on the chair. I just threw it there."

"It's not there. Don't trouble yourself. I know where it is—here," Alyosha said, finding a clean, folded, unused towel by Ivan's dressing table in the other corner of the room. Ivan looked at the towel strangely; memory seemed to flicker back to him for an instant.
"Wait"—he got up from the sofa—"an hour ago I took that new towel from over there and wet it. I wrapped it around my head and threw it down here.... How is it dry? There was no other one."
"You put that towel on your head?" Alyosha asked.
"Yes, and walked up and down the room an hour ago.... Why have the candles burned down so far? What time is it?"
"Nearly midnight."

"No, no, no!" Ivan suddenly cried. "It wasn't a dream. He was here—he was sitting right here, on that sofa. When you knocked at the window, I threw a glass at him... this one. Wait a moment. I was asleep last time, but this dream wasn't a dream. It's happened before. I have dreams now, Alyosha... only they're not dreams, they're reality. I walk around, I talk, I see... even though I'm asleep. But he was sitting right there, on that sofa.... He's frightfully stupid, Alyosha, frightfully stupid." Ivan suddenly laughed and began pacing the room.
"Who's stupid? Who are you talking about, brother?" Alyosha asked again, anxiously.

"The devil! He's taken to visiting me. He's been here twice, almost three times. He teased me for being angry that he's just an ordinary devil and not Satan, with scorched wings, thunder and lightning. But he's not Satan—that's a lie. He's an impostor. He's simply a devil—a petty, trivial devil. He goes to the bathhouse. If you stripped him down, you'd surely find he has a tail, long and smooth like a Great Dane's, a yard long, dun-colored.... Alyosha, you're cold. You've been out in the snow. Would you like some tea? What—is it cold out? Should I have her bring some? C'est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors...."
Alyosha ran to the washstand, wet the towel, got Ivan to sit back down, and wrapped the wet towel around his head. He sat down beside him.

"What were you telling me just now about Lise?" Ivan began again. (He'd grown very talkative.) "I like Lise. I said something nasty about her. It was a lie. I like her... I'm afraid of Katya tomorrow. I'm more afraid of her than of anything. On account of the future. She'll cast me off tomorrow and trample me underfoot. She thinks I'm destroying Mitya out of jealousy over her! Yes, that's what she thinks! But it isn't so. Tomorrow, the cross, but not the gallows. No, I won't hang myself. Do you know, Alyosha, I could never kill myself. Is it because I'm base? I'm not a coward. Is it from love of life? How did I know Smerdyakov had hanged himself? Yes—it was he who told me."
"And you're quite convinced someone was really here?" Alyosha asked.

"Yes, on that sofa, in the corner. You would have chased him off. You did chase him off—he vanished the moment you got here. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know I loved your face? And he is myself, Alyosha. Everything base in me, everything mean and contemptible. Yes, I'm a romantic. He guessed that... though it's slander. He's frightfully stupid, but that works to his advantage. He's got cunning, animal cunning—he knew how to drive me into a fury. He kept taunting me with believing in him, and that's how he got me to listen to him. He played me like a child. He told me a great deal of truth about myself, though—things I'd never have admitted to myself. Do you know, Alyosha," Ivan added, in an intensely earnest, confidential tone, "I'd be terribly glad to think it was him and not me."
"He's worn you out," Alyosha said, looking at his brother with compassion.

"He's been teasing me. And you know, he does it so cleverly, so cleverly. 'Conscience! What is conscience? I make it up for myself. Why does it torment me? Out of habit. From mankind's universal habit, seven thousand years running. So let's give it up, and we'll be gods.' That was him saying it, him!"

"And not you, not you?" Alyosha couldn't help crying out, looking his brother straight in the eye. "Never mind him, anyway—be done with him, forget him. Let him take with him everything you're cursing now, and never come back!"

"Yes, but he's spiteful. He laughed at me. He was insolent, Alyosha," Ivan said, with a shudder of offense. "But he was unfair to me, unfair about a great many things. He told lies about me, to my face. 'Oh, you're about to perform an act of heroic virtue—confessing that you murdered your father, that the valet murdered him at your urging.'"
"Brother," Alyosha broke in, "control yourself. It wasn't you who murdered him. It isn't true!"

"That's what he says, he does, and he knows it. 'You're about to perform an act of heroic virtue, and you don't even believe in virtue—that's what torments you and makes you angry, that's why you're so full of spite.' He said that about me, and he knows exactly what he's saying."
"It's you saying that, not him," Alyosha said, mournfully, "and you're saying it because you're ill and delirious, tormenting yourself."

"No, he knows what he's saying. 'You're going out of pride,' he says. 'You'll stand up and say it was you who killed him, so why do you writhe in horror? You're lying! I despise your opinion, I despise your horror!' He said that about me. 'And do you know you're longing for their praise—"he's a criminal, a murderer, but what a generous soul; he wanted to save his brother, and he confessed."' That's a lie, Alyosha!" Ivan suddenly cried, his eyes blazing. "I don't want the praise of the rabble, I swear I don't! That's a lie! That's why I threw the glass at him, and it shattered against his ugly face."
"Brother, calm down, stop!" Alyosha begged him.

"Yes, he knows how to torment a man. He's cruel," Ivan went on, not listening. "I had a hunch from the start what he'd come for. 'Granting that you're going out of pride, you still had hope that Smerdyakov might be convicted and sent to Siberia, and Mitya would be acquitted, while you'd only face moral condemnation' ('Do you hear that?' he laughed then)—'and some people will even praise you. But now Smerdyakov's dead, he's hanged himself, and who's going to believe you alone now? And yet you're going, you're going, you'll go all the same, you've already decided to go. What are you going for now?' That's horrible, Alyosha. I can't stand questions like that. Who dares to ask me questions like that?"

"Brother," Alyosha broke in—his heart sank with dread, but he still seemed to hope he could bring Ivan back to his senses—"how could he have told you about Smerdyakov's death before I even got here, when no one knew about it yet, and there wasn't time for anyone to know?"

"He told me," Ivan said firmly, refusing to allow any doubt. "It was all he talked about, if you want to know. 'And it would be all right if you actually believed in virtue,' he said. 'It wouldn't matter if they didn't believe you, you'd be going for the sake of principle. But you're a little piglet, just like Fyodor Pavlovitch, and what do you want with virtue? Why go sticking your nose in, if your sacrifice does no one any good? Because you don't even know yourself why you're going! Oh, you'd give a great deal to know yourself why you're going! And have you really made up your mind? You haven't made up your mind. You'll sit up all night deliberating whether to go or not. But you'll go—you know you'll go. You know that no matter which way you decide, the decision doesn't actually depend on you. You'll go because you won't dare not to go. Why won't you dare? You can work that riddle out for yourself. There's a puzzle for you!' He got up and left. You arrived, and he left. He called me a coward, Alyosha! Le mot de l'énigme is that I'm a coward. 'Eagles like that don't soar above the earth.' That was him adding that—him! And Smerdyakov said the same thing. He has to be killed! Katya despises me. I've seen it for a month now. Even Lise will start despising me! 'You're going in order to be praised.' That's a brutal lie! And you despise me too, Alyosha. Now I'm going to hate you again! And I hate the monster too! I hate the monster! I don't want to save the monster. Let him rot in Siberia! He's taken up singing hymns! Oh, tomorrow I'll go, I'll stand in front of them, and spit in their faces!"

He jumped up in a frenzy, flung off the towel, and went back to pacing the room. Alyosha remembered what he'd just said. "I seem to be asleep while awake.... I walk, I talk, I see, but I'm asleep." That seemed to be exactly what was happening now. Alyosha didn't leave his side. The thought crossed his mind to run for a doctor, but he was afraid to leave his brother alone—there was no one he could leave him with. Gradually, Ivan finally lost consciousness altogether. He kept talking, on and on, without stopping, but quite incoherently now, and even had trouble forming the words. Suddenly he staggered violently, but Alyosha caught him in time. Ivan let himself be led to bed. Alyosha undressed him as best he could and put him to bed. He sat watching over him for another two hours. The sick man slept soundly, without stirring, breathing softly and evenly. Alyosha took a pillow and lay down on the sofa, without undressing.

As he drifted off to sleep, he prayed for Mitya and for Ivan. He was beginning to understand Ivan's illness now. "The anguish of a proud will. An earnest conscience!" God, whom Ivan disbelieved in, and His truth, were gaining the upper hand in his heart, a heart that still refused to submit. "Yes," the thought drifted through Alyosha's mind as it rested on the pillow, "yes, if Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan's testimony; but he'll go and give it all the same." Alyosha smiled softly. "God will win out!" he thought. "He'll either rise up into the light of truth, or... he'll perish in hatred, taking revenge on himself and on everyone else for having served a cause he doesn't believe in," Alyosha added, bitterly, and once more he prayed for Ivan.

title: I. The Fatal Day
paragraphs: At ten o'clock in the morning, the day after the events I've just described, the trial of Dmitri Karamazov began in our district court.

I want to say right away that I'm far from claiming to be capable of reporting everything that took place at the trial in full detail, or even in the actual order it happened. I imagine that setting down everything, with a complete explanation of it all, would fill a whole volume—a very large one, at that. So I trust I won't be blamed for sticking to what struck me most. I may have picked out, as most interesting, things that were actually of secondary importance, and left out the most prominent and essential details. But I can see it's better not to apologize any further. I'll do my best, and the reader will see for themselves that I've done what I could.

To begin with, before I get into the courtroom itself, I want to mention what surprised me most that day. As it turned out later, everyone else was surprised by it too. We all knew the case had stirred up enormous interest, that everyone was burning with impatience for the trial to start, that it had been the subject of talk, guesswork, exclamations, and speculation in local society for the past two months. Everyone also knew the case had become known across all of Russia—but even so, we hadn't imagined it had stirred up such burning, intense interest in everyone, not just here among us, but all over the country. That became obvious at the trial that day.

Visitors had arrived not just from the provincial capital, but from several other Russian towns, as well as from Moscow and Petersburg. Among them were lawyers, ladies, and even a few distinguished figures. Every admission ticket had been snatched up. A special area behind the table where the three judges sat had been set aside for the most distinguished and important of the male visitors; a row of armchairs had been placed there—something quite exceptional, never allowed before. A large portion of the audience—not less than half—were women. There were so many lawyers from all over that no one knew where to seat them, since every ticket had long since been eagerly sought out and handed out. At the back of the room, behind the platform, I saw a special partition hastily thrown up, behind which all these lawyers were let in, and they counted themselves lucky just to find standing room there, since every chair had been cleared away to save space, and the crowd behind the partition stood packed shoulder to shoulder the entire time.

Some of the women, especially those who'd traveled from farther off, appeared in the gallery dressed very smartly, but most of the women there had given no thought to dress at all. Their faces betrayed a hysterical, intense, almost morbid curiosity. A peculiar fact—confirmed afterward by a great many observers—was that nearly all the women, or at least the vast majority of them, were on Mitya's side, and in favor of his acquittal. This was probably owing mostly to his reputation as a conqueror of women's hearts. It was known that two rival women would appear in the case. One of them—Katerina Ivanovna—was an object of general fascination. All sorts of extraordinary stories were told about her, astonishing anecdotes about her passion for Mitya despite his crime. Her pride and her "aristocratic connections" were especially dwelt upon (she'd called on hardly anyone in town). People said she meant to petition the government for permission to follow the convict to Siberia and marry him there, somewhere among the mines. Grushenka's appearance in court was awaited with no less impatience. The public was looking forward, with anxious curiosity, to the meeting of the two rivals—the proud, aristocratic young woman and "the courtesan." But Grushenka was a far more familiar figure to the ladies of the district than Katerina Ivanovna. They'd already seen "the woman who ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his unfortunate son," and almost without exception, everyone wondered how father and son could both have fallen so hard for "such an utterly common, ordinary Russian girl, who wasn't even pretty."

In short, there was no end of talk. I know for a fact that several serious family quarrels broke out in our town over Mitya's case. Many wives fought bitterly with their husbands over differing opinions about the terrible affair, and it's only natural that the husbands of these women, far from feeling well disposed toward the prisoner, walked into the courtroom bitterly prejudiced against him. In fact, one can say with fair confidence that the male half of the audience, unlike the female half, was biased against the prisoner. There were plenty of stern, frowning, even vindictive faces. Mitya had, in fact, managed to offend a great many people during his time in town. Some of the visitors, of course, were in excellent spirits and entirely indifferent to Mitya's personal fate. But everyone was interested in the trial itself, and most of the men were certainly hoping to see the criminal convicted—except, perhaps, the lawyers, who were more interested in the legal side of the case than the moral one.

Everyone was excited by the presence of the celebrated lawyer Fetyukovitch. His talent was well known, and this wasn't the first time he'd defended a notorious criminal case out in the provinces. And whenever he defended such a case, it became famous and long remembered across all of Russia. There were stories, too, about our prosecutor and the President of the Court. It was said that Ippolit Kirillovitch was trembling at the thought of facing Fetyukovitch, and that the two had been rivals since the very start of their careers in Petersburg—that our sensitive prosecutor, who always felt someone in Petersburg had wronged him by failing to appreciate his talents properly, was keenly worked up over the Karamazov case, and was even dreaming of rebuilding his flagging fortunes on the strength of it, while Fetyukovitch, people said, was his one great worry. But these rumors weren't quite fair. Our prosecutor wasn't the kind of man to lose heart in the face of danger. On the contrary, his self-confidence grew right along with the danger. It should be noted that our prosecutor was, in general, rather too hasty and morbidly sensitive. He'd throw his whole soul into a case and work at it as if his entire fate and fortune depended on the outcome. This was the subject of some ridicule in legal circles, since it was precisely this trait that had earned our prosecutor a wider reputation than his modest standing would otherwise have warranted. People laughed especially at his passion for psychology. In my opinion, they were wrong, and our prosecutor was, I believe, a man of greater depth than was generally credited. But with his delicate health, he'd failed to make his mark at the outset of his career, and had never quite made up for it since.

As for the President of our Court, I can only say he was a humane, cultured man, with a practical grasp of his work and progressive views. He was fairly ambitious, but didn't concern himself much with his future career. The great aim of his life was to be a man of advanced ideas. He was also a man of good connections and property. He felt, as we learned afterward, rather strongly about the Karamazov case—but from a social standpoint, not a personal one. He was interested in it as a social phenomenon, in how it might be classified, in its character as a product of our social conditions, as typical of the national character, and so on, and so forth. His attitude toward the personal side of the case, its tragic significance, and the people caught up in it, including the prisoner, was fairly indifferent and abstract—which was perhaps, indeed, fitting.

The courtroom was packed and overflowing long before the judges appeared. Our courtroom is the finest hall in town—spacious, high-ceilinged, and good for carrying sound. To the right of the judges, who sat on a raised platform, a table and two rows of chairs had been set up for the jury. On the left was the place for the prisoner and the counsel for the defense. In the middle of the courtroom, near the judges, stood a table holding the "material evidence." On it lay Fyodor Pavlovitch's white silk dressing gown, stained with blood; the fatal brass pestle used in the supposed murder; Mitya's shirt, with its blood-stained sleeve; his coat, stained with blood in patches around the pocket where he'd kept his handkerchief; the handkerchief itself, stiff with blood and by now gone quite yellow; the pistol Mitya had loaded at Perhotin's, meaning to kill himself, and quietly taken from him at Mokroe by Trifon Borissovitch; the envelope the three thousand roubles had been kept in for Grushenka, the narrow pink ribbon it had been tied with, and a number of other items I don't recall. Farther back in the hall stood the seats for the public. But just in front of the railing, a few chairs had been set out for witnesses who remained in the courtroom after giving their testimony.

At ten o'clock the three judges arrived—the President, one honorary justice of the peace, and one other. The prosecutor, of course, came in right after them. The President was a short, stout, thickset man of about fifty, with a dyspeptic complexion, dark hair going gray and cut short, and a red ribbon on his coat, of some order or other I don't remember. The prosecutor struck me, and everyone else too, as looking particularly pale, almost greenish. His face seemed to have grown thinner all of a sudden, perhaps overnight, since I'd seen him looking perfectly normal only two days before. The President began by asking the court whether all the jurymen were present.

But I can see I can't keep going on like this—partly because there were things I didn't hear, others I didn't notice, and others I've since forgotten, but mostly because, as I said before, I simply have neither the time nor the space to record everything that was said and done. I only know that neither side raised many objections to the jurors. I remember the twelve jurymen: four were minor town officials, two were merchants, and six were peasants and tradesmen from the town. I remember that long before the trial, people kept asking, with some surprise, especially the ladies: "Can such a delicate, complicated, psychological case really be handed over for decision to petty officials, and even peasants?" and "What could an official, let alone a peasant, possibly understand about a matter like this?" All four of the officials on the jury were, in fact, men of no particular consequence, low in rank. Except for one who was somewhat younger, they were all gray-headed men, little known in society, who'd spent their lives vegetating on pitiful salaries, and who probably had aging, unremarkable wives and swarms of children, some of them likely without shoes or stockings. At best, they spent their free time over cards, and had certainly never read a single book. The two merchants looked respectable enough, but were strangely silent and stolid. One was clean-shaven, dressed in the European style; the other wore a small gray beard, with a red ribbon and some sort of medal around his neck. There's no need to say much about the tradesmen and peasants. The tradesmen of Skotoprigonyevsk are practically peasants themselves, and even work the land. Two of them wore European dress too, and, perhaps for that very reason, looked dirtier and less presentable than the rest. So that one might well wonder, as I did the moment I looked them over, "what could men like that possibly make of a case like this?" And yet their faces left a strangely commanding, almost menacing, impression; they were stern, and frowning.

At last the President opened the case concerning the murder of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. I don't quite recall exactly how he described it. The court usher was told to bring in the prisoner, and Mitya appeared. A hush fell over the courtroom. You could have heard a fly buzz. I don't know how it struck others, but Mitya made a thoroughly unfavorable impression on me. He looked like an absolute dandy in a brand-new frock coat. I heard afterward that he'd ordered it specially from his own tailor in Moscow, who kept his measurements on file. He wore immaculate black kid gloves and exquisite linen. He walked in with his long, yard-length strides, staring stiffly straight ahead, and sat down in his place looking entirely unruffled.

At that same moment, the counsel for the defense, the celebrated Fetyukovitch, walked in, and a kind of hushed murmur passed through the courtroom. He was a tall, lean man, with long, thin legs, extremely long, thin, pale fingers, a clean-shaven face, neatly combed, rather short hair, and thin lips that would occasionally curl into something between a sneer and a smile. He looked to be about forty. His face would have been pleasant enough if not for his eyes—small and inexpressive in themselves, set remarkably close together, with only his thin, long nose dividing them. There was, in fact, something strikingly bird-like about his whole face. He wore evening dress and a white tie.

I remember the President's first questions to Mitya—about his name, his occupation, and so on. Mitya answered sharply, and his voice came out so unexpectedly loud that it made the President start and look at the prisoner in surprise. Then came a reading of the list of people who would take part in the proceedings—that is, the witnesses and experts. It was a long list. Four of the witnesses weren't present—Miüsov, who'd given testimony at the preliminary inquiry but was now in Paris; Madame Hohlakov and Maximov, both absent through illness; and Smerdyakov, on account of his sudden death, of which an official police statement was submitted. The news of Smerdyakov's death set off a sudden stir and murmur through the room. Many in the audience, of course, hadn't yet heard about the sudden suicide. What struck people most of all was Mitya's sudden outburst. The instant the statement about Smerdyakov's death was read out, he cried out loudly from his seat:
"He was a dog, and he died like a dog!"

I remember how his counsel rushed over to him, and how the President addressed him, warning him that strict measures would follow if such an outburst happened again. Mitya nodded, and in a subdued voice repeated several times, abruptly, to his counsel, showing no sign of regret:
"I won't do it again, I won't. It slipped out. I won't do it again."

And of course, this brief episode did him no good at all with the jury or the public. His character had shown itself, and it spoke for itself. It was still under the influence of this incident that the opening statement was read out. It was fairly short, but detailed. It set out only the chief reasons he'd been arrested, why he had to stand trial, and so on. And yet it made a great impression on me. The clerk read it loudly and clearly. The whole tragedy suddenly unfolded before us, concentrated, sharply outlined, in a fatal and pitiless light. I remember how, immediately after it was read, the President asked Mitya, in a loud, impressive voice:
"Prisoner, do you plead guilty?"
Mitya suddenly rose from his seat.

"I plead guilty to drunkenness and dissipation," he exclaimed, again in a startling, almost frenzied voice, "to idleness and debauchery. I meant to become an honest man for good, right at the very moment fate struck me down. But I am not guilty of that old man's death—my enemy, my father. No, no, I'm not guilty of robbing him! I couldn't be. Dmitri Karamazov is a scoundrel, but he's no thief."

He sat back down, visibly trembling all over. The President again, briefly but firmly, warned him to answer only what was asked and not go off into irrelevant outbursts. Then he ordered the proceedings to continue. All the witnesses were brought forward to take the oath. That was when I saw them all together for the first time. The prisoner's brothers, however, were permitted to give testimony without taking the oath. After a few words from the priest and the President, the witnesses were led out and seated as far apart from one another as possible. Then they began calling them up, one by one.

title: II. Dangerous Witnesses
paragraphs: I don't know whether the witnesses for the defense and the prosecution were sorted into groups by the President, or whether some set order had been arranged for calling them. But no doubt it was. I only know the prosecution's witnesses were called first. I'll say again that I don't mean to describe every single question step by step. Besides, my account would be somewhat redundant, since the whole course of the testimony was gathered up and cast in a sharp, telling light in the closing speeches for the prosecution and the defense, and I took down parts of those two remarkable speeches in full, which I'll quote in due course, along with one extraordinary and entirely unexpected episode that occurred just before the closing speeches, and which undoubtedly shaped the grim and fateful outcome of the trial.

I'll only note that from the very first moments of the trial, one peculiar feature of the case stood out and was noticed by everyone: the overwhelming strength of the prosecution's case compared to what the defense had to work with. Everyone realized from the first moment that the facts were falling into place around a single point, and the whole horrifying, bloody crime was gradually being laid bare. Everyone, I think, felt from the start that the matter was beyond dispute, that there was no real doubt about it, that there could hardly be any argument, and that the defense was purely a formality, and that the prisoner was guilty—plainly, conclusively guilty. I imagine even the ladies, so impatiently hoping for the acquittal of their fascinating prisoner, were nonetheless, every one of them, convinced of his guilt. What's more, I believe they'd have been disappointed if his guilt hadn't been so firmly established, since that would have taken the edge off the final scene of the criminal's acquittal. That he would be acquitted, all the ladies, strange as it sounds, were absolutely certain, right up to the very last moment. "He's guilty, but he'll be acquitted, out of humanity, in keeping with the new ideas, the new sentiments now in fashion," and so on, and so forth. And that's why they'd crowded into the courtroom so impatiently. The men were more interested in the contest between the prosecutor and the famous Fetyukovitch. Everyone wondered, and asked themselves, what even a talent like Fetyukovitch's could possibly make of such a hopeless case; and so they followed his moves, step by step, with rapt attention.

But Fetyukovitch remained a mystery to everyone right up to the very end, up to his closing speech. Experienced observers suspected he had some plan, that he was working toward some particular goal, but it was almost impossible to guess what it was. His confidence and self-assurance, though, were unmistakable. People noted, too, with a certain pleasure, that after such a short stay among us—no more than three days, perhaps—he'd managed to master the case so thoroughly, had "studied it down to the last detail." Afterward, people described with real relish how cleverly he'd "taken apart" all the prosecution's witnesses, tripping them up wherever he could, and, what's more, had cast doubt on their characters, and so diminished the weight of their testimony. But it was assumed he was doing this more or less for sport, so to speak, for professional glory, to show that nothing in the standard playbook had been left out, since everyone was convinced he couldn't achieve any real good by discrediting the witnesses this way, and that he probably knew that better than anyone, having some plan of his own held in reserve, some hidden weapon of defense he'd spring at the right moment. But in the meantime, aware of his own strength, he seemed to simply be amusing himself.

So, for instance, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch's old servant, who'd given the most damning piece of testimony about the open door, was examined, the defense counsel practically pounced on him when his turn came to question him. It should be noted that Grigory entered the hall composed, almost stately, not in the least fazed by the grandeur of the court or the vast audience listening to him. He gave his evidence as confidently as if he were talking with his own Marfa—perhaps a bit more respectfully. It was impossible to trip him into contradicting himself. The prosecutor first questioned him in detail about the Karamazov family's domestic life. The family picture that emerged was garish and unflattering. It was plain, to both ear and eye, that the witness was guileless and impartial. Despite his deep reverence for the memory of his late master, he still testified that the master had been unjust to Mitya, and "hadn't raised his children the way he should have. He'd have been eaten alive by lice as a boy, if it hadn't been for me," he added, describing Mitya's early childhood. "And it wasn't right of the father, either, to cheat his son out of his mother's property, which was rightfully his."

When the prosecutor asked what grounds he had for claiming Fyodor Pavlovitch had wronged his son in their financial dealings, Grigory, to everyone's surprise, had no proof at all to offer, yet he still insisted the arrangement with the son had been "unfair," that he "ought to have paid him several thousand roubles more." I should note, incidentally, that the prosecutor put this same question—whether Fyodor Pavlovitch had really withheld part of Mitya's inheritance—with marked persistence to every witness who might conceivably know, Alyosha and Ivan included, but got no precise information out of anyone; all of them claimed it was true, but none could produce any definite proof. Grigory's account of the scene at the dinner table, when Dmitri had burst in and beaten his father, threatening to come back and kill him, left a sinister impression on the court, especially since the old servant's composure in telling it, his sparing use of words, and his peculiar turns of phrase, carried as much weight as eloquence would have. He noted that he wasn't angry at Mitya for knocking him down and striking him in the face; he'd forgiven him long ago, he said. Of the late Smerdyakov, crossing himself, he remarked that the boy had been a capable lad, but slow-witted and afflicted, and, worse still, a nonbeliever—and that it was Fyodor Pavlovitch and his eldest son who'd taught him to be that way. But he defended Smerdyakov's honesty with something close to warmth, and recounted how Smerdyakov had once found his master's money lying in the yard, and, instead of hiding it, had brought it straight to his master, who'd rewarded him with a gold piece for it, and trusted him completely from that day forward. He stubbornly insisted the door to the garden had been open. But he was asked so many questions I can't remember them all.

At last the defense counsel began to cross-examine him, and his very first question was about the envelope Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have put three thousand roubles into, for "a certain person." "Have you ever actually seen it—you, who waited so closely on your master for so many years?" Grigory answered that he hadn't seen it, and had never heard a word about the money from anyone, "until it was on everybody's lips." Fetyukovitch put this same question about the envelope to everyone who could conceivably have known of it, just as persistently as the prosecutor had pressed his question about Dmitri's inheritance, and got the same answer from all of them: no one had seen the envelope, though many had heard talk of it. From the very start, everyone noticed how doggedly Fetyukovitch stuck to this subject.

"Now, with your permission, I'll ask you a question," Fetyukovitch said, suddenly and unexpectedly. "What exactly was that balsam, or rather decoction, made of, which, as we've learned from the preliminary inquiry, you used that evening to rub into your lumbago, hoping to cure it?"
Grigory stared blankly at the questioner, and after a brief pause muttered, "There was saffron in it."
"Just saffron? Nothing else you can recall?"
"There was milfoil in it too."
"And pepper, perhaps?" Fetyukovitch asked.
"Yes, there was pepper too."
"And so on. All dissolved in vodka?"
"In spirits."
A faint ripple of laughter passed through the courtroom.
"You see—in spirits. After rubbing your back, I believe, you drank what was left in the bottle, along with a particular pious prayer, known only to your wife?"
"I did."
"Did you drink much? Roughly speaking—a glass, two glasses?"
"Might have been a whole tumbler."
"A whole tumbler, even. Maybe a tumbler and a half?"
Grigory didn't answer. He seemed to see where this was going.
"A glass and a half of pure spirits—that's not bad at all, is it? You might well have seen the gates of heaven open, not just a door into the garden?"
Grigory stayed silent. There was another laugh in the courtroom. The President stirred.
"Do you know, as a fact," Fetyukovitch pressed on, "whether you were awake or not, when you saw that open door?"
"I was on my feet."
"That's not proof you were awake." (More laughter in the court.) "Could you have answered, at that very moment, if someone had asked you a question—say, what year it was?"
"I don't know."
"And do you know what year it is now, Anno Domini?"
Grigory stood there with a baffled expression, staring straight at his tormentor. Strangely enough, it seemed he really didn't know what year it was.
"But perhaps you can at least tell me how many fingers you have on your hands?"
"I'm a servant," Grigory said suddenly, in a loud, clear voice. "If my betters see fit to make a fool of me, it's my duty to bear it."

Fetyukovitch seemed slightly taken aback, and the President stepped in, reminding him to keep to more relevant questions. Fetyukovitch bowed with dignity and said he had no further questions for the witness. The public and the jury were, of course, left with a seed of doubt about the testimony of a man who, while undergoing a certain kind of treatment, might have seen "the gates of heaven," and who didn't even know what year he was living in. But before Grigory left the stand, one more thing happened. The President, turning to the prisoner, asked whether he had anything to say about the last witness's testimony.

"Except about the door, everything he's said is true," Mitya cried, in a loud voice. "For picking the lice off me, I thank him; for forgiving my blows, I thank him. The old man has been honest his whole life, and as loyal to my father as seven hundred poodles."
"Prisoner, mind your language," the President warned him.
"I'm no poodle," Grigory muttered.
"Fine, then I'm the poodle," Mitya cried. "If it's an insult, I'll take it on myself, and I beg his pardon. I was a beast to him, and cruel. I was cruel to Aesop too."
"What Aesop?" the President asked, sternly, again.
"Oh, Pierrot... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch."
The President warned Mitya again, and yet again, firmly and very sternly, to be more careful in his language.
"You are hurting yourself in the eyes of your judges."

The defense counsel proved just as skillful in handling Rakitin's testimony. I should mention that Rakitin was one of the prosecution's leading witnesses, one the prosecutor placed great weight on. It turned out he knew everything; his knowledge was astonishing, he'd been everywhere, seen everything, talked to everyone, knew every detail of Fyodor Pavlovitch's biography and that of every Karamazov. As for the envelope, true, he'd only heard about it from Mitya himself. But he described Mitya's exploits at the Metropolis down to the smallest detail—every compromising thing he'd said and done—and told the story of Captain Snegiryov's "wisp of tow." Even Rakitin, though, couldn't say anything definite about Mitya's inheritance, and stuck to contemptuous generalities on that point.

"Who could say which of them was in the wrong, which owed the other, with that mad Karamazov habit of tangling everything up so no one could make heads or tails of it?" He attributed the tragic crime to habits ingrained over generations of serfdom, and to the distressed state of Russia, caused by the lack of proper institutions. He was, in fact, given a certain latitude to speak freely. This was the first occasion on which Rakitin got to show what he could do, and he drew real attention. The prosecutor knew the witness was preparing a magazine article on the case, and later, in his own closing speech, as we'll see, quoted several ideas straight from that article, showing he'd already seen it. The picture the witness painted was a dark and sinister one, and it considerably strengthened the case for the prosecution. On the whole, Rakitin's speech captivated the public with its independence of thought and the extraordinary nobility of its ideas. There were even two or three bursts of applause when he spoke of serfdom and the distressed state of Russia.

But Rakitin, in his youthful enthusiasm, made a small slip, which the defense counsel at once shrewdly seized on. Answering certain questions about Grushenka, and swept up in the loftiness of his own sentiments and in his own success, which he was, of course, well aware of, he went so far as to refer to Agrafena Alexandrovna rather contemptuously as "Samsonov's kept mistress." He'd have given a great deal to take those words back afterward, because Fetyukovitch caught him out on it immediately. And all because Rakitin hadn't reckoned on the lawyer managing to become so intimately acquainted with every detail in such a short time.

"Allow me to ask," the defense counsel began, with the most affable, even respectful smile, "are you, by any chance, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, The Life of the Late Elder Father Zossima, published by the diocesan authorities, full of profound and pious reflections, and preceded by an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I've just had the pleasure of reading?"
"I didn't write it for publication... it was published afterward," Rakitin muttered, oddly rattled, almost ashamed.

"Oh, excellent! A thinker like yourself can, and indeed should, take the broadest possible view of every social question. Your highly instructive pamphlet has circulated widely, thanks to the bishop's patronage, and has done a good deal of visible good.... But here's the main thing I wanted to learn from you. You just stated that you were very closely acquainted with Madame Svyetlov." (I should note that Grushenka's surname was Svyetlov. I heard it for the first time that day, during the trial.)
"I can't answer for every one of my acquaintances.... I'm a young man... and who can be held responsible for everyone they happen to meet?" Rakitin cried, flushing all over.

"I understand, I understand perfectly," Fetyukovitch cried, as if he too were embarrassed, and hurrying to excuse himself. "You, like anyone else, might well take an interest in getting acquainted with a young, beautiful woman who was happy to entertain the cream of the local young men, but... I only wanted to know... It's come to my attention that Madame Svyetlov was especially eager, a couple of months ago, to make the acquaintance of the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and promised you twenty-five roubles if you'd bring him to her in his monastic robes. And that this actually took place on the very evening the terrible crime now under investigation was committed. You did bring Alexey Karamazov to Madame Svyetlov—and did you receive the twenty-five roubles from Madame Svyetlov as your reward? That's what I'd like to hear from you."
"It was a joke.... I don't see what interest that could possibly hold for you.... I took it as a joke... meaning to give it back later...."
"So you did take it—but you haven't given it back yet... or have you?"
"That's beside the point," Rakitin muttered. "I refuse to answer questions like that.... Of course I'll give it back."

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch announced he had no further questions for the witness. Mr. Rakitin left the witness box not entirely without a stain on his reputation. The effect of his lofty idealism was somewhat dulled, and the look on Fetyukovitch's face as he watched him walk away seemed to suggest to the public, "here's a fine specimen of the high-minded people accusing him." I recall that this episode, too, didn't pass without an outburst from Mitya. Enraged by the tone Rakitin had used about Grushenka, he suddenly shouted "Bernard!" When, after Rakitin's cross-examination, the President asked the prisoner if he had anything to say, Mitya cried out loudly:
"Since I've been arrested, he's borrowed money from me! He's a contemptible Bernard, and an opportunist, and he doesn't believe in God—he took the bishop for a fool!"

Mitya was, of course, reprimanded again for his intemperate language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov's testimony was also a failure, though for an entirely different reason. He appeared in ragged, filthy clothes, muddy boots, and despite the watchfulness and practiced eye of the court officers, turned out to be hopelessly drunk. Asked about Mitya's assault on him, he refused to answer.
"God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will make it up to me, over there."
"Who told you not to tell? Who are you talking about?"
"Ilusha, my little boy. 'Father, father, how he insulted you!' He said that, at the stone. He's dying now...."

The captain suddenly broke into sobs, and dropped to his knees in front of the President. He was hurriedly led away, amid laughter from the public. Whatever effect the prosecutor had hoped for fell entirely flat.

Fetyukovitch kept seizing every opportunity, astonishing people more and more with his minute grasp of the case. Trifon Borissovitch's testimony, for instance, made a strong impression—one that, naturally, was very damaging to Mitya. He calculated, practically on his fingers, that on his first visit to Mokroe, Mitya must have spent three thousand roubles, "or not far off it. Just think what he threw away on those gypsy girls alone! And as for our poor peasants, it wasn't a matter of tossing a half rouble into the street—he gave them presents of twenty-five roubles a man, at the very least, never less than that. And how much money was simply stolen from him! And if anyone did steal, he never left a receipt behind. How could you ever catch the thief, when he was flinging money around the whole time? Our peasants are thieves, you know, they've no care at all for their souls. And the way he carried on with the girls, our village girls! They've been living high ever since, I tell you, they used to be poor as church mice." He recalled, in fact, every single item of expense, and added it all up. So the notion that only fifteen hundred had actually been spent, and the rest set aside in a little pouch, came to seem inconceivable.

"I saw three thousand roubles, plain as day, right there in his hands, I saw it with my own eyes; I should think I know how to count money," Trifon Borissovitch cried, doing his level best to satisfy "his betters."

When it was Fetyukovitch's turn to cross-examine him, he barely bothered trying to refute the testimony itself, and instead began asking about an incident during the first bout of carousing at Mokroe, a month before the arrest, when Timofey and another peasant named Akim had picked a hundred roubles up off the floor in the hallway, dropped by Mitya while he was drunk, and handed it over to Trifon Borissovitch, receiving a rouble each for their trouble. "Well," the lawyer asked, "did you give that hundred roubles back to Mr. Karamazov?" Trifon Borissovitch squirmed uselessly.... He was forced, once the peasants had been questioned, to admit to finding the hundred roubles, only adding that he'd returned every kopeck of it to Dmitri Fyodorovitch, "in perfect honesty, and it's only because his honor was in his cups at the time that he doesn't remember it." But since he'd denied the whole business of the hundred roubles until the peasants were called in to prove it, his claim about returning the money to Mitya was, naturally, met with great suspicion. So one more of the prosecution's most dangerous witnesses was discredited.

The same thing happened with the Poles. They took a proud, independent stance; they loudly declared they'd both served the Crown, and that "Pan Mitya" had offered them three thousand roubles "to buy their honor," and that they'd seen a great deal of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch peppered his sentences with a tremendous number of Polish words, and seeing that this only raised his standing in the eyes of the President and the prosecutor, grew more and more pompous, and finally switched entirely to Polish. But Fetyukovitch caught them too, in his snares. Trifon Borissovitch, recalled to the stand, was forced, despite all his dodging, to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had swapped in a different deck of cards for the one he'd supplied, and that Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated during the game. Kalganov confirmed this, and both Poles left the witness box with their reputations in tatters, amid laughter from the public.

Then exactly the same thing happened with almost every one of the prosecution's most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to cast a shadow over every one of them, dismissing them one after another with a certain quiet mockery. The lawyers and legal experts were lost in admiration, though they couldn't quite work out what good purpose it all served, since everyone, I repeat, felt the prosecution's case couldn't really be refuted, that it was only growing more overwhelming and tragic by the moment. But from the confidence of this "great magician," they could see he remained perfectly serene, and they waited, sensing that "a man like that" hadn't come all the way from Petersburg for nothing, and wasn't the sort to go home empty-handed.

title: III. The Medical Experts And A Pound Of Nuts
paragraphs: The testimony of the medical experts, too, did the prisoner little good. And it turned out later that Fetyukovitch hadn't been counting on it for much. The medical line of defense had only been pursued at Katerina Ivanovna's insistence, since she'd specially sent for a celebrated doctor from Moscow. The defense, of course, stood to lose nothing by it, and might, with luck, gain something. There was, however, a distinctly comic element to it, owing to the doctors' disagreement among themselves. The medical experts were the famous Moscow doctor, our own Doctor Herzenstube, and the young Doctor Varvinsky. The latter two also appeared as witnesses for the prosecution.

The first called as an expert witness was Doctor Herzenstube. He was a gray, bald old man of seventy, of medium height and sturdy build. Everyone in town held him in great esteem and respect. He was a conscientious doctor, an excellent and devout man, a Herrnhuter, or Moravian Brother—I'm not entirely sure which. He'd lived among us for many years and carried himself with remarkable dignity. He was kind-hearted and humane. He treated the poor and the peasants for nothing, visited them in their slums and huts, and left money behind for medicine, but he was as stubborn as a mule. Once an idea had lodged in his head, nothing could shake it loose. Nearly everyone in town knew, incidentally, that the famous Moscow doctor had, within his first two or three days among us, made some extremely insulting remarks about Doctor Herzenstube's competence. Although the Moscow doctor charged twenty-five roubles a visit, several people in town were glad to take advantage of his presence, and rushed to consult him no matter the cost. All of them, naturally, had previously been Doctor Herzenstube's patients, and the celebrated doctor had criticized his treatment with real harshness. In the end, he'd taken to asking each patient the moment he saw them, "Well, who's been stuffing you full of nostrums? Herzenstube? Heh heh!" Doctor Herzenstube, of course, heard about all this, and now all three doctors appeared, one after another, to be examined.

Doctor Herzenstube flatly declared that the abnormality of the prisoner's mental faculties was self-evident. Then, giving his reasons for this opinion, which I'll skip over here, he added that the abnormality wasn't only apparent in many of the prisoner's past actions, but was visible even now, at this very moment. Asked to explain how it was apparent right now, the old doctor, with simple, guileless directness, pointed out that the prisoner, on entering the courtroom, had worn "an extraordinary expression, remarkable given the circumstances"; that he'd "marched in like a soldier, staring straight ahead, though it would have been more natural for him to look to the left, where the ladies were sitting among the public, seeing as he's such a great admirer of the fair sex, and must be very curious what the ladies are saying about him just now," the old man concluded, in his peculiar way of speaking.

I should add that he spoke Russian fluently, but every sentence came out shaped in the German style, which didn't trouble him in the least, since it had always been one of his particular vanities to believe he spoke Russian perfectly—better, in fact, than Russians themselves. He was also very fond of Russian proverbs, always insisting that Russian proverbs were the finest, most expressive sayings in the whole world. I might note, too, that in conversation, through simple absent-mindedness, he often forgot the most ordinary words, which sometimes slipped clean out of his head, even ones he knew perfectly well. The same thing happened when he spoke German, and at such moments he'd always wave a hand in front of his face, as if trying to catch the missing word out of the air, and nothing could persuade him to go on speaking until he'd found it. His remark that the prisoner ought to have looked at the ladies when he entered set off an amused murmur in the audience. All our ladies were quite fond of the old doctor; they also knew that, having spent his whole life a bachelor and a devout man of exemplary conduct, he regarded women as lofty, elevated creatures. So his unexpected remark struck everyone as very odd indeed.

The Moscow doctor, questioned in his turn, repeated firmly and emphatically that he considered the prisoner's mental state abnormal in the highest degree. He spoke at length, and with great erudition, about "aberration" and "mania," arguing that from all the facts gathered, the prisoner had undoubtedly been in a state of mental aberration for several days before his arrest, and that if he had in fact committed the crime, it must, even if he was conscious of it at the time, have been nearly involuntary, since he lacked the power to control the morbid impulse gripping him.

But setting aside temporary aberration, the doctor also diagnosed a mania, which, in his words, threatened to lead to complete insanity down the road. (I should note I'm reporting this in my own words; the doctor himself used highly learned, technical language.) "All his actions run contrary to common sense and logic," he went on. "Setting aside what I haven't personally witnessed—that is, the crime itself and the whole catastrophe—the day before yesterday, while speaking with me, he had an inexplicably fixed look in his eyes. He burst out laughing unexpectedly, when there was nothing at all to laugh at. He showed constant, unaccountable irritability, using strange words—'Bernard!' 'Ethics!'—and others equally out of place." But the doctor detected the mania most clearly, he said, in the fact that the prisoner couldn't even mention the three thousand roubles he believed he'd been cheated out of without extraordinary agitation, even though he could speak comparatively calmly about other misfortunes and grievances. By all accounts, in the past too, whenever the subject of the three thousand roubles came up, he'd fly into an absolute frenzy—and yet he was, by all reports, a man indifferent to money, not at all grasping.

"As for my learned colleague's opinion," the Moscow doctor added, ironically, in closing, "that the prisoner, on entering the courtroom, would naturally have looked at the ladies rather than straight ahead, I'll only say that, setting aside the sheer whimsy of the theory, it's fundamentally unsound. Because while I fully agree that the prisoner, entering the courtroom where his fate is to be decided, wouldn't naturally stare straight ahead in that fixed way, and that this may indeed be a sign of his abnormal mental state, I maintain, at the same time, that he wouldn't naturally look to the left, toward the ladies, but rather to the right, to find his legal counsel, on whose help all his hopes rest, and on whose defense his entire future depends." The doctor delivered his opinion with firm, emphatic conviction.

But it was the unexpected pronouncement of Doctor Varvinsky that added the final touch of comedy to the experts' disagreement. In his opinion, the prisoner was now, and had been all along, in a perfectly normal state, and although he'd certainly been nervous and exceedingly agitated before his arrest, this could be traced to several perfectly obvious causes—jealousy, anger, continual drunkenness, and so on. But this nervous state wouldn't amount to the mental aberration just described. As for whether the prisoner should have looked to the left or the right upon entering the courtroom, "in his modest opinion," the prisoner would naturally look straight ahead on entering, exactly as he had done, since that was where the judges sat, the men on whom his fate depended. So it was precisely by looking straight ahead that he'd shown his perfectly normal state of mind at present. The young doctor closed out his "modest" testimony with a touch of heat.
"Bravo, doctor!" Mitya cried, from his seat. "Exactly so!"

Mitya was, of course, reprimanded, but the young doctor's opinion had a decisive effect on the judges and the public, and, as it turned out later, everyone agreed with him. But Doctor Herzenstube, called as a witness, proved quite unexpectedly useful to Mitya. As a longtime resident of the town who'd known the Karamazov family for years, he offered a few facts of considerable value to the prosecution, and then suddenly, as if recalling something, added:

"But the poor young man might have had a very different life, for he had a good heart both as a child and after childhood—that much I know. But the Russian proverb says, 'One head is good, but if another clever man comes to visit him, it'd be even better, for then there'd be two heads instead of just one.'"

"One head is good, but two are better," the prosecutor put in, impatiently. He knew the old man's habit of speaking slowly and deliberately, indifferent to the impression he made or the delay he caused, and prizing his flat, dull, ever-gleeful German wit far too highly. The old man loved cracking jokes.

"Oh yes, that's just what I say," he went on, stubbornly. "One head is good, but two are much better, only he never met that second clever head, and his wits went astray. Where did they go? I've forgotten the word." He went on, waving his hand in front of his eyes, "Oh, yes—spazieren."
"Wandering?"

"Oh, yes, wandering, that's just what I say. Well, his wits went off wandering and fell into such a deep hole that he lost himself entirely. And yet he was a grateful, sensitive boy. Oh, I remember him very well, a little fellow so high, left neglected by his father in the back yard, running around without shoes on his feet, his little breeches hanging by a single button."
A note of real feeling and tenderness suddenly crept into the honest old man's voice. Fetyukovitch genuinely started, as if catching a scent, and pounced on it at once.

"Oh, yes, I was a young man then.... I was... well, forty-five, I think, and had only just arrived here. And I felt so sorry for the boy at the time; I asked myself, why shouldn't I buy him a pound of... a pound of what? I've forgotten what it's called. A pound of the thing children love so much, what is it, what is it?" The doctor began waving his hands again. "It grows on a tree, it's gathered, and given out to everyone...."
"Apples?"
"Oh, no, no. You buy apples by the dozen, not the pound.... No, there are lots of them, all small. You put them in your mouth and crack them."
"Nuts?"

"Just so, nuts, that's what I'm saying," the doctor repeated, perfectly calm, as if he'd never been at a loss for the word at all. "And I bought him a pound of nuts, because no one had ever bought that boy a pound of nuts before. And I raised my finger and said to him, 'Boy, Gott der Vater.' He laughed and said, 'Gott der Vater.'... 'Gott der Sohn.' He laughed again and lisped, 'Gott der Sohn.' 'Gott der heilige Geist.' Then he laughed and said, as best he could, 'Gott der heilige Geist.' I went off, and two days later I happened to be passing by, and he called out to me on his own, 'Uncle, Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn,' and he'd only forgotten 'Gott der heilige Geist.' But I reminded him, and I felt sorry for him all over again. But then he was taken away, and I never saw him again. Twenty-three years passed. I'm sitting one morning in my study, a white-haired old man, when a blooming young man walks into the room, whom I'd never have recognized, but he raised his finger and said, laughing, 'Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn, and Gott der heilige Geist. I've just arrived, and I've come to thank you for that pound of nuts, because no one else ever bought me a pound of nuts—you're the only one who ever did.' And then I remembered my own happy youth, and the poor child in the yard, with no shoes on his feet, and my heart was touched, and I said, 'You're a grateful young man, for having remembered your whole life the pound of nuts I bought you as a child.' And I embraced him, and blessed him. And I shed tears. He laughed, but he shed tears too... because a Russian will often laugh when he really ought to be weeping. But he did weep, I saw it. And now, alas!..."
"And I'm weeping now too, German, I'm weeping now too, you saintly man," Mitya suddenly cried.

In any case, the story left a certain favorable impression on the public. But the real sensation in Mitya's favor came from Katerina Ivanovna's testimony, which I'll describe directly. Indeed, once the witnesses for the defense began giving their evidence, fortune seemed all at once to turn noticeably in Mitya's favor, and, most strikingly, this came as a surprise even to the defense counsel himself. But before Katerina Ivanovna was called, Alyosha was examined, and he recalled a fact that seemed to offer solid evidence against one important point in the prosecution's case.

title: IV. Fortune Smiles On Mitya
paragraphs: It came as quite a surprise even to Alyosha himself. He wasn't required to take the oath, and I recall that both sides addressed him very gently and sympathetically. It was plain that his reputation for goodness had gone before him. Alyosha gave his testimony modestly and with restraint, though his warm sympathy for his unhappy brother was unmistakable. Asked one question, he described his brother's character as that of a man, perhaps hot-tempered and carried away by his passions, but at the same time honorable, proud, and generous, capable of self-sacrifice if it came to that. He admitted, though, that through his passion for Grushenka and his rivalry with their father, his brother had lately been living in an unbearable position. But he pushed back indignantly against any suggestion that his brother could have committed murder for the sake of money, though he acknowledged that the three thousand roubles had become almost an obsession for Mitya, that he regarded it as part of the inheritance their father had cheated him of, and that, careless as he usually was about money, he couldn't even speak of that three thousand without flying into a fury. As for the rivalry between the two "ladies," as the prosecutor put it—that is, Grushenka and Katya—he answered evasively, and was even unwilling to answer one or two questions at all.
"Did your brother ever tell you, in any case, that he meant to kill your father?" the prosecutor asked. "You may decline to answer, if you think it necessary," he added.
"He never told me so outright," Alyosha answered.
"How's that? Did he tell you indirectly?"
"He spoke to me once of his hatred for our father, and his fear that, at some extreme moment... in a moment of fury, he might perhaps kill him."
"And you believed him?"

"I'm afraid I have to say I did. But I never once doubted that some higher feeling would always save him at the critical moment—and indeed it did save him, since it wasn't him who killed our father," Alyosha said, firmly, in a loud voice that carried through the whole courtroom.
The prosecutor started, like a warhorse at the sound of a trumpet.

"Let me assure you I fully believe in the complete sincerity of your conviction, and I don't attribute it merely to, or equate it with, your affection for your unfortunate brother. Your particular view of this whole tragic episode is already known to us from the preliminary investigation. I won't try to hide from you that it's highly unusual, and contradicts all the other evidence the prosecution has gathered. And so I think it essential to press you to tell me exactly what facts have led you to this conviction of your brother's innocence, and of the guilt of another person, against whom you gave testimony at the preliminary inquiry?"
"I only answered the questions put to me at the preliminary inquiry," Alyosha replied, slowly and calmly. "I made no accusation against Smerdyakov on my own."
"And yet you gave testimony against him?"

"I was led to it by my brother Dmitri's own words. I was told what happened at his arrest, and how he'd pointed to Smerdyakov before I was even questioned. I believe absolutely that my brother is innocent, and if he didn't commit the murder, then—"
"Then Smerdyakov? Why Smerdyakov? And why are you so completely convinced of your brother's innocence?"
"I can't help believing my brother. I know he wouldn't lie to me. I could see from his face that he wasn't lying."
"Only from his face? Is that the whole of your proof?"
"I have no other proof."
"And of Smerdyakov's guilt, you have no proof whatsoever, beyond your brother's word and the look on his face?"
"No, I have no other proof."

The prosecutor dropped the questioning there. The impression Alyosha's testimony left on the public was thoroughly disappointing. There'd been talk about Smerdyakov before the trial; someone had heard something, someone else had pointed out something else, and it was said Alyosha had assembled some extraordinary proof of his brother's innocence and Smerdyakov's guilt—and in the end there was nothing, no evidence at all beyond certain moral convictions, natural enough in a brother.

But then Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. When he asked Alyosha exactly when the prisoner had told him of his hatred for their father and that he might kill him—whether he'd heard it, say, at their last meeting before the catastrophe—Alyosha started as he answered, as though only just now recollecting and grasping something.
"I remember one detail now that I'd completely forgotten myself. It wasn't clear to me at the time, but now—"

And, evidently struck by the thought for the very first time, he recounted eagerly how, at his last meeting with Mitya that evening under the tree, on the road to the monastery, Mitya had struck himself on the chest—"the upper part of the chest"—and had repeated several times that he had a way to restore his honor, that the way lay right here, here on his chest. "I thought, when he struck his chest, he meant it was in his heart," Alyosha went on, "that he might find in his heart the strength to save himself from some terrible disgrace hanging over him, one he didn't even dare confess to me. I'll admit that at the time I thought he was talking about our father, that the disgrace he shuddered at was the thought of going to our father and doing him some violence. And yet it was right then that he pointed to something on his chest, so I remember the thought striking me at the time that the heart isn't located in that part of the chest, but lower, and that he was striking himself much too high, just below the neck, and kept pointing to that same spot. My idea seemed foolish to me at the time, but perhaps he was pointing to that little pouch where he kept the fifteen hundred roubles!"
"Exactly right," Mitya cried from his seat. "That's right, Alyosha, it was the little pouch I struck with my fist."

Fetyukovitch rushed over to him in a hurry, pleading with him to stay quiet, and in the same instant pounced on Alyosha. Alyosha, swept up himself in the memory, warmly laid out his theory that this disgrace was most likely that very fifteen hundred roubles on him, money he could have returned to Katerina Ivanovna as half of what he owed her, but which he'd nonetheless decided not to repay, meaning instead to use it for another purpose—namely, to run off with Grushenka, if she agreed.

"That's it, it has to be that," Alyosha exclaimed, suddenly excited. "My brother cried out several times that half of the disgrace—half of it (he said 'half' several times)—he could free himself from right away, but that he was so wretched in his weakness of will that he wouldn't do it... that he knew beforehand he was incapable of doing it!"
"And you clearly, confidently remember that he struck himself right in this part of the chest?" Fetyukovitch asked, eagerly.

"Clearly and confidently, because I thought at the time, 'Why is he striking himself up there, when the heart is lower down?' and the thought seemed silly to me right then... I remember it seeming silly... it flashed through my mind. That's what brought it all back to me just now. How could I have forgotten it until now? That's the pouch he meant when he said he had the means but wouldn't give back that fifteen hundred. And when he was arrested at Mokroe he cried out—I know, I was told about it—that he considered it the most shameful act of his life that when he had the means to repay Katerina Ivanovna half—half, mind you—of what he owed her, he still couldn't bring himself to give the money back, and chose instead to remain a thief in her eyes rather than part with it. And what torment, what torment that debt has been to him!" Alyosha finished, exclaiming.

The prosecutor, of course, stepped in. He asked Alyosha to describe once more exactly how it had happened, and pressed the question several times: "Did the prisoner appear to be pointing at something specific? Or might he simply have struck himself on the chest with his fist?"
"But it wasn't with his fist," Alyosha cried; "he pointed with his fingers, and pointed right here, very high up.... How could I have so completely forgotten it until this very moment?"

The President asked Mitya what he had to say about the last witness's testimony. Mitya confirmed it, saying he'd been pointing to the fifteen hundred roubles he kept on his chest, just below the neck, and that this, of course, was the disgrace. "A disgrace I can't deny, the most shameful act of my entire life," Mitya cried. "I could have paid it back and didn't pay it back. I chose to remain a thief in her eyes rather than give it back. And the most shameful part of it was that I knew beforehand I wouldn't give it back! You're right, Alyosha! Thank you, Alyosha!"

With that, Alyosha's cross-examination came to an end. What mattered, what stood out about it, was that at least one fact had come to light, and even if it was only a small scrap of evidence, a mere hint at evidence, it did go some way toward proving the pouch had really existed and had really held fifteen hundred roubles, and that the prisoner hadn't been lying at the preliminary inquiry when he'd claimed, at Mokroe, that the fifteen hundred roubles were "his own." Alyosha was glad. Flushed, he made his way back to the seat set aside for him. He kept repeating to himself: "How did I forget? How could I have forgotten it? And what made it come back to me just now?"

Katerina Ivanovna was called to the witness box. As she entered, something extraordinary happened in the courtroom. The ladies clutched their lorgnettes and opera glasses. A stir passed through the men; some stood up for a better view. Everyone said afterward that Mitya had gone "white as a sheet" the moment she entered. Dressed entirely in black, she came forward modestly, almost timidly. Nothing in her face betrayed her agitation; but there was a resolute glint in her dark, brooding eyes. I should note that many people remarked afterward how especially beautiful she looked at that moment. She spoke softly but clearly, so that she could be heard throughout the whole courtroom. She expressed herself with composure, or at least made every effort to appear composed. The President began questioning her discreetly, with great respect, as though afraid to touch on "certain chords," showing consideration for her great unhappiness. But in answer to one of his first questions, Katerina Ivanovna stated firmly that she had once been engaged to the prisoner, "until he left me, of his own accord..." she added, quietly. When they asked her about the three thousand roubles she'd entrusted to Mitya to post to her relatives, she said firmly, "I didn't give him the money simply to have it mailed off. I could tell at the time that he was in great need of money.... I gave him the three thousand on the understanding that he'd mail it within the month, if he chose to. There was no need for him to worry himself over that debt afterward."
