I won't repeat every question put to her and every answer she gave, in full detail. I'll only give the substance of her testimony.

"I was firmly convinced he'd send that sum off the moment he got money from his father," she went on. "I've never doubted his disinterestedness, or his honesty... his scrupulous honesty... in money matters. He felt quite certain he'd receive the money from his father, and spoke to me about it several times. I knew he was at odds with his father, and I always believed his father had treated him unfairly. I don't recall his ever making any threat against his father. He certainly never made any such threat in front of me. If he'd come to see me around that time, I'd have set his mind at rest at once about that unlucky three thousand roubles, but he'd stopped coming to see me... and I myself was placed in a position... where I couldn't invite him to.... And I really had no right, in any case, to be exacting about that money," she added suddenly, a note of resolve ringing in her voice. "I was once indebted to him myself, for a sum of assistance greater than three thousand, and I accepted it, even though at the time I couldn't have foreseen I'd ever be in a position to repay that debt."
There was a note of defiance in her voice. It was at this point that Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination.

"Did that take place not here, but at the very beginning of your acquaintance?" Fetyukovitch suggested, cautiously, feeling his way, catching the scent of something favorable at once. I should mention, in passing, that although Fetyukovitch had been brought from Petersburg partly at Katerina Ivanovna's own urging, he knew nothing at all about the episode of the four thousand roubles Mitya had given her, and of her "bowing to the ground before him." She'd concealed this from him, said not a word about it, and that was strange. One can fairly safely assume she herself hadn't known, until the very last minute, whether she'd speak of that episode in court, and had simply waited for the inspiration of the moment.

No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything—the whole episode Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reasons for it. She spoke of her father, and of going to see Mitya, and never once, not by a single word or hint, suggested that Mitya himself, through her sister, had proposed that they "send Katerina Ivanovna to him" to fetch the money. She generously kept that hidden, and wasn't ashamed to let it appear as though she'd run to the young officer entirely on her own impulse, trusting to something... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The courtroom fell silent, straining to catch every word. It was something unheard of. Even from a woman as strong-willed and contemptuously proud as she was, such a completely frank confession, such a sacrifice, such self-immolation, seemed almost unbelievable. And for what, for whom? To save the man who'd deceived and insulted her, and to help, in however small a way, secure his rescue, by building up a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, bowing respectfully to the innocent girl, handed over his last four thousand roubles—everything he had in the world—was cast in a very sympathetic, appealing light, but... I had an uneasy foreboding in my heart! I sensed that slander might come of this later (and it did, in fact, it did). Afterward, it went round the whole town, repeated with spiteful laughter, that the story might not be entirely complete—that is, that the claim the officer had let the young lady leave "with nothing but a respectful bow" left something out. There were hints that something had been left unsaid.

"And even if nothing had been left out, even if that were the whole story," the most highly respected of our ladies insisted, "it's still very doubtful whether it was proper for a young woman to behave that way, even to save her father."

And could Katerina Ivanovna, with her intelligence, her morbid sensitivity, have failed to understand that people would talk that way? She must have understood it—and yet she made up her mind to tell everything anyway. Of course, all these nasty little suspicions about the truth of her story only surfaced afterward, and in the first moment everyone was deeply moved by it. As for the judges and lawyers, they listened to Katerina Ivanovna in a reverent, almost shame-faced silence. The prosecutor didn't dare risk even a single question on the subject. Fetyukovitch bowed low to her. Oh, he was nearly triumphant! A great deal of ground had been won. For a man to hand over his last four thousand roubles on a generous impulse, and then for that same man to murder his father just to rob him of three thousand—the idea seemed simply too incongruous. Fetyukovitch felt that the charge of theft, at least, was now as good as disproved. "The case" had been thrown into an entirely different light. A wave of sympathy for Mitya swept through the room. As for him... I was told that once or twice, while Katerina Ivanovna was giving her testimony, he jumped up from his seat, sank back down again, and buried his face in his hands. But once she'd finished, he suddenly cried out, in a sobbing voice:
"Katya, why have you ruined me?"—and his sobs could be heard throughout the whole courtroom. But he checked himself instantly, and cried out again:
"Now I'm condemned!"

Then he sat rigid in his place, teeth clenched, arms crossed over his chest. Katerina Ivanovna remained in the courtroom, taking her seat. She was pale, and sat with her eyes cast down. Those sitting near her said afterward that for a long time she shivered all over, as if in the grip of a fever. Grushenka was called.

I'm coming now to the sudden catastrophe that was, perhaps, the final blow that sealed Mitya's ruin. For I'm convinced, as is everyone—every lawyer said the same thing afterward—that if this episode hadn't happened, the prisoner would at the very least have been recommended for mercy. But more on that later. First, a few words about Grushenka.

She too was dressed entirely in black, her magnificent black shawl draped over her shoulders. She walked to the witness box with her smooth, silent step, that slightly swaying gait common to women of a full figure. She looked steadily at the President, her eyes turning neither right nor left. To my mind she looked quite beautiful at that moment, not at all pale, as the ladies claimed afterward. They also insisted she wore a tight, spiteful expression. I believe she was simply irritated, painfully conscious of the contemptuous, curious eyes of our scandal-hungry public fixed on her. She was proud, and couldn't stand being looked down on. She was one of those people who flare up in anger, eager to strike back, at the mere hint of contempt. There was an element of timidity in her too, of course, and inward shame at her own timidity, so it wasn't strange that her tone kept shifting. At one moment it was angry, contemptuous, harsh; the next, there was a genuine note of self-reproach. At times she spoke as though taking a desperate plunge, as though thinking, 'I don't care what happens, I'll say it....' Speaking of her acquaintance with Fyodor Pavlovitch, she remarked curtly, "That's all nonsense—was it my fault he wouldn't leave me alone?" But a minute later she added, "It was all my fault. I was laughing at both of them—at the old man, and at him too—and I brought them both to this. It all happened on account of me."

Samsonov's name came up somehow. "That's nobody's business," she snapped at once, with a kind of insolent defiance. "He was my benefactor; he took me in when I didn't have a shoe to my name, when my own family had thrown me out." The President reminded her, politely but firmly, that she must answer the questions directly, without wandering off into irrelevant details. Grushenka flushed crimson, her eyes flashing.

The envelope with the money in it, she hadn't seen herself—she'd only heard from "that wicked wretch" that Fyodor Pavlovitch had an envelope with three thousand in notes inside it. "But that was all foolishness. I was only laughing. I'd never have gone to him for anything."
"Who are you referring to as 'that wicked wretch'?" the prosecutor asked.
"The lackey, Smerdyakov, who murdered his master and hanged himself last night."
She was, of course, immediately asked what grounds she had for such a definite accusation; but it turned out she had no grounds for it either.

"Dmitri Fyodorovitch told me so himself; you can believe him. The woman who came between us ruined him—she's the cause of all of it, I'll tell you that," Grushenka added. She seemed to be quivering with hatred, a vindictive edge in her voice.
She was asked again whom she meant.
"That young lady there, Katerina Ivanovna. She sent for me, offered me chocolate, tried to win me over. There's not much real shame in her, I can tell you that...."
At this point the President cut her off sternly, asking her to moderate her language. But the jealous woman's heart was on fire, and she no longer cared what she did.

"When the prisoner was arrested at Mokroe," the prosecutor asked, "everyone saw and heard you run out of the next room and cry out, 'It's all my fault! We'll go to Siberia together!' So you already believed, at that point, that he'd murdered his father?"

"I don't remember what I felt at the time," Grushenka answered. "Everyone was shouting that he'd killed his father, and I felt it was my fault, that it was on my account he'd murdered him. But when he said he wasn't guilty, I believed him at once, and I believe him now, and I always will believe him. He's not the kind of man to lie."

Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. I remember that, among other things, he asked her about Rakitin and the twenty-five roubles "you paid him for bringing Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov to see you."

"There was nothing strange about him taking the money," Grushenka sneered, with angry contempt. "He was always coming to me for money—he used to get at least thirty roubles a month out of me, mostly for little luxuries; he had plenty to live on without my help."
"What made you so generous toward Mr. Rakitin?" Fetyukovitch asked, despite an uneasy stir from the President.
"Why, he's my cousin. His mother was my mother's sister. But he's always begged me not to tell anyone here about it—he's so dreadfully ashamed of me."

This fact came as a complete surprise to everyone; no one in town, nor at the monastery, not even Mitya, had known about it. I was told Rakitin turned purple with shame where he sat. Grushenka had somehow heard, before coming into the courtroom, that he'd testified against Mitya, and that had made her angry. Whatever effect Rakitin's speech had left on the public—his noble sentiments, his attacks on serfdom and Russia's political disorder—was now, this time, finally and thoroughly ruined. Fetyukovitch was satisfied; it was another gift from heaven. Grushenka's cross-examination didn't last long, and there was, of course, nothing particularly new in her testimony. She left a very unpleasant impression on the public; hundreds of contemptuous eyes were fixed on her as she finished testifying and took her seat again in the courtroom, at a good distance from Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya stayed silent through the whole of her testimony. He sat as though turned to stone, his eyes fixed on the floor.
Ivan was called to give evidence.

title: V. A Sudden Catastrophe
paragraphs: I should note he'd actually been called before Alyosha. But the court usher had informed the President that, owing to some kind of attack or fit, the witness couldn't appear just then, though he'd be ready to testify as soon as he recovered. But no one seemed to have caught this, and it only came out later.

For the first moment, his entrance went almost unnoticed. The main witnesses, especially the two rival women, had already been questioned. Curiosity was, for the time being, satisfied; the public felt almost worn out. A few more witnesses still had to be heard, who probably had little to add after everything already said. Time dragged on. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness, looking at no one, his head bowed, as if sunk in gloomy thought. He was impeccably dressed, but his face left a painful impression, on me at least—there was something earthen in it, something like the look of a dying man. His eyes were dull; he raised them and let them travel slowly around the courtroom. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and let out a groan, "Ah!" I remember that, though it went almost unnoticed.

The President began by informing him he was testifying without the oath, that he could answer or decline to answer, but that of course he must bear witness according to his conscience, and so on, and so forth. Ivan listened, staring at him blankly, but his face gradually relaxed into a smile, and the moment the President, watching him in astonishment, finished speaking, he burst out laughing.
"Well, and what else?" he asked, loudly.
A hush fell over the courtroom; there was a sense that something was wrong. The President showed signs of unease.
"You... are perhaps still unwell?" he began, glancing around for the usher.
"Don't trouble yourself, your excellency, I'm well enough, and I can tell you something interesting," Ivan answered, with sudden calm and courtesy.
"You have some particular statement to make?" the President went on, still uncertain.
Ivan looked down, waited a few seconds, and, lifting his head, answered, almost stammering:
"No... I don't. I have nothing in particular."

They began putting questions to him. He answered, as it were, reluctantly, with extreme brevity, with a kind of disgust that grew more and more visible, though his answers made sense. To a great many questions he simply said he didn't know. He knew nothing of his father's financial dealings with Dmitri. "I wasn't interested in the subject," he added. Threats to kill his father, he'd heard from the prisoner. About the money in the envelope, he'd heard from Smerdyakov.
"The same thing, over and over," he suddenly broke in, with a look of exhaustion. "I have nothing particular to tell the court."
"I can see you're unwell, and I understand your feelings," the President began.
He turned to the prosecutor and defense counsel to invite them to question the witness, if they wished, when Ivan suddenly asked, in an exhausted voice:
"Let me go, your excellency, I feel very ill."

And with those words, without waiting for permission, he turned to walk out of the courtroom. But after four steps, he stopped short, as though he'd reached some decision, smiled slowly, and turned back.

"I'm like the peasant girl, your excellency... you know how it goes? 'I'll stand up if I like, and I won't if I don't.' They were trying to dress her in her sarafan, to take her to church to be married, and she said, 'I'll stand up if I like, and I won't if I don't.'... It's in some book about the peasants."
"What do you mean by that?" the President asked, severely.

"Why, this," Ivan suddenly pulled out a roll of banknotes. "Here's the money... the notes that were in that envelope" (he nodded toward the table holding the material evidence), "the money our father was murdered for. Where should I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it."
The court usher took the whole roll and handed it to the President.
"How did this money come into your possession, if it's the same money?" the President asked, in astonishment.

"I got it from Smerdyakov, from the murderer, yesterday.... I was with him just before he hanged himself. It was he, not my brother, who killed our father. He murdered him, and I put him up to it... Who doesn't wish for his own father's death?"
"Are you in your right mind?" burst involuntarily from the President.

"I should think I'm in my right mind... in the same nasty mind as all of you... as all these... ugly faces." He turned suddenly to the audience. "My father's been murdered, and they pretend to be horrified," he snarled, with furious contempt. "They keep up the sham with each other. Liars! Every one of them wants their fathers dead. One reptile devours another.... If there'd been no murder, they'd have gone home angry and out of sorts. It's a spectacle they want! Panem et circenses. Though who am I to talk! Is there any water? Give me a drink, for Christ's sake!" He suddenly clutched his head.

The usher hurried over to him at once. Alyosha jumped up and cried, "He's ill. Don't believe him—he has brain fever." Katerina Ivanovna rose abruptly from her seat and, frozen in horror, stared at Ivan. Mitya stood up and stared hungrily at his brother, listening to him with a wild, strange smile.
"Don't trouble yourselves. I'm not mad—I'm only a murderer," Ivan began again. "You can't expect eloquence from a murderer," he added suddenly, for no clear reason, and laughed a strange laugh.

The prosecutor bent toward the President, visibly alarmed. The two other judges exchanged agitated whispers. Fetyukovitch listened with his ears pricked up; the hall sat hushed, waiting. The President seemed to suddenly pull himself together.

"Witness, your words are incomprehensible and out of place here. Calm yourself, if you can, and tell your story... if you really have something to tell. How can you back up your statement... if you're not, in fact, delirious?"

"That's exactly it. I have no proof. That cur Smerdyakov isn't going to send you proof from the other world... in an envelope. All you people think about is envelopes—one's enough. I have no witnesses... except perhaps one," he smiled, thoughtfully.
"Who is your witness?"

"He has a tail, your excellency, and that would be irregular! Le diable n'existe point! Pay no attention to him: he's a petty, pitiful devil," he added suddenly. He'd stopped laughing now and spoke almost confidentially. "He's here somewhere, no doubt—under that table with the material evidence on it, perhaps. Where else would he sit? Listen to me. I told him I don't want to keep quiet, and he went on about the geological cataclysm... idiocy! Come, let the monster go... he's been singing a hymn. That's because his heart is light! Like a drunk man in the street bawling about how 'Vanka went to Petersburg,' and I'd give a quadrillion quadrillions for two seconds of joy. You don't know me! Oh, how stupid this whole business is! Take me instead of him! I didn't come here for nothing.... Why, why is everything so stupid?..."

And he began again, slowly, as if reflecting, looking around him once more. But by now the whole courtroom was in an uproar. Alyosha rushed toward him, but the court usher had already grabbed Ivan by the arm.

"What are you doing?" he cried, staring into the man's face, and suddenly seizing him by the shoulders, he flung him violently to the floor. But the police were right there, and he was seized. He screamed furiously. And the whole time he was being carried out, he shouted and screamed something incoherent.

The whole courtroom fell into confusion. I don't remember every detail of what happened. I was too worked up myself to follow it all. I only know that afterward, once everything had quieted down and everyone understood what had happened, the court usher was called in for a reprimand, though he explained quite reasonably that the witness had seemed perfectly well, that a doctor had examined him an hour before, when he'd had a brief spell of dizziness, but that right up until he'd entered the courtroom, he'd spoken quite coherently, so there'd been no way to foresee this—and that he had, in fact, insisted on giving evidence. But before everyone had fully regained their composure and recovered from this scene, another one followed it. Katerina Ivanovna had an attack of hysterics. She sobbed, shrieking loudly, but refused to leave the courtroom, struggling, begging them not to remove her. Suddenly she cried out to the President:

"There's more evidence I have to give right now... right now! Here's a document, a letter... take it, read it, quickly, quickly! It's a letter from that monster... that man there, there!" She pointed at Mitya. "It was he who killed his father, you'll see it in a moment. He wrote to me how he'd kill his father! But the other one is ill, he's ill, he's delirious!" she kept crying, beside herself.

The court usher took the document she was holding out and handed it to the President, and she, sinking back into her chair, burying her face in her hands, began sobbing convulsively and silently, shaking all over, stifling every sound for fear she'd be thrown out of the courtroom. The document she'd handed up was that letter Mitya had written at the Metropolis tavern, the one Ivan had called "mathematical proof." Alas, its mathematical force was borne out, and if it hadn't been for that letter, Mitya might have escaped his fate, or at least that fate might have been less terrible. It was, I repeat, hard to catch every detail. What followed is still a blur in my mind. The President must, I suppose, have passed the document at once to the judges, the jury, and the lawyers on both sides. I only remember how they began questioning the witness. Gently asked by the President whether she'd recovered enough, Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed, impetuously:

"I'm ready, I'm ready! I'm perfectly capable of answering you," she added, evidently still afraid she'd somehow be prevented from giving her testimony. She was asked to explain in detail what this letter was, and under what circumstances she'd received it.

"I received it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it's written on the back of some kind of bill!" she cried, breathlessly. "He hated me at that time, because he'd behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature... and because he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! He was humiliated by that three thousand, on account of his own low character! Here's how it happened, with that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, to hear me out. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to see me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he needed it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I already knew by then that he'd been unfaithful to me and meant to leave me, and it was I, I, who gave him that money, offered it to him under the pretext that he'd send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it to him, I looked him straight in the face and told him he could send it whenever he liked—'in a month's time would do.' How, how could he have failed to understand that I was practically telling him, to his very face, 'You need money to betray me with your creature, so here's the money for you. I'm giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor left as to take it!' I wanted to prove to myself what he really was, and what happened? He took it—he took it, and squandered it on that creature in a single night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew everything about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I'd given him that money to test him, to see whether he'd sunk so low he'd take it from me. I looked into his eyes, and he looked into mine, and he understood everything, and he still took it—he carried off my money!"

"That's true, Katya," Mitya roared suddenly. "I looked into your eyes and I knew you were dishonoring me with it, and I took your money anyway. Despise me as a scoundrel, despise me, all of you! I've earned it!"
"Prisoner," the President cried, "one more word and I'll have you removed."

"That money tormented him," Katya went on, with impulsive haste. "He wanted to pay it back to me. He truly wanted to, that's true; but he needed money for that creature too. So he murdered his father, and still didn't repay me, and ran off with her to that village where he was arrested. There, once again, he squandered the money he'd stolen after murdering his father. And the day before the murder, he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it. I saw that right away, at the time. He wrote it out of spite, absolutely certain, positively certain, that I'd never show it to anyone—even if he did kill him—or else he'd never have written it. Because he knew I wouldn't want revenge, wouldn't want to destroy him! But read it, read it carefully—more carefully, please—and you'll see he described it all, in that letter, all of it beforehand: how he'd kill his father, and where the money was kept. Look, please, don't skip over it, there's one phrase there: 'I'll kill him the moment Ivan's gone.' So he'd worked it all out beforehand, exactly how he'd kill him," Katerina Ivanovna pointed out to the court, with venomous, malicious triumph. Oh, it was plain she'd studied every line of that letter, picked apart every hidden meaning in it. "If he hadn't been drunk, he'd never have written to me; but look, it's all written there beforehand, exactly as he carried it out afterward. A complete plan of it!" she cried, frantically.

She was past caring now about any consequences to herself, though no doubt she'd foreseen them even a month before, since even then, perhaps, shaking with anger, she'd already been weighing whether to produce it at the trial or not. Now she'd taken the fatal plunge. I remember the letter was read aloud by the clerk, right afterward, I believe. It made an overwhelming impression. They asked Mitya whether he admitted to writing the letter.

"It's mine, mine!" Mitya cried. "I wouldn't have written it if I hadn't been drunk!... We've hated each other over so many things, Katya, but I swear, I swear I loved you even while I hated you, and you never loved me!"

He sank back into his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and the defense counsel began cross-examining her, mainly to establish what had led her to conceal such a document, and to give her testimony in such a different tone and spirit only a short while before.

"Yes, yes. I was lying just now. I was lying against my own honor, against my own conscience, but I wanted to save him, because he's hated me and despised me so!" Katya cried, wildly. "Oh, he's despised me horribly, he's always despised me, and do you know, he's despised me from the very moment I bowed down to him for that money. I saw it.... I felt it immediately, at the time, but for a long time I refused to believe it. How many times I've read it in his eyes: 'You came of your own accord, though.' Oh, he didn't understand, he had no idea why I ran to him, he can't imagine anything but baseness, he judged me by himself, he thought everyone was just like him!" Katya hissed furiously, in an absolute frenzy. "And he only wanted to marry me because I'd inherited a fortune, because of that, only because of that! I always suspected it was because of that! Oh, he's a brute! He was always convinced I'd tremble with shame in front of him my whole life, because I'd gone to him that once, and that he had the right to despise me for it forever, to hold himself above me forever—that's why he wanted to marry me! That's how it is, that's exactly how it is! I tried to win him over with my love—a love without limits. I even tried to forgive his unfaithfulness; but he understood nothing, nothing! How could he understand, really? He's a monster! I only got that letter the next evening: it was brought to me from the tavern—and only that morning, only that very morning, I wanted to forgive him everything, everything—even his betrayal!"

The President and the prosecutor, of course, tried to calm her down. I can't help thinking they felt ashamed of taking advantage of her hysteria, of listening to such confessions. I remember hearing them say to her, "We understand how difficult this is for you; believe us, we can sympathize," and so on, and so forth. And yet they went on drawing testimony out of this raving, hysterical woman. In the end she described, with an extraordinary clarity that often appears, if only for a moment, in states of overwrought emotion like this, how Ivan had very nearly been driven out of his mind over the past two months, trying to save "the monster and murderer," his brother.

"He tortured himself," she exclaimed, "he was always trying to minimize his brother's guilt, confessing to me that he too had never loved his father, and perhaps had wished for his death himself. Oh, he has such a tender, over-tender conscience! He tormented himself with it! He told me everything, everything! He came every day and talked to me as his only friend. I have the honor of being his only friend!" she suddenly cried, with a kind of defiance, her eyes flashing. "He'd been to see Smerdyakov twice. One day he came to me and said, 'If it wasn't my brother, but Smerdyakov, who committed the murder' (since the rumor was spreading everywhere that Smerdyakov had done it), 'then maybe I'm guilty too, because Smerdyakov knew I didn't love my father, and might have believed I wanted my father dead.' Then I brought out that letter and showed it to him. He became entirely convinced his brother had done it, and it crushed him. He couldn't bear the thought that his own brother was a parricide! Just a week ago, I saw it was making him ill. Over these past few days he's talked incoherently in front of me. I could see his mind was giving way. He wandered around, raving; people saw him muttering to himself in the streets. The doctor from Moscow, at my request, examined him the day before yesterday, and told me he was on the verge of brain fever—and all on his account, all because of this monster! And last night he learned Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock it drove him out of his mind... and all because of this monster, all for the sake of saving the monster!"

Oh, of course, an outpouring like that, a confession like that, is only possible once in a lifetime—at the hour of death, say, on the way to the scaffold! But it was entirely in keeping with Katya's character, and this was just such a moment in her life. It was the same impetuous Katya who'd once thrown herself on the mercy of a young libertine to save her father; the same Katya who, only moments before, in her pride and purity, had sacrificed herself and her maidenly modesty in front of this whole crowd, telling of Mitya's generous conduct, hoping to soften his fate just a little. And now, once again, she sacrificed herself—but this time for someone else, and perhaps only now, perhaps only in this very moment, did she feel and understand how dear that someone else truly was to her! She'd sacrificed herself in terror for him, suddenly imagining he'd destroyed himself with his confession that he, not his brother, had committed the murder; she'd sacrificed herself to save him, to save his good name, his reputation!

And yet one terrible doubt occurred to me: was she lying in her account of her earlier relationship with Mitya? That was the question. No, she hadn't slandered him on purpose when she cried out that Mitya despised her for bowing down to him! She believed it herself. She'd been firmly convinced, probably ever since that bow, that simple-hearted Mitya, who even then adored her, was laughing at her, despising her. She'd loved him with a hysterical, "lacerated" love, born only of pride, of wounded pride, and that love wasn't really love at all, but closer to revenge. Oh, perhaps that lacerated love might have grown into real love; perhaps that was all Katya had ever longed for; but Mitya's unfaithfulness had wounded her to the very bottom of her heart, and her heart couldn't forgive him for it. The moment of revenge had come upon her suddenly, and everything that had been building up, for so long and so painfully, in that wounded woman's breast burst out all at once, unexpectedly. She betrayed Mitya, but she betrayed herself too. And the instant she'd given full voice to her feelings, the tension broke, and she was overcome with shame. The hysterics started up again: she collapsed to the floor, sobbing, screaming. She was carried out. At that moment Grushenka, with a wail, rushed toward Mitya before anyone could stop her.

"Mitya," she wailed, "your serpent has destroyed you! There, she's shown you what she is!" she shouted at the judges, shaking with rage. At a signal from the President, they seized her and tried to remove her from the courtroom. She wouldn't allow it. She fought and struggled to get back to Mitya. Mitya let out a cry and struggled to reach her. He was overpowered.

Yes, I think the ladies who'd come for the spectacle must have gone home satisfied—it had certainly been a varied show. Then, I recall, the Moscow doctor appeared on the scene. I believe the President had earlier sent the court usher to arrange medical help for Ivan. The doctor announced to the court that the sick man was suffering from a dangerous attack of brain fever, and had to be removed at once. Answering questions from the prosecutor and defense counsel, he said the patient had come to see him of his own accord the day before yesterday, and that he'd warned him an attack like this was coming, though the patient had refused to be looked after. "He certainly wasn't in a normal state of mind: he told me himself that he saw visions while wide awake, that he met several people in the street who were dead, and that Satan came to visit him every evening," the doctor concluded. Having given his testimony, the celebrated doctor withdrew. The letter produced by Katerina Ivanovna was added to the material evidence. After some deliberation, the judges decided to proceed with the trial, and to enter both unexpected pieces of testimony—Ivan's and Katerina Ivanovna's—into the record.

But I won't go into detail about the testimony of the other witnesses, who only repeated and confirmed what had already been said, each in their own characteristic way. I repeat, it was all drawn together in the prosecutor's closing speech, which I'll quote shortly. Everyone was worked up, everyone was electrified by this latest catastrophe, and all were waiting for the closing speeches, for the prosecution and the defense, with intense impatience. Fetyukovitch was visibly shaken by Katerina Ivanovna's testimony. But the prosecutor was triumphant. Once all the evidence had been heard, the court adjourned for nearly an hour. I believe it was just eight o'clock when the President returned to his seat, and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his closing speech.
